title: Many Histories
scope: 228 selected histories, 27 contextual entries and 189 detailed topics. All named reference-poster topics are indexed; world history itself is not exhaustive. Full window 4500 BCE–2026 CE; Modern era window 1450–2026 CE. Earlier origins are indicated and explained in the reader.
dateConvention: Negative historical years are BCE; positive years are CE. No year zero. Approximate dates are plotting anchors. ongoing=true means the bar continues beyond the editorial cutoff, not a prediction. Selected phases and interruptions are explained in entry notes.

histories.title: Ancient Egyptian dynasties
histories.summary: Dynastic kingdoms, changing royal centres and periods of foreign rule shaped the Nile Valley.
histories.note: This groups many dynasties and interruptions. The Roman annexation in 30 BCE did not end Egyptian people or culture.

histories.title: Nubian kingdoms
histories.summary: Kerma, Napata and Meroe were distinct centres of political power, trade and artistic production.
histories.note: An umbrella range for successive states, not one uninterrupted kingdom. These societies interacted with Egypt on changing terms.

histories.title: Nok culture
histories.dates: c. 1500 BCE–start of the Common Era
histories.summary: Archaeological evidence records farming communities, ironworking and a distinctive terracotta tradition.
histories.note: Recent research places the culture earlier than older museum timelines. The range describes material evidence, not a known royal dynasty.

histories.title: Jenne-jeno
histories.summary: A long-lived urban settlement brought together specialised crafts and exchange across the Niger floodplain.
histories.note: The plotted range covers occupation at the old settlement. Later Jenne developed nearby; urban life in the region continued.

histories.title: Ghana / Wagadu
histories.location: Western Sahel · mainly present-day Mauritania and Mali
histories.summary: A Soninke-associated polity connected communities and trans-Saharan trade in the western Sahel.
histories.note: Origins and endpoints are disputed. The Met’s broad c. 300–1200 range is used here; it is not the modern Republic of Ghana.

histories.title: Aksum
histories.location: Horn of Africa · present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea
histories.summary: Monumental stelae and royal coinage attest to an influential kingdom in the Horn of Africa.
histories.note: Uses UNESCO’s 1st–8th-century period, rounded for plotting. Political and cultural changes continued after this range.

histories.title: Great Zimbabwe
histories.summary: Ancestors of Shona communities built a major stone city with imposing enclosures and residential complexes.
histories.note: This dates the principal medieval city, not the beginning or end of Shona history. Century boundaries are plotting anchors.

histories.title: Kingdom of Benin
histories.summary: Benin City was the centre of a kingdom renowned for court art and extensive earthworks.
histories.note: 1897 marks British military conquest, not the disappearance of Edo culture or the monarchy. The royal institution continues.

histories.title: Mali Empire
histories.location: Western Sahel · across several present-day countries
histories.summary: A major Mande-led empire grew around the upper Senegal and Niger river regions.
histories.note: 1235 conventionally marks Sundiata’s consolidation. Decline was gradual; sources vary on when imperial power ended.

histories.title: Songhai Empire
histories.summary: An empire centred on Gao expanded under Sonni Ali and later Askia rulers.
histories.note: The range marks imperial expansion to the Moroccan invasion. Earlier Songhai states and later successor powers lie outside it.

histories.title: Uruk · early urban growth
histories.summary: Monumental buildings and early accounting tablets illuminate the growth of a major city.
histories.note: A selected early urban phase, not the city’s full lifespan. Uruk continued to develop after 3000 BCE.

histories.title: Akkadian period
histories.summary: Rulers of Agade brought rival cities under their authority through conquest.
histories.note: Uses the broad archaeological period in the Met’s chronology. More specific reign dates depend on chronological convention.
posterNotes: Middle-chronology conventional dates; competing chronologies differ. Existing chart uses rounded 2350–2150 BCE.

histories.title: Achaemenid Persian Empire
histories.summary: An imperial dynasty governed a diverse realm extending across several regions.
histories.note: The empire also included lands in Africa and Europe. Placement in this row identifies its core, not its full territory.
posterNotes: The poster steps conquest dates across regions: Lydia 546, Egypt 525, Babylon 539. These are accessions of territory, not multiple founding dates; Iranian rule continued under successor powers.

histories.title: Abbasid caliphate · Baghdad
histories.summary: Baghdad became a major political and cultural centre under the Abbasid dynasty.
histories.note: Dates refer to the Baghdad caliphate. Political authority varied, and a later Abbasid caliphal line continued in Cairo.
posterNotes: Cairo-based Abbasid caliphs later continued under Mamluk patronage 1261–1517; Baghdad’s fall 1258 ends this selected ruling phase.

histories.title: Ottoman Empire
histories.location: Anatolia, Southeast Europe, North Africa & West Asia
histories.summary: A long-lived empire linked territories across the Mediterranean and neighbouring regions.
histories.note: The founding date is conventional. The sultanate ended in 1922; the caliphate survived until 1924.
posterNotes: Conventional origin around 1299; Ottoman expansion into Byzantine, Mamluk and Iraqi territories occurred at different dates. Sultanate abolished 1922; republic proclaimed 1923.

histories.title: Indus · Mature Harappan phase
histories.summary: Cities and a distinctive seal tradition characterised the mature urban phase of the Indus civilisation.
histories.note: This range covers the mature phase. Earlier and later Harappan communities extend beyond these dates.
posterNotes: The poster’s 3300 BCE start is Early Harappan, while the existing chart shows Mature Harappan 2600–1900 BCE. Add Early and Late phases explicitly; decline of urban centres did not end all Harappan traditions 1500 BCE.

histories.title: Mauryan Empire
histories.summary: An empire centred on Magadha supported monumental inscriptions and religious patronage under Ashoka.
histories.note: The Met uses c. 323 BCE; 322 or 321 BCE also appears in other chronologies. Borders changed over time.
posterNotes: Traditional dates 322/321–185 BCE; exact founding chronology varies. Not an empire covering every part of the Indian subcontinent.

histories.title: Gupta period
histories.summary: Influential artistic traditions developed in a period of Gupta rule and patronage.
histories.note: A broad period convention. Gupta power did not encompass all South Asia, and its decline was uneven.
posterNotes: Conventional imperial/art-historical phase; political decline and regional artistic influence have different end dates.

histories.title: Mughal dynasty
histories.summary: Court workshops brought Persian, South Asian and European artistic traditions into dialogue.
histories.note: This follows the Met’s dynastic period. Effective control contracted long before the final emperor’s removal.
posterNotes: Interrupted by the Sur dynasty 1540–1555. Imperial power contracted greatly before 1858, while regional kingdoms and Company rule overlapped.

histories.title: Han dynasties
histories.location: East Asia · centred in present-day China
histories.summary: Western and Eastern Han rulers shaped a durable model of imperial government.
histories.note: The broad span includes an interruption: the Xin dynasty ruled in 9–23 CE, before Eastern Han was established in 25.
posterNotes: Western and Eastern Han, interrupted by the Xin dynasty 9–23 CE and subsequent civil war. Territorial reach and rule varied.

histories.title: Tang dynasty
histories.location: East Asia · centred in present-day China
histories.summary: The Tang period connected an imperial court with wide-ranging artistic and cultural exchange.
histories.note: A dynastic span, not uninterrupted rule: Wu Zetian’s Zhou dynasty intervened in 690–705 CE.
posterNotes: Interrupted by Wu Zhou 690–705; regional warlords and rival states increasingly constrained late-Tang rule.

histories.title: Angkor · Khmer capitals
histories.summary: A succession of Khmer capitals produced extensive temple and urban landscapes.
histories.note: UNESCO dates these capitals to the 9th–15th centuries. These bounds do not describe the full lifespan of Khmer culture.

histories.title: Song dynasties
histories.summary: Northern and Southern Song courts governed changing territories across this period.
histories.note: The division into Northern and Southern Song is grouped here; other contemporary states occupied parts of what is now China.
posterNotes: Northern Song 960–1127 and Southern Song 1127–1279 coexisted with Liao, Western Xia and Jin powers. Yuan proclaimed 1271 before Song’s final defeat 1279.

histories.title: Joseon dynasty
histories.summary: A long-lived Korean dynasty supported distinctive court arts and institutions.
histories.note: The broad museum convention includes the Korean Empire proclaimed in 1897; dynastic and state labels are not identical.

histories.title: Edo / Tokugawa period
histories.summary: Tokugawa government and regional domains shaped the Edo period.
histories.note: Sources start the period in 1600, 1603 or 1615 depending on definition. This follows the British Museum’s 1603 convention.
posterNotes: Tokugawa shogunal rule began 1603 and ended 1867–1868. International contact was controlled and restricted, never wholly absent.

histories.title: Minoan culture
histories.summary: A Bronze Age island culture developed maritime connections and elaborate palace traditions.
histories.note: An archaeological umbrella with several phases. It does not describe one continuously unified Cretan state.
posterNotes: The website already covers the Cretan component. This does not by itself cover all Cycladic or mainland Aegean histories.

histories.title: Classical Greek world
histories.summary: Independent and competing communities shared artistic and cultural traditions across the Greek world.
histories.note: A period convention, not a unified Greek nation or the complete lifespan of Greek civilisation.
posterNotes: The poster starts this label around 800 BCE, combining Archaic and Classical Greece. Classical Greece conventionally begins around 480 BCE; city-states were independent and often at war.

histories.title: Roman imperial rule · West
histories.summary: Roman imperial institutions ruled changing territories around the Mediterranean.
histories.note: This endpoint concerns the Western Empire. The Eastern Roman Empire continued; the two entries intentionally overlap.
posterNotes: 27 BCE marks the conventional beginning of the principate. 476 CE concerns western imperial government; the Eastern Roman state continued. The poster’s cross-column shape is not a precise territorial map.

histories.title: Eastern Roman / Byzantine Empire
histories.summary: The Roman state continued around Constantinople through late antiquity and the medieval centuries.
histories.note: 330 marks Constantinople’s dedication, not a clean break with Rome. Includes the 1204–1261 Latin occupation and Byzantine successor states.
posterNotes: The empire was Roman in its own identity. The poster’s 395 start marks a division of imperial courts; Constantinople’s dedication in 330 is the website’s selected frame. The Latin conquest interrupted rule in Constantinople in 1204–1261.

histories.title: Carolingian imperial period
histories.summary: Carolingian rulers held an imperial title while their realms underwent repeated political division.
histories.note: Uses Mayke de Jong’s 800–888 frame. Partitions and changes of ruler mean this was not a single unchanging state.

histories.title: Caral-Supe
histories.summary: Monumental platforms and circular courts record an early centre of complex society in the Americas.
histories.note: Uses the wider radiocarbon range in UNESCO’s statement. Some accounts use a narrower c. 2600–2000 BCE range.

histories.title: Olmec traditions
histories.summary: Centres such as San Lorenzo and La Venta developed major sculptural traditions.
histories.note: Olmec is an archaeological designation, not proof of one empire controlling all Mesoamerica.

histories.title: Teotihuacan
histories.summary: A monumental city developed around major pyramids and repeated building campaigns.
histories.note: Selected monumental urban phase; settlement and later engagement with the site extend beyond this range.

histories.title: Maya · Classic period
histories.location: Present-day Mexico, Guatemala, Belize & neighbouring areas
histories.summary: Maya courts commissioned artworks, inscriptions and buildings across many distinct cities.
histories.note: 900 CE marks a period boundary, not the disappearance of Maya peoples. Maya communities and languages continue today.

histories.title: Cahokia
histories.summary: A major Mississippian centre joined monumental earthworks with an agricultural urban society.
histories.note: Uses UNESCO’s Mississippian occupation range at this site. The population peak was around 1050–1150 CE.

histories.title: Aztec Triple Alliance
histories.summary: Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan formed an alliance that dominated much of central Mexico.
histories.note: 1521 marks conquest of Tenochtitlan by Spanish and Indigenous allied forces; it did not end Nahua people or culture.

histories.title: Inca imperial expansion
histories.summary: An Andean state expanded across a large and environmentally diverse region.
histories.note: 1532 marks the Spanish capture of Atahualpa. An Inca successor state survived at Vilcabamba until 1572; Andean cultures continue.

histories.title: Aboriginal Australian cultures
histories.summary: Diverse peoples sustain long histories of connection to Country, community and culture.
histories.note: The deep-time date is an approximate archaeological anchor, not a precise founding year. The bar extends before and beyond the displayed window.

histories.title: Lapita traditions
histories.summary: Distinctive pottery accompanies evidence of eastward settlement into the Pacific.
histories.note: A material-culture range. It does not mark the beginning or end of Pacific peoples or all Oceanian settlement.

histories.title: Nan Madol · major construction
histories.location: Pohnpei · present-day Federated States of Micronesia
histories.summary: Basalt and coral structures formed a ceremonial centre associated with Saudeleur rule.
histories.note: The bar covers the major building period described by UNESCO, not all occupation or continuing ceremonial significance.

histories.title: Māori settlement & cultures
histories.summary: East Polynesian voyagers settled Aotearoa, where distinctive Māori societies developed and continue.
histories.note: First settlement is dated to approximately 1250–1300 CE. The bar uses 1250 as a plotting anchor, not an exact arrival date.

histories.title: Early Dynastic city-states
histories.summary: Independent city-states developed royal institutions and exchanged luxury materials through trade and conquest.
histories.note: This is a regional archaeological period, not one united state. Cities such as Uruk existed before and after it.

histories.title: Old Babylonian dynasty
histories.summary: Babylonian rulers, including Hammurabi, governed changing territories in southern Mesopotamia.
histories.note: Uses the Met’s dynastic range. The broader Old Babylonian archaeological period is sometimes dated from around 2000 BCE.
posterNotes: Selected First Dynasty of Babylon, not all southern Mesopotamian states in this era.

histories.title: Middle Babylonian / Kassite period
histories.summary: Kassite rulers participated in a wider diplomatic world linking Babylonia with neighbouring courts.
histories.note: The Hittite sack of Babylon is the conventional boundary in this chronology; this does not imply immediate Kassite control everywhere.
posterNotes: Traditional period boundary 1595 BCE reflects the Hittite sack; the earliest establishment of Kassite rule is imperfectly documented.

histories.title: Neo-Assyrian Empire
histories.summary: Assyrian rulers expanded an imperial realm centred in northern Mesopotamia.
histories.note: Follows the Met’s conventional range ending with the fall of Nineveh. It does not date all later resistance or Assyrian cultural history.
posterNotes: Nineveh fell 612 BCE; remaining Assyrian royal resistance at Harran continued until 609 BCE. Existing entry uses 612 for the fall of its capital.

histories.title: Vedic / Indo-Gangetic cultures
histories.summary: Regional communities and traditions developed across the northern subcontinent during this broad cultural period.
histories.note: Uses the Met’s early Indo-Gangetic periodisation. Vedic traditions have other chronological definitions; this was not a single state covering South Asia.
posterNotes: Conventional textual-cultural frame 1500–500 BCE; dates are approximate, regional and debated. Vedic cultures coexisted with Late Harappan and other traditions; not a single state.

histories.title: Liangzhu
histories.summary: A rice-cultivating regional society built a city, waterworks and socially differentiated cemeteries.
histories.note: Dates follow UNESCO’s archaeological range for the city and related sites, not the beginning of all Chinese civilisation.
posterNotes: Archaeological culture 3300–2300 BCE; the poster uses 3000 and extends it toward Xia. Liangzhu is not a dynastic predecessor ruling all China.

histories.title: Shang dynasty
histories.summary: A Bronze Age dynasty is represented in archaeological material and written evidence.
histories.note: These are conventional dynastic boundaries. Different chronologies use different starting dates, and Shang rule did not encompass all present-day China.
posterNotes: The later Shang is securely attested by oracle-bone writing. The beginning around 1600 BCE and transition date 1046 are conventional archaeological-historical dates.

histories.title: Zhou dynasties
histories.summary: Western and Eastern Zhou span a long period of changing royal and regional authority.
histories.note: Western Zhou and Eastern Zhou are grouped together. Especially in the later centuries, many competing states held effective political power.
posterNotes: Western and Eastern Zhou with changing royal power; Spring and Autumn and Warring States polities coexisted under increasingly nominal Zhou kingship.

histories.title: Archaic Greek world
histories.summary: Greek communities developed distinctive pottery, sculpture and architectural traditions in contact with their neighbours.
histories.note: Follows the Museum of Cycladic Art’s art-historical range. Broader historical chronologies sometimes start the Archaic period around 800 BCE.
posterLabels: Classical Greek City-States · earlier Archaic component
posterNotes: An expanded conventional frame covering the earlier portion of the poster’s combined Greek band. The existing site uses the narrower art-historical start c. 700 BCE; either convention needs an explicit note.

histories.title: Ife · artistic flourishing
histories.summary: Ife became a major Yoruba centre of naturalistic terracotta and metal sculpture.
histories.note: The city’s origins reach back to at least the sixth century. This bar selects its major medieval artistic phase; Ife remains a living city.

histories.title: Oyo · imperial expansion
histories.location: Yoruba region · present-day Nigeria and Benin
histories.summary: Oyo developed a powerful cavalry-based empire and extensive regional political and commercial connections.
histories.note: This shows the principal imperial phase, not the disputed date of Oyo’s founding. The Alaafin’s institution and Yoruba societies continued after imperial collapse.

histories.title: Asante Empire
histories.summary: An Akan state developed influential political institutions, trade networks and court arts.
histories.note: 1701 marks consolidation after the defeat of Denkyira. British annexation was proclaimed in 1901 and took effect in 1902; the Asante monarchy and culture continued.

histories.title: Kingdom of Kongo
histories.location: West-central Africa · present-day Angola and the two Congos
histories.summary: A major Central African kingdom developed regional networks and a long, changing relationship with Portugal.
histories.note: The foundation date is approximate. Sovereignty weakened before formal suppression of the kingship in 1914; Kongo peoples and traditions continued.

histories.title: Kilwa · Swahili trading city
histories.summary: Kilwa linked the East African coast with commerce across the Indian Ocean.
histories.note: UNESCO places occupation between the ninth and nineteenth centuries, with prosperity peaking in the thirteenth and fourteenth. These are century anchors, not exact founding and ending dates.

histories.title: Solomonic Ethiopia
histories.location: Horn of Africa · present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea
histories.summary: Solomonic rulers presided over a long history of changing imperial authority in the Ethiopian highlands.
histories.note: A dynastic frame including interruptions and periods of fragmented authority. The bar does not imply that Ethiopian statehood or culture began in 1270.

histories.title: Kanem Empire
histories.location: Lake Chad basin · mainly present-day Chad
histories.summary: A Sahelian state connected communities around Lake Chad with trans-Saharan networks.
histories.note: Early chronology is uncertain. The late-fourteenth-century endpoint marks a shift of the ruling dynasty towards Bornu, rather than the disappearance of the region’s societies.

histories.title: Bornu Empire
histories.location: Lake Chad basin · mainly present-day Nigeria
histories.summary: Bornu became a major centre of power west of Lake Chad under rulers linked to the earlier Kanem state.
histories.note: The foundation date is rounded. The fall of the capital to Rabih in 1893 marks an important political rupture; later Borno institutions continued.

histories.title: Hittite kingdom and empire
histories.summary: Hittite rulers developed a major Anatolian state and participated in the diplomacy of the Late Bronze Age.
histories.note: The bar groups changing phases of Hittite rule. Later Neo-Hittite states and communities continued after the imperial collapse.
posterNotes: Kingdom begins around 1650 BCE, not simply 1700; the imperial New Kingdom is a narrower phase.

histories.title: Phoenician city-states
histories.summary: Maritime city-states including Tyre, Sidon and Byblos maintained extensive Mediterranean connections.
histories.note: This is a selected period of city-state history, not one Phoenician empire. Alexander’s conquest of Tyre is not an end date for Phoenician or Punic peoples.

histories.title: Sasanian Empire
histories.summary: An Iranian empire competed and exchanged ideas with Rome and other neighbouring powers.
histories.note: The dynasty’s political ending does not mark the end of Iranian society, religion or administrative traditions.
posterNotes: Founded 224. Arab conquest proceeded over several decades;651 marks the death of YazdegerdIII, not the disappearance of Iranian society.

histories.title: Rashidun caliphate
histories.summary: The first caliphs led a rapidly expanding state after the death of Muhammad.
histories.note: This is a political period in early Islamic history. It is not the beginning or end of Islam as a religious tradition.

histories.title: Umayyad caliphate · Damascus
histories.location: West Asia, North Africa and Iberia
histories.summary: A dynasty based in Damascus governed a realm extending across several world regions.
histories.note: The Damascus caliphate ended in 750, while an Umayyad dynasty continued in Iberia. Placement identifies a centre of rule, not its territorial extent.

histories.title: Great Seljuq Empire
histories.summary: A Turkic-led empire shaped political and cultural life across much of the Iranian world.
histories.note: The dates concern the Great Seljuq polity; Seljuq successor states, including the Sultanate of Rum, had different lifespans.

histories.title: Safavid Iran
histories.summary: Safavid rulers established a major Iranian state and sponsored influential court arts.
histories.note: The dynasty lost effective control of its capital in 1722. The 1736 endpoint refers to formal replacement; it does not imply uniform control throughout.
posterNotes: Conventional dynasty 1501–1736. Effective control collapsed after the Afghan conquest 1722; residual Safavid claimants and restoration attempts continued until Nader’s coronation.

histories.title: Kushan Empire
histories.location: Central and South Asia · Afghanistan, Pakistan and northern India
histories.summary: Kushan rulers connected major trading and cultural networks, including centres of Buddhist patronage.
histories.note: A broad museum-style period range. The chronology and limits of effective rule vary, and later Kushan-related polities are not all represented.

histories.title: Medieval Chola dynasty
histories.location: Southern India, Sri Lanka and the Bay of Bengal
histories.summary: Chola rulers sponsored major temples, sculpture and maritime connections across the Bay of Bengal.
histories.note: This selects the medieval imperial phase. Chola names and lineages occur earlier; the dates do not describe all Tamil history.

histories.title: Delhi Sultanate
histories.location: Northern Indian subcontinent and changing adjoining territories
histories.summary: Successive ruling dynasties based in Delhi governed changing parts of South Asia.
histories.note: Five major dynasties are grouped here. The extent of their rule varied; southern states and other independent powers coexisted.
posterNotes: Several ruling dynasties with shifting territories; a northern Indian political frame rather than all-India rule.

histories.title: Vijayanagara Empire
histories.location: Southern India · capital at present-day Hampi
histories.summary: A major southern Indian empire developed a monumental capital and extensive regional networks.
histories.note: The defeat of 1565 transformed the empire, but successor rulers continued beyond the destruction of the main capital.

histories.title: Maratha polity
histories.location: Indian subcontinent · centred in the western Deccan
histories.summary: Maratha rulers and confederated houses became major powers in the subcontinent.
histories.note: The frame runs from Shivaji’s coronation to the defeat of the Peshwa. Several Maratha-ruled princely states continued after 1818.

histories.title: Qin dynasty
histories.summary: A short-lived dynasty unified competing states under an imperial ruler.
histories.note: The Qin state existed before 221 BCE. This short bar represents the imperial dynasty; it remains selectable even when its label needs magnification.
posterNotes: Unification 221 BCE, correcting the poster’s tiny 217 BCE label. Qin as a regional state existed much earlier.

histories.title: Sui dynasty
histories.summary: The Sui reunited northern and southern realms before the Tang dynasty.
histories.note: Dynastic dates should not be confused with uniform control across all regions for the entire period.
posterNotes: Dynasty founded 581; reunification of north and south 589. The poster uses 589 for the territorial milestone.

histories.title: Mongol Empire · unified phase
histories.location: Founded in Mongolia · expansion across Eurasia
histories.summary: Mongol armies and rulers connected an exceptionally extensive Eurasian imperial realm.
histories.note: 1260 marks a conventional transition into competing khanates. Mongol states continued much longer, including the Yuan dynasty shown separately.

histories.title: Yuan dynasty
histories.location: East Asia · centred in present-day China
histories.summary: Kublai Khan proclaimed the Yuan dynasty during the wider history of Mongol rule.
histories.note: 1271 is the dynastic proclamation; conquest of the Southern Song was completed in 1279. Northern Yuan rulers continued after losing China in 1368.
posterNotes: Proclaimed 1271, Southern Song conquered 1279. Ming seized Dadu 1368 but Northern Yuan rule continued beyond the poster’s endpoint.

histories.title: Ming dynasty
histories.summary: Ming rulers governed a major imperial state with extensive regional and maritime connections.
histories.note: 1644 marks the fall of Beijing and the main dynasty. Southern Ming regimes continued after that date.
posterNotes: Beijing fell 1644, while Southern Ming regimes continued to 1662 and related resistance longer. Ming did not simply become Qing everywhere at once.

histories.title: Qing dynasty
histories.summary: A Manchu-led dynasty governed an expansive and diverse empire.
histories.note: 1644 marks entry into Beijing rather than the dynasty’s 1636 proclamation. Some art chronologies end in 1911; the emperor abdicated in 1912.
posterNotes: Qing dynastic name proclaimed 1636 before its 1644 seizure of Beijing; conquest continued regionally thereafter. Abdication 1912.

histories.title: Heian period
histories.summary: Court culture developed around Heian-kyō while political institutions changed over time.
histories.note: This is a historical period, not the full lifespan of a single Japanese state. Alternative endpoints include 1192.
posterNotes: Conventional ending 1185 with the emergence of warrior government;1192 is another common boundary emphasizing the shogunal appointment.

histories.title: Goryeo dynasty
histories.summary: A Korean dynasty supported influential Buddhist, ceramic and printing traditions.
histories.note: 918 marks the dynasty’s foundation; unification of the later Three Kingdoms was completed in 936.

histories.title: Srivijaya
histories.location: Maritime Southeast Asia · centred on Sumatra
histories.summary: A maritime polity linked ports, Buddhist institutions and commercial networks across Southeast Asia.
histories.note: Origins, centres of power and the end of the polity are debated. This broad range should not imply continuous control of all regional shipping.

histories.title: Majapahit
histories.location: Maritime Southeast Asia · centred on Java
histories.summary: A Javanese court cultivated political and commercial relationships across the archipelago.
histories.note: Claims of influence should not be treated as a map of uniformly administered territory. The decline and final endpoint remain debated.

histories.title: Mycenaean societies
histories.summary: Palatial centres and Linear B records illuminate the Late Bronze Age Greek world.
histories.note: This is an archaeological period grouping several centres. The collapse of palace systems did not end Greek-speaking communities.
posterNotes: An archaeological period of multiple mainland palace centres, rather than a single uniformly governed Greek nation.

histories.title: Roman Republic
histories.summary: Republican institutions accompanied Rome’s expansion into a major Mediterranean power.
histories.note: 509 BCE is a traditional date for the republic’s foundation; 27 BCE is the conventional beginning of the principate, not an instant change in every institution.
posterNotes: Traditional republican frame; the Republic conquered territories at different times rather than inheriting all the coloured columns at its foundation.

histories.title: Hellenistic kingdoms
histories.summary: Successor kingdoms emerged after Alexander’s death and fostered interconnected cultural worlds.
histories.note: This groups independent and competing kingdoms across several regions. The 31 BCE endpoint follows a common period convention.
posterNotes: The poster’s Greek column ends at Roman conquest in 146 BCE. Hellenistic kingdoms elsewhere continued; 31 BCE is a common wider period endpoint, with Egypt annexed in 30 BCE.
A family of rival states following Alexander; selected separate Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Parthian histories are required for the poster’s named blocks.

histories.title: Holy Roman Empire
histories.location: Central Europe and changing neighbouring territories
histories.summary: An imperial framework connected many kingdoms, principalities and cities in Central Europe.
histories.note: Some histories begin with Charlemagne in 800. This bar uses Otto I’s coronation in 962; the empire was not a modern centralised nation-state.
posterNotes: Otto I’s 962 coronation is the selected start; some imperial narratives begin with 800. This was a changing framework of many states and cities, not a modern German nation-state.

histories.title: Kyivan Rusʹ
histories.location: Eastern Europe · centred on Kyiv and other cities
histories.summary: A network of principalities developed political, commercial and religious connections across Eastern Europe.
histories.note: The conventional frame simplifies regional fragmentation and the Mongol invasions. It does not assign the medieval polity exclusively to one modern nation.

histories.title: Moche traditions
histories.summary: Regional communities produced monumental adobe centres and distinctive ceramic and metal arts.
histories.note: Moche is an archaeological designation encompassing changing regional centres, not proof of one uninterrupted empire.

histories.title: Nazca traditions
histories.summary: Communities developed distinctive ceramics, textiles and monumental geoglyphs.
histories.note: Period boundaries vary. The geoglyphs include work from different communities and phases, and do not define the entire history of the region.

histories.title: Chaco Canyon
histories.location: Southwestern North America · present-day United States
histories.summary: Ancestral Pueblo communities built major ceremonial and residential centres connected across the region.
histories.note: This selects the major Chacoan phase. Pueblo peoples and their cultural traditions continue; the endpoint does not mean their disappearance.

histories.title: Wari · expansion
histories.summary: Urban centres and regional networks expanded around the Wari state and its material traditions.
histories.note: This selects the main expansion phase. Some archaeological periodisations begin Wari material traditions earlier; the degree of state control varied across regions.

histories.title: Tiwanaku
histories.location: Lake Titicaca basin · present-day Bolivia and neighbouring areas
histories.summary: A major highland centre influenced religious and regional networks around Lake Titicaca.
histories.note: This selects a period of expansion and florescence. Settlement at the site began earlier, and regional communities continued afterward.

histories.title: Tuʻi Tonga
histories.location: Tonga and wider western Polynesian networks
histories.summary: Tongan chiefly authority developed extensive political and cultural relationships across the Pacific.
histories.note: The early chronology draws heavily on genealogies. The bar groups changing chiefly arrangements rather than asserting direct administration of a single Pacific empire.

histories.title: Rapa Nui · monumental phase
histories.location: Rapa Nui / Easter Island · southeastern Pacific
histories.summary: Rapa Nui communities constructed monumental platforms and moai within a distinctive island society.
histories.note: A selected broad monumental phase. Initial settlement and monument chronologies remain subjects of research; Rapa Nui people and culture continue.

histories.title: Kingdom of England
histories.note: 927 is a conventional unification date. Republican rule interrupted the monarchy in 1649–1660; the 1707 union did not end English society.

histories.title: Kingdom of Scotland
histories.note: 843 is a traditional, disputed origin convention rather than a precise founding date. The crowns were shared from 1603; parliamentary union followed in 1707.

histories.title: Kingdom of France
histories.note: This selects the Capetian and subsequent royal frame from 987, not the earliest Frankish kingdom. The monarchy was abolished in 1792 and later restored in different forms.
posterNotes: 987 marks Hugh Capet’s accession and the selected royal frame. France was not a uniformly centralised nation-state throughout this period.

histories.title: France · revolutionary and modern eras
histories.note: A modern-period grouping, not an uninterrupted French republic: empires, restored monarchies, occupation and successive republics fall within it. The First Republic was proclaimed in 1792.
posterNotes: Modern France includes republics, empires and restored monarchies. The poster’s 1946 boundary is the Fourth Republic; the Fifth Republic began in 1958.

histories.title: Spain · composite monarchy and modern eras
histories.note: 1479 marks the dynastic union of Castile and Aragon under their joint rulers, not immediate administrative unification. This groups later monarchies, republics and dictatorship.
posterNotes: Country-level frame that distinguishes the late medieval dynastic union from later monarchy, republican, dictatorial and democratic governments.

histories.title: Kingdom of Great Britain
histories.note: The 1707 Acts of Union united England and Scotland. The 1801 union with Ireland created the United Kingdom. Britain and the British Empire are distinct entries.

histories.title: United Kingdom
histories.note: The 1801 union created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Most of Ireland left in 1922; the present state name was adopted in 1927. This is not the lifespan of the British Empire.
posterNotes: The United Kingdom was created in 1801, not 1917. Most of Ireland left in 1922; the present state name dates to 1927. The royal family adopted the Windsor name in 1917.

histories.title: British Empire · major overseas phase
histories.location: Britain and territories across several continents
histories.note: A selected overseas phase, from the permanent Jamestown settlement to the Hong Kong handover. English imperial ventures began earlier; British Overseas Territories continue after 1997. The end is a transition marker, not a claim that all colonial relationships ended then.

histories.title: Russian Empire
histories.note: The imperial title was adopted in 1721. The monarchy fell in 1917; the subsequent civil war and formation of the USSR are separate developments. Its territories extended across Europe and Asia.

histories.title: Soviet Union / USSR
histories.location: Europe and Asia · a union of changing constituent republics
histories.note: The USSR was founded in 1922 and dissolved in 1991. It was not simply another name for Russia; multiple successor states emerged.

histories.title: Russian Federation
histories.note: This frame starts with the end of the USSR. The Russian republic and its institutions existed earlier. Placement does not endorse territorial claims or imply that other Soviet republics became Russia.

histories.title: Germany · modern state eras
histories.note: 1871 marks imperial unification. This modern grouping includes imperial, Weimar and Nazi regimes, postwar division into two states, and reunification in 1990; it does not imply one uninterrupted government.
posterNotes: A broad modern frame including empire, republic, dictatorship, occupation, two states and reunification in 1990. It is not one uninterrupted government.

histories.title: Italy · kingdom and republic
histories.note: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861; unification proceeded in stages. The republic dates from 1946. Earlier Italian societies and states long predate this frame.
posterNotes: A modern country frame beginning with proclamation of the kingdom. The republic dates to 1946, and the republican constitution entered into effect in 1948.

histories.title: British America
histories.note: This groups English and later British colonies before the 1783 peace settlement. Britain retained colonies afterward. It is not a state called Anglo-America, and it does not replace Indigenous histories.

histories.title: Spanish America · colonial rule
histories.location: The Caribbean and changing parts of North, Central and South America
histories.note: Colonisation developed after the 1492 voyage; 1493 marks permanent settlement on Hispaniola. Territorial control was highly uneven. Most mainland colonies became independent much earlier than 1898, when Spain lost its remaining major American colonies. Indigenous peoples and cultures continued throughout.

histories.title: New France
histories.location: North America · changing French colonial territories
histories.note: 1534 is a conventional beginning with Cartier’s voyage, not continuous settlement everywhere. Mainland territories were transferred in stages; small French territories in North America continued.

histories.title: Portuguese America · Brazil
histories.note: 1500 marks Portuguese arrival; substantial colonisation developed later. Brazil became a kingdom united with Portugal in 1815, before independence in 1822. This groups those changing relationships. Slavery persisted until 1888. Indigenous societies did not begin with European arrival.

histories.title: United States
histories.location: North America · one of the countries commonly grouped as Anglo-America
histories.note: 1776 marks the declaration of independence; British recognition followed in 1783 and the present Constitution took effect in 1789. Anglo-America is a variable cultural-geographic term, not a unified country, empire or description of every inhabitant.

histories.title: Canada · from Confederation
histories.location: North America · often included in Anglo-America, with diverse linguistic and Indigenous communities
histories.note: Confederation in 1867 created the Dominion of Canada. Autonomy and territory developed in stages, including the Statute of Westminster in 1931 and constitutional patriation in 1982. Canada is not wholly English-speaking.

histories.title: Mexico · independent eras
histories.note: 1821 marks independence from Spain. Empires, republics, civil conflicts and changing borders followed; this is not the beginning of the region’s peoples or cultures.

histories.title: Brazil · empire and republic
histories.note: This begins with independence in 1822. The empire became a republic in 1889; later political regimes varied. Slavery continued until 1888.

histories.title: Haiti · independent eras
histories.note: Haiti declared independence in 1804 after a revolution against slavery and French colonial rule. The date does not imply uninterrupted sovereignty or constitutional continuity; US occupation followed in 1915–1934.

histories.title: East India Company rule
histories.location: Changing parts of the Indian subcontinent
histories.note: 1757 is a conventional starting point after Plassey; Company trading posts existed earlier and territorial control expanded gradually. Many princely states retained indirect or independent arrangements.

histories.title: British Raj
histories.note: Direct British Crown rule followed Company rule in 1858. This includes directly governed provinces and princely states under different arrangements, not uniform administration. Partition accompanied independence in 1947.
posterNotes: The poster correctly uses 1858 for Crown rule. Company territorial rule began earlier and is separately represented; princely states had distinct arrangements.

histories.title: India · independent state
histories.note: Independence dates from 1947; the republic from 1950. India’s earlier societies long predate this political frame. Partition, disputed borders and later territorial changes are not depicted as settled by the block.
posterNotes: Independent Dominion 1947–1950, Republic from 1950. Independence is a political milestone, not the beginning of Indian cultures.

histories.title: Pakistan
histories.note: Pakistan became independent in 1947, initially including East Pakistan. Bangladesh became independent in 1971. The republic dates from 1956; governments and constitutional arrangements changed.
posterNotes: Independence 1947; East Pakistan became Bangladesh 1971. Constitutions and political regimes changed within this continuing national history.

histories.title: Bangladesh
histories.note: 1971 marks independence after the liberation war. The region had earlier histories as part of Bengal, British India and East Pakistan.

histories.title: Japan · modern eras
histories.note: 1868 marks the Meiji Restoration, not Japan’s founding. Imperial expansion, the Second World War, occupation and the postwar constitutional state are different phases within this modern frame.

histories.title: Republic of China · mainland era
histories.note: The republic was founded in 1912. After civil-war defeat on the mainland in 1949 its government continued in Taiwan, where it had assumed administration in 1945. The endpoint concerns mainland rule, not dissolution of the republic.
posterNotes: Founded 1912. The government relocated to Taiwan 1949 and the Republic of China continues there; it did not cease to exist with the PRC’s mainland victory.

histories.title: Republic of China · Taiwan era
histories.location: East Asia · Taiwan and other administered islands
histories.note: 1949 marks the relocation of the ROC central government after civil-war defeat on the mainland. ROC administration in Taiwan began in 1945. This frame does not date the island’s settlement or resolve sovereignty, recognition or territorial claims.

histories.title: People’s Republic of China
histories.location: East Asia · mainland China and administered territories
histories.note: 1949 marks the PRC’s proclamation, not the beginning of Chinese history. The Republic of China continued separately. Block placement does not adjudicate borders or sovereignty claims.
posterNotes: PRC proclaimed 1949. Its government has never administered Taiwan; the site’s separate Taiwan/ROC history preserves this distinction.

histories.title: South Korea
histories.note: The Republic of Korea was established in 1948 after the peninsula’s division. Korea’s earlier history is not limited to this modern state; the Korean War began in 1950.

histories.title: North Korea
histories.note: The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was established in 1948 after the peninsula’s division. The 1953 armistice suspended fighting without a final peace settlement.

histories.title: Indonesia
histories.note: 1945 marks the declaration of independence; Dutch transfer of sovereignty followed in 1949. Territorial incorporation and international recognition developed in stages.

histories.title: Vietnam · reunified state
histories.note: 1976 marks formal reunification as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. The 1945 independence declaration and earlier rival governments are earlier phases, not absent Vietnamese history.

histories.title: Africa · high colonial era
histories.location: Africa · different European empires and local political orders
histories.note: A selected period of rapid partition and colonial rule, not a single African state or uniform continental timeline. Colonialism began earlier in several regions and ended later in others; Ethiopia and Liberia had distinct histories.

histories.title: Nigeria · independent state
histories.note: Independence dates from 1960 and the republic from 1963. The colonial amalgamation was in 1914. Earlier kingdoms and communities are separate histories; the civil war and changes between military and civilian rule are within this frame.

histories.title: Ghana · independent state
histories.note: Independence dates from 1957 and the republic from 1960. Modern Ghana is distinct from the medieval Ghana/Wagadu Empire shown elsewhere.

histories.title: Egypt · modern independent eras
histories.note: The 1922 declaration of independence was limited by British reserved powers and continued military presence. The republic dates from 1953; withdrawal and sovereignty developed in stages.

histories.title: South Africa · union and republic
histories.note: The Union dates from 1910, the republic from 1961 and the first universal-suffrage national election from 1994. This broad political span does not equate segregation and apartheid with the later democratic order.

histories.title: Kenya · independent state
histories.note: Independence dates from 1963 and the republic from 1964. Earlier communities and political orders are not dated by the modern state’s formation.

histories.title: Republic of Türkiye / Turkey
histories.note: The republic was proclaimed in 1923 after the Ottoman sultanate ended in 1922. This does not date the beginning of Anatolian societies or imply unchanged borders.
posterNotes: Republic proclaimed 1923; the empire and republic are distinct phases.

histories.title: Iran · Pahlavi and republican eras
histories.note: This selects the Pahlavi dynasty from 1925 and the Islamic Republic from 1979. Iran’s history and state traditions began long before this modern frame.

histories.title: Saudi Arabia
histories.note: 1932 marks the proclamation of the unified kingdom, not the start of Saudi rule or the peninsula’s history. Earlier Saudi states are distinct phases.

histories.title: Israel
histories.note: 1948 marks the declaration of statehood. The accompanying war and Palestinian displacement are essential context. This block does not endorse disputed territorial claims or define settled borders.

histories.title: State of Palestine · declaration
histories.note: 1988 marks the declaration of statehood, not the beginning of Palestinian society or the achievement of full territorial sovereignty. Recognition, occupation and borders are separate questions; the block does not resolve them.

histories.title: Australia · federation
histories.note: 1901 marks federation of six British colonies. Constitutional independence developed gradually; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories long predate the federation and continue alongside it.

histories.title: New Zealand · Dominion and later state
histories.note: 1907 marks Dominion status, not a single complete independence event. Self-government, the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi, the 1947 adoption of the Statute of Westminster and the 1986 Constitution Act belong to different phases. Māori histories continue alongside the state.

histories.title: Fiji · independent state
histories.note: 1970 marks independence from Britain; the republic was declared in 1987. Earlier Indigenous histories and later constitutional changes are not erased by this statehood frame.

histories.title: Iron Age Britain · Celtic-speaking communities
histories.note: Selected pre-Roman Iron Age frame; Celtic languages and identities did not disappear in 43 CE. Stonehenge belongs to the much earlier Neolithic and Bronze Age, rather than to the origin of a Celtic state.

histories.title: Lusitanians and neighbouring Iron Age communities
histories.note: An approximate Iron Age frame, not a single kingdom founded in 600 BCE. Roman writers attest Lusitanians later; the Lusitanian War ended in 139 BCE but regional conquest continued.

histories.title: Iberian and Celtiberian communities
histories.note: A broad grouping of distinct peoples, languages and regional societies. Iberian culture is usually identified from the first millennium BCE; Rome completed its wider Iberian conquests in 19 BCE, not in 218 BCE.

histories.title: Carthaginian Iberia · Barcid expansion
histories.note: Selected Barcid territorial phase beginning with Hamilcar Barca in 237 BCE. Phoenician and Punic settlements predate it; Rome expelled the main Carthaginian forces from Iberia in 206 BCE.

histories.title: Gaul · Iron Age communities
histories.note: An approximate regional Iron Age frame, not one Celtic state. Caesar campaigned in 58–50 BCE; southern Gaul had already come under Roman rule.

histories.title: Italic peoples · early Italian peninsula
histories.note: An approximate early grouping of several languages and peoples. Etruscans were not linguistically Italic, Greek colonies were distinct, and Italic communities continued after the Roman monarchy began.

histories.title: Roman Kingdom · traditional chronology
histories.note: 753 BCE and 509 BCE are traditional foundation and transition dates transmitted by later Roman historians, not archaeologically proven day-one boundaries.

histories.title: Central European Celtic and Germanic communities
histories.note: A regional, approximate cultural frame spanning many communities. These categories are linguistic and historical labels, not one government or an unbroken ethnic ancestry.

histories.title: Hallstatt culture · early Iron Age phases
histories.note: The selected Iron Age Hallstatt C–D phases date approximately 800–450 BCE. Broader Hallstatt A–B material belongs to the earlier Bronze Age; the culture was not a unitary state.

histories.title: Kingdom of Noricum
histories.note: The Norican kingdom or federation consolidated around the second century BCE; the poster’s c. 400 BCE better describes earlier regional Celtic culture. Roman annexation began in 15 BCE; later provincial institutions continued.

histories.title: Aegean Bronze Age cultures
histories.note: An archaeological umbrella including Cycladic, Minoan and Mycenaean cultures with different chronologies; it was not one empire or an exclusive origin story for later Greeks.

histories.title: Early Iron Age Greece · Greek Dark Ages
histories.note: A conventional archaeological period following palace collapse. The label does not imply an absence of communities, creativity or contact; boundaries vary between regions.

histories.title: Sub-Roman Britain
histories.note: Approximate transition after the withdrawal of Roman imperial administration, conventionally around 410. Regional British polities continued alongside incoming and established communities; 500 is not a universal end date.

histories.title: First County of Portugal
histories.note: A conventional first-county frame beginning with the recovery of Porto in 868. The first comital line ended with Nuno Mendes’s defeat in 1071. Royal administration and later reorganisation preceded Henry of Burgundy’s county around 1096; this was not an uninterrupted independent state.

histories.title: Second County of Portugal
histories.note: The second county is usually dated from Henry of Burgundy’s appointment around 1096. Afonso Henriques’ kingship in 1139 and recognition in 1143 and 1179 mark different steps toward independence.

histories.title: Kingdom of Portugal
histories.note: A long political frame with dynastic and constitutional changes, including the Iberian Union of 1580–1640. The colonial link shown here is a selected episode.

histories.title: Portugal · modern republican eras
histories.note: A modern country frame including the First Republic, military and Estado Novo dictatorships, and the democratic transition. Democracy began after 1974; the present constitution took effect in 1976.

histories.title: Kingdom of the Suebi
histories.note: The Suebi established rule in northwestern Iberia after crossing the Rhine and entering Iberia. The Visigoths annexed their kingdom in 585; this was not a kingdom encompassing all Iberia.

histories.title: Visigothic Kingdom
histories.note: The kingdom began in Aquitaine in 418 and shifted toward Iberia. The Suebi were annexed in 585; Byzantine-controlled southern areas remained separate until the seventh century. After 711, remnants continued in Septimania into the 720s.

histories.title: Al-Andalus
histories.note: An umbrella for changing Muslim-ruled Iberian territories, not a single state lasting throughout 711–1492. The emirate, caliphate, taifas and later dynasties overlap with northern Christian kingdoms.

histories.title: Kingdom of Asturias
histories.note: 718 is a traditional royal origin date. The court and political centre shifted to León in 910, while distinct Asturian royal claims continued to 924; chronology depends on whether one tracks title, court or territory.

histories.title: Kingdom of León
histories.note: A selected independent royal frame. León and Castile were joined and separated at several points; permanent dynastic union in 1230 did not erase León’s regional institutions.

histories.title: Frankish realms · Merovingian and Carolingian periods
histories.note: 481 marks Clovis I’s accession, not the first existence of Franks. Frankish realms were repeatedly divided; imperial coronation in 800 and partition in 843 are distinct events.

histories.title: West Francia
histories.note: A kingdom created by the partition of 843. The Capetian accession in 987 is a dynastic convention, not an instant creation of French society.

histories.title: Western Roman Empire · late phase
histories.note: The selected late phase follows the 395 division of imperial courts. Roman institutions and communities did not disappear in 476.

histories.title: Ostrogothic Kingdom in Italy
histories.note: Theodoric took control of Italy in 493. 553 is a conventional endpoint after Byzantine victories; warfare and residual resistance continued.

histories.title: Kingdom of the Lombards
histories.note: The Lombard kingdom ruled much of the peninsula after 568 and was conquered by Charlemagne in 774. Southern Lombard duchies continued afterward.

histories.title: Italian states · medieval communes and regional powers
histories.note: A regional umbrella for many states, cities and jurisdictions, not one state. Venice, Genoa, the Papal States, imperial territories and southern kingdoms had distinct histories.

histories.title: Kingdom of Sicily
histories.note: Founded in 1130. After 1282 the island and mainland crowns were politically divided, with both claiming Sicilian titles; they were formally combined as the Two Sicilies in 1816. The poster’s 1494 boundary is not the kingdom’s end.

histories.title: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
histories.note: The poster’s 1815 restoration relates to the post-Napoleonic settlement. The unified Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was formally created in 1816 and incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

histories.title: Germanic-speaking communities in late antiquity
histories.note: A selected late antique migration frame encompassing many groups and political formations. Language labels do not imply one people, one kingdom or an unbroken ancestry for modern Germany.

histories.title: Migration Period · late antique Europe
histories.note: A broad conventional span used by the Metropolitan Museum; other historians use narrower fourth-to-sixth-century ranges. Migration involved warfare, settlement, Roman service and changing identities rather than a single population replacement.

histories.title: Post-Roman kingdoms in the eastern Alpine region
histories.note: A selected regional transition among successor authorities, including Ostrogothic influence and emerging Bavarian power. It is not a single named kingdom founded in 476.

histories.title: Early Duchy of Bavaria
histories.note: The first Bavarian duchy is conventionally traced to the mid-sixth century; Charlemagne deposed Tassilo III in 788. Later Bavarian duchies continued under different political arrangements.

histories.title: East Francia
histories.note: The map selects the kingdom before Otto I’s imperial coronation. The kingdom and later empire developed through successive changes.

histories.title: Margraviate of Austria
histories.note: The Babenberg march was established in 976 and elevated to a duchy in 1156. This was a frontier territory within a wider imperial framework, not an independent modern Austria.

histories.title: Duchy of Austria
histories.note: The Privilegium Minus elevated the march to a duchy in 1156. The archducal title was invented in the fourteenth century but officially recognised in 1453.

histories.title: Habsburg Austria · archducal and composite monarchy phases
histories.note: 1453 marks formal recognition of the archducal title, not the beginning of Habsburg rule in Austria (which dates to the late thirteenth century). The wider Habsburg monarchy accumulated distinct crowns and territories.

histories.title: Austrian Empire
histories.note: The Austrian imperial title was proclaimed in 1804, while the Holy Roman Empire still existed until 1806. The Dual Monarchy replaced this framework in 1867.

histories.title: Austria-Hungary
histories.note: The 1867 Compromise established a dual monarchy with separate Austrian and Hungarian institutions and shared affairs. Its dissolution in 1918 produced several successor states, not simply modern Austria.

histories.title: Austria · modern republican eras
histories.note: A modern country frame covering the First Republic, authoritarian Federal State, Nazi annexation, restored republic and Allied occupation. Full sovereignty was restored in 1955, not the first existence of the republic.

histories.title: Greece · modern state eras
histories.note: Independence was internationally recognised in 1830 and the kingdom established in 1832. The democratic Third Republic dates to 1974, with its constitution in 1975; the poster’s 1973 marker refers to a junta-controlled abolition of monarchy.

histories.title: Ptolemaic Kingdom
histories.note: A Hellenistic kingdom based in Egypt. The royal title dates to 305 BCE; Ptolemy had governed Egypt earlier.

histories.title: Fatimid Caliphate
histories.note: Founded in North Africa 909; conquest of Egypt and establishment of Cairo occurred 969. The poster’s 969 start represents the Egyptian phase, not the caliphate’s founding.

histories.title: Ayyubid Sultanate
histories.note: Ayyubid government ended in Egypt 1250; regional Ayyubid rulers in Syria continued through 1260 and some local branches longer. Use 1171–1250 for a strictly Egyptian subperiod.

histories.title: Mamluk Sultanate · Egypt and Syria
histories.note: Egyptian rule began 1250; control of Syria expanded by 1260. Ottoman conquest 1516–1517 ended the sultanate, although Mamluk elites persisted.

histories.title: Egypt · Muhammad Ali dynasty
histories.note: The dynasty continued across the British occupation, protectorate and Kingdom of Egypt; these were overlapping political dimensions. The poster cuts the dynasty at 1882.

histories.title: Syro-Hittite / Neo-Hittite kingdoms
histories.note: Multiple Luwian and Aramaean kingdoms followed the Hittite imperial collapse; no single successor empire. Final incorporation into Assyria varied by kingdom.

histories.title: Lydia · Mermnad kingdom
histories.note: Selected well-attested Mermnad phase begins around 680 BCE. Earlier Lydian traditions and rulers predate it; Cyrus’s conquest is conventionally dated 547/546 BCE.

histories.title: Sumer · cities and writing
histories.note: Selected urban Sumerian cultural history, not a single united empire. The poster’s 4500 BCE start is an overly precise ethnic-cultural founding date: Ubaid settlement traditions are earlier, while Uruk urbanization and writing developed during the fourth millennium. Ur III ended 2004 BCE; Sumerian language and traditions persisted.

histories.title: Assyria · Middle Assyrian period
histories.note: The poster’s broad Assyrian band combines Middle and Neo-Assyrian periods. This earlier phase complements existing Neo-Assyria; power and territory fluctuated.

histories.title: Neo-Babylonian Empire
histories.note: Nabopolassar’s kingdom began 626 BCE; imperial expansion followed Assyria’s collapse 612–609. Conquered by Cyrus 539 BCE.

histories.title: Elam · kingdoms of southwest Iran
histories.note: A sequence of kingdoms and cultural phases, not one uninterrupted empire. Elamite history did not simply end 1500 BCE with the appearance of Iranian-speaking groups; these histories overlapped.

histories.title: Early Iranian-speaking peoples
histories.note: A selected approximate pre-Achaemenid frame, not a state or a single dated migration. Western-Iranian groups are securely attested in Assyrian records by the ninth centuryBCE; their languages and societies continued after 550 BCE.

histories.title: Medes · kingdom and debated empire
histories.note: Conventional traditional frame only. The extent, political unity and chronology of a Median empire remain debated; no claim that a securely documented empire was founded in 678 BCE.

histories.title: Alexander’s empire
histories.note: This selects the period of expansion into the Achaemenid realm. Alexander became king in 336 BCE; successor kingdoms emerged through prolonged wars after his death.

histories.title: Seleucid Empire
histories.note: One of several Hellenistic successor kingdoms. Its territory contracted over time, and it did not encompass all of Alexander’s former realm.

histories.title: Parthian Empire
histories.note: Parthian rulers expanded gradually into Seleucid-held territories and were later overthrown by the Sasanians.

histories.title: Sultanate of Rûm
histories.note: An Anatolian Seljuk state distinct from the Great Seljuq Empire already in the chart. Autonomy weakened after defeat by the Mongols 1243.

histories.title: Iran and Iraq · Mongol and regional dynasties
histories.note: A regional overview, not a single successor state. Includes Ilkhanid, Jalayirid, Timurid and Turkmen powers with different and overlapping dates; Ilkhanid rule began before 1258 and several regional histories continued after 1501.

histories.title: Ilkhanate
histories.note: A regional Mongol khanate. The united dynasty fragmented in 1335; later claimants and successor states continued. Some art chronologies extend to 1353.

histories.title: Timurid Empire
histories.note: Specific major power within the poster’s umbrella band; western Iranian territory also passed to Turkmen dynasties. Their dates do not define a single 1258–1501 empire.

histories.title: Afsharid Iran
histories.note: Nader Shah’s empire fragmented after his death 1747. Afsharid government in Khorasan survived until 1796, overlapping the Zands and rising Qajars.

histories.title: Qajar Iran
histories.note: Start dates 1786,1789,1794 and 1796 reflect different stages of consolidation and coronation. Use conventional 1789 for the dynasty and explain 1796 coronation; the poster selects 1796.

histories.title: Kingdom of Iraq
histories.note: Monarchy established 1921 under British control; mandate ended and independence recognized 1932. Monarchy overthrown 14 July 1958.

histories.title: Iraq · republican eras
histories.note: A succession of republics and regimes, with major changes 1968,2003 and 2005. The state and Iraqi society did not originate 1958.

histories.title: Mahājanapadas
histories.note: Multiple kingdoms and oligarchic republics, principally in northern South Asia; conventional sixth–fourth centuryBCE frame. Mauryan expansion incorporated different states at different times.

histories.title: Post-Mauryan South Asian kingdoms
histories.note: Period overview containing Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greek, Shaka, Satavahana and Kushan powers; many coexisted. Existing Kushan history provides one named example.

histories.title: Post-Gupta regional kingdoms
histories.note: A selected transition frame, not one polity. Regional kingdoms and post-Gupta artistic traditions began before and continued after Harsha; avoid a blanket replacement at 606.

histories.title: Harsha · northern Indian kingdom
histories.note: Harsha ruled parts of northern India 606–647, not all South Asia; southern powers including the Chalukyas remained independent.

histories.title: Early medieval South Asian kingdoms
histories.note: A broad selected frame, not one state or a cultural vacuum. Includes Pala, Pratihara, Rashtrakuta, Chalukya, Chola and Rajput polities with overlapping dates; southern kingdoms continued after 1206.

histories.title: Xia · traditional dynasty, debated identification
histories.note: These are traditional/modelled dates, not secure contemporary attestations. No surviving contemporary inscription securely identifies Erlitou as Xia; historicity and archaeological identification remain debated.

histories.title: China · Six Dynasties and divided realms
histories.note: An umbrella period, not one government. Includes Three Kingdoms, Western/Eastern Jin, Sixteen Kingdoms and Northern/Southern dynasties; brief Western Jin reunification 280–316 interrupts any claim of continuous division.

histories.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
histories.note: Northern Five Dynasties traditionally end 960 with Song’s foundation, while southern independent kingdoms continued until 979. A network of concurrent states, not five rulers of all China.
histories.wikiTitle: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

wikipedia.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period

histories.title: Jōmon period
histories.note: Starts many millennia before the chart window. The transition to Yayoi was regionally gradual from roughly 900 BCE; Jōmon traditions persisted later in northern areas. This is not Japan’s first human occupation.

histories.title: Yayoi period
histories.note: Dates vary by region and dating method. Newer chronologies place wet-rice-based Yayoi society from around 900 BCE in northern Kyushu, while older general surveys use 300 BCE. Do not present the poster’s 300 BCE as a universal secure start.

histories.title: Yamato polity · Kofun and Asuka periods
histories.note: A broad conventional Kofun/Asuka frame; the Yamato court consolidated gradually.250 is an archaeological-period anchor, not a known single state-founding date.

histories.title: Nara period
histories.note: Capital established at Heijō-kyō710; court moved to Heian-kyō794, with a brief intervening Nagaoka phase 784–794.

histories.title: Kamakura shogunate
histories.note: 1185 marks military victory and establishment of rule;1192 marks Minamoto no Yoritomo’s shogunal title. Shogunate ended 1333.

histories.title: Muromachi / Ashikaga shogunate
histories.note: Ashikaga regime 1336–1573, with a rival Southern Court 1336–1392. The later Sengoku wars overlap it; the shogunate did not continue to 1603.

histories.title: New Spain · mainland Mexican frame
histories.note: 1521 marks the fall of Tenochtitlan; the Viceroyalty of New Spain was established in 1535. Its jurisdiction extended far beyond present-day Mexico and changed over time. Spanish conquest did not end Indigenous peoples or cultures.

histories.title: Spanish colonial Río de la Plata
histories.note: 1536 marks the first, short-lived Buenos Aires settlement, not continuous control of present-day Argentina. The second foundation was in 1580. The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata existed only from 1776, and the independence process began in 1810 before the 1816 declaration. Indigenous territories were not uniformly controlled.
histories.wikiTitle: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

wikipedia.title: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata

histories.title: Australia · British colonial periods
histories.note: The British colony of New South Wales began in 1788; other colonies were established or separated later. Six colonies federated in 1901. Colonial expansion involved dispossession and conflict, while Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories continued.

histories.title: Argentina · independent eras
histories.note: 1816 marks the declaration of independence by the United Provinces, following the 1810 revolution. The Argentine state, its constitutional arrangements and territorial control developed through later conflicts and agreements. This is not an unchanged republic from 1816.

histories.title: Kingdom of Israel (Samaria)
histories.location: Southern Levant and wider Jewish communities
histories.summary: A northern Israelite kingdom, with its later capital at Samaria. Assyrian conquest ended the kingdom and deported part of its population.
histories.note: The 900 BCE start is an approximate display anchor for early state development, not a documented founding year. Origins, early chronology and the relationship with Judah remain debated. This is the ancient northern kingdom, distinct from modern Israel.

histories.title: Kingdom of Judah
histories.location: Southern Levant and wider Jewish communities
histories.summary: A southern Israelite kingdom centred on Jerusalem, important to the development of Jewish history and traditions. Babylonian conquest destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and deported many inhabitants; others remained.
histories.note: The 900 BCE start is an approximate display anchor, not an established founding date. The emergence of the kingdom and its relationship with northern Israel are debated. The fall of its government did not end Jewish communities or traditions.

histories.title: Hasmonean Judea
histories.location: Southern Levant and wider Jewish communities
histories.summary: Jewish rulers established an expanding Judean state during the Hellenistic period. Roman intervention reduced its independence before Herod took Jerusalem in 37 BCE.
histories.note: The 140 BCE start is a conventional dynastic-period boundary. The Maccabean revolt began earlier; Roman intervention in 63 BCE curtailed sovereignty before the dynasty ended. This block does not represent all Jewish communities.

connections.label: 1707 · union
connections.summary: The English and Scottish kingdoms and parliaments united as Great Britain.
connections.note: The 1603 Union of the Crowns had already created a shared monarch; parliamentary union came later.

connections.label: 1600s · overseas expansion
connections.summary: English overseas settlements and trading ventures developed into a wider imperial system.
connections.note: The British Empire was not a new country replacing England. Scottish ventures and the later British state also shaped it.

connections.label: Colonial administration
connections.summary: British America grouped colonies within the wider empire.
connections.note: The colonies had different institutions; Indigenous peoples and political orders continued alongside and under colonial expansion.

connections.label: 1801 · union
connections.summary: Great Britain and Ireland entered a parliamentary union as the United Kingdom.
connections.note: This was a political union, not the beginning of the peoples or cultures of either island.

connections.label: 1776–83 · independence & remaining colonies
connections.summary: Thirteen colonies declared independence and became the United States. Britain retained other North American colonies.
connections.note: This is a selected branching of colonial jurisdictions, not a division of the entire population into two homogeneous peoples.

connections.label: 1763 · cession of Canada
connections.summary: The Treaty of Paris transferred French Canada to British control.
connections.note: Other former French territories had different outcomes, including transfers to Spain. The arrow concerns Canada, not all New France.

connections.label: 1867 · Confederation
connections.summary: The Province of Canada, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia federated as the Dominion of Canada.
connections.note: Other colonies and territories joined later; 1867 was not a single moment of complete independence.

connections.label: 1922 · Free State established
connections.summary: The Irish Free State was established, while Northern Ireland remained within the United Kingdom.
connections.note: The Free State initially had dominion status. Later constitutional changes followed in 1937 and 1949.

connections.label: 1937 / 1949 · constitutional changes
connections.summary: A new constitution replaced the Free State framework in 1937; the republic description and departure from the Commonwealth followed in 1949.
connections.note: The constitution came into operation in December 1937. Ireland is the state name; these constitutional changes did not end the separate position of Northern Ireland.

continuations.label: Iron Age communities, Rome & post-Roman Britain

connections.label: 27 BCE · principate
connections.summary: Augustus established the principate within the continuing Roman state.
connections.note: Republican forms and institutions did not vanish overnight; this is a conventional political transition.

connections.label: 395 · separate imperial courts
connections.summary: After Theodosius I, separate emperors ruled the eastern and western courts.
connections.note: Division developed over time. The eastern empire continued to understand itself as Roman, rather than representing an unrelated new civilisation.

connections.label: 800 · Roman imperial title revived
connections.summary: Charlemagne’s coronation revived a western claim to Roman imperial authority.
connections.note: This indicates a political model and claim to legitimacy, not an uninterrupted continuation of Western Roman administration.

connections.label: War, diplomacy & exchange
connections.summary: The Roman and Sasanian states fought repeated wars and maintained diplomatic and cultural contacts.
connections.note: Neither state simply merged into the other; their frontier and relationship changed over centuries.

connections.label: 1453 · Constantinople conquered
connections.summary: Ottoman forces conquered Constantinople, ending its Byzantine imperial government.
connections.note: The Ottoman state had existed for well over a century. Byzantine successor territories and cultural traditions had separate and continuing histories.

connections.label: 843 · Treaty of Verdun
connections.summary: The Carolingian realm was partitioned into West, Middle and East Francia.
connections.note: These were dynastic kingdoms, not the present borders or founding moments of modern France, Germany and Italy. Further partitions followed.

connections.label: 987 · Capetian accession
connections.summary: Hugh Capet’s accession marks a dynastic transition in the western Frankish kingdom.
connections.note: The French kingdom did not appear from nothing in 987; institutions and society developed across this transition.

connections.label: 962 · imperial coronation
connections.summary: Otto I’s imperial coronation anchors the conventional beginning used here for the Holy Roman Empire.
connections.note: This was an evolving imperial framework, not immediate unification of a modern German nation-state.

connections.label: 1792 · monarchy abolished
connections.summary: The Revolution abolished monarchy and inaugurated a republic in France.
connections.note: The destination is a broad frame containing later empires, restored monarchies and republics. It does not imply uninterrupted republican government after 1792.

connections.label: 1806–15 · imperial end & new league
connections.summary: The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806; after Napoleonic reorganisation, the Vienna settlement created a German Confederation in 1815.
connections.note: This was a new association of states after an intervening period, not the old empire renamed. Its membership and institutions differed.

connections.label: 1804–06 · Habsburg imperial change
connections.summary: The Habsburg ruler created an Austrian imperial title in 1804, before relinquishing the separate Holy Roman title in 1806.
connections.note: The Austrian Empire concerned the Habsburg monarchy, including lands outside the Holy Roman Empire. It did not inherit the whole former empire.

connections.label: 1866–67 · new northern federation
connections.summary: War dissolved the old German Confederation; Prussia and northern allies formed a new federal state.
connections.note: Austria and the southern states were outside this new federation. The two confederations were different political frameworks.

connections.label: 1871 · enlarged German federation
