connections.summary: Southern German states joined the Prussia-led federation, forming the German Empire.
connections.note: Austria was excluded. The destination groups later German regimes, division after 1945 and reunification in 1990; it is not one unchanged government.

connections.label: 1867 · Dual Monarchy
connections.summary: The compromise reorganised the Habsburg monarchy into Austrian and Hungarian halves with shared affairs.
connections.note: This was a constitutional reorganisation of a multinational monarchy, not the merger of two homogeneous peoples.

connections.label: 1918 · one of several successor states
connections.summary: The monarchy broke apart and a republic was proclaimed in Austria.
connections.note: Austria was only one successor. Hungary, Czechoslovakia and other successor or enlarged states followed separate paths. The destination also includes dictatorship, annexation in 1938 and the restored republic after 1945.

connections.label: 1922–23 · sultanate ends; republic
connections.summary: The sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed in 1923 after war and the Lausanne settlement.
connections.note: This is one selected outcome of Ottoman dissolution. Other former Ottoman territories had different state formations and colonial mandates; the entire empire did not become Turkey.

continuations.label: Aegean networks, Greek worlds & modern independence

connections.label: 334–330 BCE · conquest
connections.summary: Alexander’s campaigns defeated Achaemenid royal power and occupied its principal territories.
connections.note: Local populations and administrative practices continued; this was not a replacement of all inhabitants or cultures.

connections.label: After 323 BCE · successor kingdoms
connections.summary: Wars after Alexander’s death produced several kingdoms, including the Seleucid and Ptolemaic realms.
connections.note: Only two selected successors are shown. They emerged through prolonged struggles, not a neat agreed two-way split in 323 BCE.

connections.label: 3rd–2nd c. BCE · territorial expansion
connections.summary: Parthian rulers expanded into territories previously controlled by the Seleucids.
connections.note: This was gradual and regional. Seleucid rule continued elsewhere after major eastern territories were lost.

connections.label: 30 BCE · Egypt annexed
connections.summary: Octavian’s forces defeated the Ptolemaic monarchy, and Egypt came under Roman rule.
connections.note: The conquest preceded the conventional 27 BCE beginning of the principate. Egyptian society continued under different rulers.

connections.label: 224 · dynasty overthrown
connections.summary: Ardashir defeated the last major Arsacid king and established Sasanian rule.
connections.note: A dynastic and political change did not erase the region’s peoples, religious communities or administrative traditions.

connections.label: 633–651 · conquest of Iran
connections.summary: Arab-Muslim armies defeated Sasanian forces, and the last Sasanian emperor died in 651.
connections.note: Conquest unfolded in stages. The caliphate already existed; Iranian institutions and cultural traditions continued in changing forms.

connections.label: 661 · Umayyad rule
connections.summary: Mu‘awiya’s rule inaugurated the Umayyad caliphate after civil war.
connections.note: This is a change in political leadership, not a new beginning for Islam or a single instantaneous transformation of every province.

connections.label: 750 · Abbasid revolution
connections.summary: The Abbasid revolution replaced the Damascus-based Umayyad caliphate.
connections.note: An Umayyad line continued in Iberia. The diagram does not imply that all Umayyad institutions or communities disappeared.

connections.label: 1258 · Baghdad conquered
connections.summary: Hülegü’s Mongol forces captured Baghdad and ended its Abbasid caliphate.
connections.note: The Ilkhanate was already taking shape. Later Abbasid caliphs in Cairo and other Islamic states are not represented by this arrow.

connections.label: 13th c. · regional khanates
connections.summary: The wider Mongol realm developed into several regional khanates, including these four major branches.
connections.note: Their origins predated the final fragmentation. This was not a single simultaneous partition in 1260, and competing claims to imperial authority continued.

connections.label: 1279 · Song conquest completed
connections.summary: Kublai Khan’s forces completed the conquest of the Southern Song.
connections.note: The Yuan dynastic name had been proclaimed in 1271. The arrow records conquest of another state, not the first formation of Yuan rule.

connections.label: 1368 · Ming takes the capital
connections.summary: Ming forces took the Yuan capital, and Yuan rulers withdrew north.
connections.note: Northern Yuan regimes continued after 1368. Dynastic replacement in China did not end Mongol societies or all Mongol states.

connections.label: 1644 · Qing enters Beijing
connections.summary: The Qing entered Beijing during the collapse of the main Ming regime.
connections.note: The Qing dynasty was proclaimed in 1636. Southern Ming resistance and the consolidation of Qing rule continued after 1644.

connections.label: 1911–12 · revolution & abdication
connections.summary: Revolution and the Qing emperor’s abdication ended the imperial system and established republican rule.
connections.note: Political fragmentation and competing governments continued; this is not a claim of immediate stable national control.

connections.label: 1949 · civil war & rival governments
connections.summary: The PRC was proclaimed on the mainland, while the ROC government relocated to Taiwan.
connections.note: ROC administration in Taiwan began in 1945. These are changes in governments and territorial control; the map does not resolve sovereignty or recognition claims.

continuations.label: Golden Horde → Muscovy, USSR & modern states

connections.label: 1757–65 · Company gains in Bengal
connections.summary: Military victories and revenue rights expanded Company control in Bengal and adjoining regions.
connections.note: Mughal imperial titles survived until 1858. This was a regional expansion of colonial power, not a merger of the entire Mughal realm into the Company.

connections.label: 1818 · Peshwa defeated
connections.summary: The Company defeated the Peshwa in the Third Anglo-Maratha War.
connections.note: Several Maratha-ruled princely states continued afterward. The event did not annex or extinguish every Maratha institution.

connections.label: Rivalry, war & negotiation
connections.summary: Mughal and Maratha powers fought and negotiated over territory and authority.
connections.note: Their polities coexisted. An encounter does not imply that one people simply transformed into the other.

connections.label: 1858 · Crown replaces Company
connections.summary: The British Crown took over the Company’s governing role in India.
connections.note: The new colonial framework included provinces under direct administration and princely states with different arrangements.

connections.label: 1947 · independence & Partition
connections.summary: British rule ended as India and Pakistan became independent, accompanied by Partition.
connections.note: Pakistan initially included geographically separated eastern and western wings. The division involved mass displacement and violence; it was not a simple peaceful branching.

connections.label: 1971 · Bangladesh independence
connections.summary: East Pakistan became Bangladesh following the liberation war.
connections.note: West Pakistan continued as Pakistan. This marks a change in sovereignty, not the beginning of Bengali society or culture.

connectionMaps.title: West Africa: several kinds of connection

connections.label: Shared regions & changing power
connections.summary: Mali and Songhai participated in overlapping Sahelian trade networks and successively controlled some of the same centres.
connections.note: Mali continued as Songhai expanded. Gao and Timbuktu had different intervening rulers; this is not a single direct transfer or merger.

connections.label: 1591 · Moroccan invasion
connections.summary: Troops sent by the Moroccan sultan defeated Songhai’s army and seized major centres.
connections.note: Authority remained contested, and Songhai resistance and successor communities continued. Morocco did not simply become a new name for the entire Songhai realm.

connections.label: Late 1300s · ruling court relocates
connections.summary: The Sayfuwa court moved from Kanem to Bornu west of Lake Chad.
connections.note: The move changed the centre of dynastic power. Kanem and Bornu had distinct regional histories, and the transfer did not erase their populations.

connections.label: Dynastic links in oral tradition
connections.summary: Benin oral traditions connect the foundation of a new royal line with Ife and Oranmiyan.
connections.note: This is a stated tradition, not proof that Benin was simply a province of Ife or that the account supplies a precisely dated political merger.

continuations.label: Continue: later realms → Mali, Senegal & Nigeria
Sahel, Yoruba cities and the Gold Coast

connections.label: 1479 · dynastic union
connections.summary: The crowns of Castile and Aragon came under the joint rule of Isabella and Ferdinand.
connections.note: Their laws, institutions and territories remained distinct. This was not immediate administrative fusion into a modern centralised nation-state.

connections.label: From 1493 · colonial expansion
connections.summary: Spanish conquest and colonisation established changing jurisdictions in the Americas.
connections.note: The broad colonial node does not imply simultaneous conquest or uniform control, and Indigenous peoples and institutions persisted.

connections.label: From 1500 · arrival & colonisation
connections.summary: Portuguese arrival was followed by settlement and colonial rule in parts of Brazil.
connections.note: Large-scale settlement developed later. Brazil’s elevation to a kingdom in 1815 preceded independence in 1822.

connections.label: 1822 · independence
connections.summary: Brazil became independent under a monarchy before becoming a republic in 1889.
connections.note: Independence did not abolish slavery, which continued until 1888, or end all colonial social and economic relationships.

connections.label: 1821 · independence
connections.summary: The independence struggle ended Spanish rule over what became independent Mexico.
connections.note: Mexico’s initial imperial and later republican forms are grouped in the destination node; its peoples and cultures predate 1821.

connections.label: 1819–22 · republic & liberation
connections.summary: A new Colombian republic formed while independence forces liberated and incorporated territories.
connections.note: Present-day Ecuador joined after liberation in 1822. Other Spanish American independence movements had different trajectories.

connections.label: 1830–31 · union dissolves
connections.summary: Venezuela and Ecuador separated, while the central provinces organised as New Granada.
connections.note: The map shows the principal successor states. Their borders and later constitutional forms continued to change.

connections.label: 1858 · federal constitution
connections.summary: New Granada adopted a federal constitution and the name Granadine Confederation.
connections.note: The population and territory did not become a new people; the event concerns constitutional arrangements.

connections.label: 1863 · new federal constitution
connections.summary: After civil war, the Rionegro constitution established the United States of Colombia.
connections.note: Transitional governments and names intervened. This map selects the lasting 1863 constitutional settlement.

connections.label: 1886 · centralising constitution
connections.summary: A new constitution replaced the federal framework and restored the name Republic of Colombia.
connections.note: Later constitutional changes followed, including the 1991 constitution. Panama remained within Colombia until 1903.

connections.label: 1903 · Panama separates
connections.summary: Panama separated from Colombia and established an independent republic.
connections.note: Colombia continued as a state. US intervention and canal negotiations were central to the circumstances of separation.

connections.label: 1910 · monarchy overthrown
connections.summary: The monarchy was replaced by a republic in Portugal.
connections.note: The later frame includes dictatorship and democratic government after 1974. The empire’s overseas territories had separate paths to independence.

connectionMaps.title: From the Ilkhanate to modern Iran

connections.label: After 1335 · regional powers
connections.summary: The united Ilkhanate fragmented after Abu Sa‘id died. Jalayirids and Muzaffarids were among the regional powers that expanded.
connections.note: Only two examples are drawn. Chobanids, Sarbadars and others also ruled; no single dynasty inherited the whole realm. Some regional dynasties had earlier origins.

connections.label: 1370 · Timur takes Transoxiana
connections.summary: Timur established power in Transoxiana within the western Chagatai political setting, founding the Timurid realm.
connections.note: This concerns the western region. Eastern Chagataid and Moghulistan histories continued separately; it is not a transfer of the entire Chagatai Khanate.

connections.label: 1380s–90s · Timurid conquests
connections.summary: Timur’s armies invaded Iran and subordinated or defeated regional rulers. His conquests also extended well beyond former Ilkhanid lands.
connections.note: This was conquest after decades of regional rule. Jalayirid rulers sometimes returned; the drawing does not imply a peaceful, complete or permanent transfer.

connections.label: 1400s · western territorial gains
connections.summary: Qara Qoyunlu rulers gained Iraq and western Iranian territories claimed by Jalayirid and Timurid rulers.
connections.note: The connection selects western territories. Timurid courts continued in the east, and the expansion occurred in stages.

connections.label: 1526 · Babur founds Mughal rule
connections.summary: Babur, a Timurid prince, established Mughal rule in northern India after victory at Panipat.
connections.note: This marks a dynastic and cultural connection across regions, rather than the entire Timurid realm moving to or merging with India.

connections.label: 1467–69 · Aq Qoyunlu victories
connections.summary: Uzun Hasan’s victories over rival confederate and Timurid forces established Aq Qoyunlu supremacy over much of Iran and Iraq.
connections.note: Both Turkoman confederations had earlier histories. This arrow selects their contest for territory, rather than the origins of their communities.

connections.label: 1501–03 · Safavid victories
connections.summary: Ismail and his Qizilbash supporters defeated Aq Qoyunlu forces and established Safavid rule at Tabriz in 1501.
connections.note: Consolidation across Iran took years, and Aq Qoyunlu resistance continued. This is not an instantaneous transfer of every territory.

connections.label: 1722 · Isfahan falls
connections.summary: Hotak forces captured Isfahan and broke the central Safavid government’s power.
connections.note: Safavid claimants continued. Hotak occupation, Ottoman and Russian interventions, and Nader’s subsequent recovery made this a period of contested rule.

connections.label: 1736 · Nader takes the throne
connections.summary: After expelling Hotak forces and ruling through Safavid claimants, Nader took the throne and founded Afsharid rule.
connections.note: The 1736 change followed military recovery and political conflict. Nader’s large empire then fragmented after his death in 1747.

connections.label: After 1747 · competing realms
connections.summary: Afsharid rulers retained Khorasan while Karim Khan Zand consolidated much of western and southern Iran.
connections.note: These are selected branches, not all territories. Zand and Afsharid rule overlapped; a separate Durrani state also emerged in Afghanistan.

connections.label: 1794 · Zand defeat
connections.summary: Agha Mohammad Khan defeated the last Zand ruler, consolidating Qajar power after a prolonged struggle.
connections.note: Qajar starting dates vary with regional rule, conquest or coronation. The timeline uses 1789 as its conventional starting frame.

connections.label: 1796 · Khorasan conquered
connections.summary: Qajar forces brought the surviving Afsharid realm in Khorasan under their control.
connections.note: A parallel conquest during Qajar consolidation, after Zand rule had already ended elsewhere.

connections.label: 1925 · Pahlavi monarchy
connections.summary: Parliament ended Qajar sovereignty and a constituent assembly established Reza Shah’s monarchy.
connections.note: The 1921 coup preceded the dynastic replacement by four years. Government, institutions and territorial control changed across these stages.

connections.label: 1979 · revolution & republic
connections.summary: Revolution brought down the Pahlavi monarchy. The Islamic Republic was proclaimed on 1 April 1979 after a referendum.
connections.note: This was a major change of government within Iran. It does not imply a new people or an ethnically uniform successor society.

connectionMaps.title: West Africa: later realms, colonial borders & independence

connections.label: 1600s–1800s · later regional histories
connections.summary: Bamana, Massina and Toucouleur states later controlled parts of the upper and middle Niger regions.
connections.note: This indicates shared geography and changing centres of power over a long interval, not direct state succession or unchanged imperial borders.

connections.label: Late 1800s · French conquest
connections.summary: French forces conquered regional states and established changing colonial jurisdictions around the Niger.
connections.note: Resistance continued, and administrative borders shifted. Colonial rule was not a merger agreed by all the region’s peoples.

connections.label: 1897 · invasion of Benin
connections.summary: British forces invaded Benin City, deposed the Oba and looted the palace. Its territory was incorporated into colonial jurisdictions.
connections.note: Edo communities and the monarchy’s cultural history continued. The Southern Nigeria administration came later; the Benin kingdom is distinct from the modern Republic of Benin.

connections.label: Around 1900 · colonial partition
connections.summary: Colonial expansion incorporated part of the former Bornu region into British Northern Nigeria.
connections.note: Intervening warfare and partition also placed other Lake Chad territories under French and German rule. This regional connection is not the entire Bornu state changing directly into Nigeria.

connections.label: 1959–60 · federation & independence
connections.summary: The Sudanese Republic and Senegal formed the Mali Federation, which gained independence from France in June 1960.
connections.note: Senegal was a separate constituent with its own colonial history; it was not part of French Sudan. Only the Sudanese branch is shown above.

connections.label: 1914 · colonial amalgamation
connections.summary: British administrators joined northern and southern jurisdictions in the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria.
connections.note: This was colonial administrative unification of many societies, not the voluntary union of just Benin and Bornu.

connections.label: 1960 · federation dissolves
connections.summary: Senegal withdrew in August; the Sudanese Republic adopted the name Republic of Mali in September.
connections.note: The two modern states followed distinct histories. Their shared federation was not a revival of the medieval Mali Empire.

connections.label: 1960 · independence
connections.summary: Nigeria became independent of British rule.
connections.note: A republic followed in 1963. Later constitutional changes, military governments and the civil war belong within the modern history reader.

continuations.label: Sahel, Yoruba cities and the Gold Coast

connectionMaps.title: Golden Horde, Muscovy & Soviet successor states

connections.label: 1400s · several successor khanates
connections.summary: The Horde fragmented into competing regional khanates; Kazan and the Great Horde are two examples.
connections.note: Crimea, Astrakhan, Nogai and other formations had separate paths. The selected branches do not exhaust the Horde’s political or cultural legacy.

connections.label: 1480 · Ugra standoff
connections.summary: The standoff between Ivan III and the Great Horde is conventionally associated with the end of Muscovite tributary subordination.
connections.note: Muscovy already existed and was not a renamed Horde. The Great Horde continued until 1502 and other khanates survived separately.

connections.label: 1547 · Ivan IV crowned tsar
connections.summary: Ivan IV’s coronation as tsar marks the conventional beginning of the Russian tsardom.
connections.note: An evolving state and title, rather than the sudden creation of a new population or all its later territory.

connections.label: 1552 · Kazan conquered
connections.summary: Ivan IV’s forces conquered Kazan, incorporating its territory into the expanding tsardom.
connections.note: Tatar communities and traditions continued. Other khanates were conquered at different times or followed other paths.

connections.label: 1721 · imperial title
connections.summary: Peter I adopted the title of emperor after the Great Northern War.
connections.note: The change of title followed long state expansion and reform; it does not date the beginning of Russian communities or every imperial territory.

connections.label: 1917–22 · revolutions, war & new union
connections.summary: The monarchy fell in 1917. Revolution, civil war and Bolshevik consolidation preceded the formation of the USSR in 1922.
connections.note: Several former imperial territories became independent. The Soviet Union was formed by constituent republics, not simply by renaming the whole Russian Empire.

connections.label: 1991 · fifteen independent states
connections.summary: The Soviet Union dissolved and its constituent republics became or re-established independent states.
connections.note: This preview shows three of fifteen states. All fifteen appear in the Soviet regional maps, accessible through Maps & coverage. Regional groupings are navigation aids, not intermediate successor states.

continuations.label: Soviet dissolution · Russia and eastern Europe

connectionMaps.title: Sudan and South Sudan: kingdoms, conquest and independence

connections.label: Context: later Nubian kingdoms
connections.summary: After Meroe’s decline, several kingdoms developed in the Nubian Nile region.
connections.note: Context link, not a documented division of one empire into three states or an assertion of unchanged institutions; Christianisation followed during the sixth century.

connections.label: Nobatia and Makuria united
connections.dates: By the early medieval period · precise date uncertain
connections.summary: Nobatia came under a ruler shared with Makuria, while retaining regional institutions.
connections.note: The date and circumstances are uncertain; this does not imply that Alodia joined them.

connections.label: Context: changing regional rule
connections.summary: The Funj sultanate rose in the central Nile region after the decline of Alodian authority.
connections.note: Context, not a secure direct succession: later chronicles associate Soba’s destruction with 1504, but the excavated city shows earlier decline, and the chronology and agents of the political transformation remain disputed.

connections.label: Egyptian conquest ends Funj rule
connections.summary: Forces sent by Muhammad Ali conquered the Funj sultanate and established Egyptian administration.
connections.note: This was conquest and new colonial government, not a peaceful dynastic inheritance; control over other Sudanese territories expanded at different times.

connections.label: Egyptian territorial expansion
connections.summary: Muhammad Ali’s Egyptian government sent armies south and imposed rule over Sudanese territories.
connections.note: The Egyptian dynasty operated within a changing Ottoman imperial framework; the term Turco-Egyptian does not imply all inhabitants were Turkish or Egyptian.

connections.label: Mahdist revolt and capture of Khartoum
connections.summary: The Mahdist movement defeated Egyptian government forces and captured Khartoum in January 1885.
connections.note: The revolt began before the capture; Egyptian and British forces retained some peripheral positions, and not every community supported the Mahdist government.

connections.label: Anglo-Egyptian conquest
connections.summary: British-led Anglo-Egyptian armies defeated the Mahdist state, and the 1899 agreements established joint colonial rule.
connections.note: The decisive defeat at Omdurman occurred in 1898; fighting continued into 1899, so military conquest and the legal creation of the condominium are distinct stages.

connections.label: British-led colonial administration
connections.summary: Sudan was administered under a formal Anglo-Egyptian condominium in which British authority predominated.
connections.note: This was legally distinct from simply annexing Sudan as an ordinary British colony; Egyptian claims and participation persisted.

connections.label: Sudan becomes independent
connections.summary: Sudan became independent of the Anglo-Egyptian condominium.
connections.note: The independent state initially included the territory that later became South Sudan; independence did not resolve internal conflicts or guarantee one continuous constitutional order.

connections.label: South Sudan secedes after referendum
connections.summary: South Sudan became an independent state after the January 2011 referendum.
connections.note: Sudan continued as a state after the separation; this was not the replacement of Sudan by South Sudan, and it does not imply that all boundary questions were resolved.

continuations.label: Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers
Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states

connectionMaps.title: Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers

connections.label: Trade, migration and conflict
connections.summary: Nubian societies and Egyptian kingdoms exchanged goods and people and fought over access and authority along the Nile.
connections.note: The relationship changed direction over time; neither region was permanently subordinate or culturally uniform.

connections.label: Kushite pharaohs in Egypt
connections.summary: Kushite kings extended their rule into Egypt and formed its Twenty-fifth Dynasty.
connections.note: This selected episode sits within both broad timeline frames; Kushite rule did not begin all Egyptian or Nubian history.

connections.label: Persian conquest of Egypt
connections.summary: Cambyses defeated Egypt’s last Twenty-sixth-Dynasty ruler and brought Egypt into Achaemenid rule.
connections.note: Egypt later regained independence before a second Persian conquest; this was not uninterrupted Persian government until Alexander.

connections.label: Alexander enters Egypt
connections.summary: Alexander took Egypt from Achaemenid control during his campaigns against the Persian Empire.
connections.note: The Persian Empire and Alexander’s campaigns extended far beyond Egypt. Egyptian communities and institutions continued.

connections.label: Ptolemaic kingship
connections.summary: The struggles among Alexander’s successors produced Ptolemaic kingship in Egypt.
connections.note: Ptolemy governed Egypt before adopting the royal title; other successor kingdoms emerged elsewhere.

connections.label: Egypt annexed by Rome
connections.summary: Octavian’s conquest ended Ptolemaic royal government and placed Egypt under Roman administration.
connections.note: Annexation occurred before the conventional imperial starting date of 27 BCE. Roman government did not end Egyptian culture.

connections.label: Eastern Roman government
connections.summary: Egypt remained within the Roman state as its eastern imperial administration centred on Constantinople.
connections.note: This is overlapping periodisation within a continuing empire, not an Egyptian state newly founded or a clean cultural break in 330 or 395.

connections.label: Arab-Muslim conquest
connections.summary: Arab-Muslim armies conquered Byzantine Egypt and established government based at Fustat.
connections.note: Military and administrative change did not cause immediate universal conversion; Coptic Christian communities continued.

connections.label: Egypt under Umayyad rule
connections.summary: Egypt became a province of the Damascus-based Umayyad caliphate.
connections.note: This was a change of ruling authority within the early Islamic state, not the origin of Egypt’s population or all its traditions.

connections.label: Abbasid provincial rule
connections.summary: The Abbasid revolution brought Egypt under the new caliphal dynasty.
connections.note: Egypt’s provincial connection should not be read as uninterrupted direct Baghdad control throughout the Abbasid period.

connections.label: Autonomous and restored governments
connections.summary: Egypt passed through Tulunid government, restored direct Abbasid rule and Ikhshidid government.
connections.note: These are three successive arrangements grouped in one explicitly labelled transition frame, with continuing Abbasid religious allegiance.

connections.label: Fatimids conquer Egypt
connections.summary: Fatimid forces took Egypt and established Cairo, later making it their capital.
connections.note: The Fatimid caliphate began in North Africa in 909; 969 dates its Egyptian expansion rather than the foundation of the dynasty.

connections.label: Saladin ends Fatimid rule
connections.summary: Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate and established Ayyubid government in Egypt.
connections.note: A political and religious reorientation did not replace all inhabitants or erase Fatimid institutions and artistic traditions.

connections.label: Mamluks take power in Egypt
connections.summary: Mamluk leaders overthrew the last independent Ayyubid sultan in Egypt and established their own sultanate.
connections.note: Ayyubid branches continued in Syria and elsewhere; the Egyptian event does not end every Ayyubid polity in 1250.

connections.label: Ottoman conquest
connections.summary: Ottoman campaigns defeated the Mamluk sultanate and incorporated Syria and Egypt into the Ottoman Empire.
connections.note: Mamluk elites and institutions persisted after the sultanate ended; Ottoman rule had regional variation.

connections.label: Muhammad Ali appointed
connections.summary: Muhammad Ali became Ottoman governor of Egypt in 1805 and founded a dynasty whose hereditary rule was formally recognised in 1841.
connections.note: This followed French occupation and renewed Ottoman intervention; growing Egyptian autonomy did not immediately end Ottoman suzerainty.

connections.label: British occupation
connections.summary: Britain occupied Egypt while the Muhammad Ali dynasty remained in office.
connections.note: Occupation, dynastic rule and Ottoman suzerainty overlapped; Britain declared a protectorate only in 1914.

connections.label: Limited independence recognised
connections.summary: Britain ended its formal protectorate and recognised Egypt as a sovereign state while reserving several matters for later agreement.
connections.note: British military presence and restrictions remained; this was not complete immediate withdrawal.

connections.label: Monarchy ends; republic declared
connections.summary: The 1952 revolution was followed by abolition of the monarchy and proclamation of a republic in 1953.
connections.note: The destination frame begins with limited independence in 1922 and includes this later constitutional rupture; the two timeline blocks intentionally overlap.

connections.label: Augustus and imperial government
connections.summary: Octavian received the title Augustus as Roman government took the form conventionally called the Principate.
connections.note: The conventional start of the Roman Empire did not create a new Egyptian population or end every republican institution.

continuations.label: Sudan and South Sudan: kingdoms, conquest and independence
Horn of Africa and the Indian Ocean coast
Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states

connectionMaps.title: Horn of Africa and the Indian Ocean coast

connections.label: Trade and Christian networks
connections.summary: Aksum and the eastern Roman world participated in commercial, religious and artistic networks across the Red Sea and eastern Mediterranean.
connections.note: Contact did not mean Aksum was a Byzantine province or that African Christianity had only one origin.

connections.label: Later highland Christian kingdoms
connections.summary: Later highland kingdoms including the Zagwe preserved and developed Christian traditions after Aksumite political power declined.
connections.note: The intervening political sequence is incompletely known: this is a qualified cultural and regional connection, not proven unbroken dynastic succession.

connections.label: Solomonic dynasty takes power
connections.summary: Yekuno Amlak displaced Zagwe rule and established the dynasty conventionally called Solomonic.
connections.note: The dynasty’s claim to descend from biblical Solomon is a legitimising tradition, not an independently demonstrated genealogy.

connections.label: Monarchy overthrown
connections.summary: The Derg deposed Haile Selassie and replaced imperial government with military rule.
connections.note: This begins a broad post-monarchical frame containing later changes of regime, not a single uninterrupted republic.

connections.label: Eritrean independence
connections.summary: Eritrean military victory and a UN-supervised referendum led to recognised independence from Ethiopia.
connections.note: Ethiopia continued as a state; the modern Eritrean border and independence process are not a simple redivision of ancient Aksum.

connections.label: Gold and Indian Ocean trade
connections.summary: Great Zimbabwe was connected through long-distance trade to the Indian Ocean coast, with Kilwa coins among its imported finds.
connections.note: Goods travelled through networks and intermediaries; an imported coin is not proof that Great Zimbabwe was ruled by Kilwa or that every shipment went directly between the two cities.

connections.label: Portuguese fort and occupation
connections.summary: Portuguese forces established a fort at Kilwa during their expansion along the East African coast.
connections.note: Their occupation was limited and contested; the Portuguese kingdom did not originate in Kilwa, and Swahili communities continued.

connections.label: Omani and Zanzibar authority
connections.summary: Omani Busaidi rulers based in Zanzibar later exercised authority at Kilwa and adapted its buildings for their administration.
connections.note: This selected later episode follows intervening local histories; coastal authority varied and does not imply all Swahili cities formed one uninterrupted empire.

connections.label: German mainland expansion
connections.summary: German colonial expansion displaced local authorities and acquired control of mainland coastal jurisdictions associated with Zanzibar.
connections.note: The mainland and island sultanate had different legal histories; Zanzibar itself did not become part of German East Africa.

connections.label: Postwar partition and mandate
connections.summary: The postwar division of German East Africa placed the mainland territory later called Tanganyika under British administration.
connections.note: Rwanda and Burundi went to Belgian administration and the Kionga Triangle to Portugal; Tanganyika was only one successor jurisdiction.

connections.label: Tanganyika independent
connections.summary: Tanganyika became independent from British administration.
connections.note: It became a republic in 1962 before union with Zanzibar; the event does not date the beginning of its peoples or communities.

connections.label: Tanganyika and Zanzibar unite
connections.summary: Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined to form the union later named Tanzania.
connections.note: Zanzibar retained institutions within the union; its independence in 1963 and revolution in January 1964 preceded the agreement.

connections.label: Coastal protectorate administered
connections.summary: Britain administered the Sultan of Zanzibar’s mainland coastal protectorate together with colonial Kenya.
connections.note: The coastal protectorate had a legal status distinct from the inland colony until independence; the edge does not place all Zanzibar under Kenyan government.

connections.label: Kenya independent
connections.summary: Kenya became independent of British rule and the separate coastal arrangement ended.
connections.note: A republic followed in 1964; the modern state joined regions with diverse earlier histories.

connections.label: Independence and revolution
connections.summary: Zanzibar became independent under a sultanate before the January 1964 revolution replaced the monarchy with a republic.
connections.note: This concerns the islands and their government, not all territories formerly influenced by Omani or Zanzibar rulers along the mainland coast.

continuations.label: Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states
Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers

connectionMaps.title: Sahel, Yoruba cities and the Gold Coast

connections.label: Changing Sahelian centres
connections.summary: Mali rose within western Sahelian trading and political networks that had earlier sustained Ghana/Wagadu.
connections.note: This is regional reconfiguration, not proof that Ghana uniformly merged into Mali on one date; Ghana’s decline and Mali’s expansion were uneven.

connections.label: Inland Niger urban networks
connections.summary: Jenne-jeno and the surrounding Inland Niger Delta formed part of the commercial and political landscape of the Mali era.
connections.note: The archaeological city and later Jenne are distinct settlements; urban communities had their own histories and were not created by imperial conquest.

connections.label: Later Jenne under Songhai
connections.summary: Songhai expanded its authority over the Inland Niger Delta and later Jenne after the main occupation phase of Jenne-jeno.
connections.note: The plotted Jenne-jeno block ends around 1400; this link explicitly follows the neighbouring city and regional urban history rather than claiming the old settlement remained the same imperial capital.

connections.label: Royal traditions connect Yoruba cities
connections.summary: Ife and Oyo are linked in Yoruba royal traditions associated with Oranmiyan.
connections.note: Oral dynastic traditions are not proof that Oyo simply descended as a state from Ife; the Oyo timeline selects its much later imperial expansion.

connections.label: Niger-to-Ife trade routes
connections.summary: Oyo channelled goods from Niger-region trading networks towards Ife and other Yoruba centres.
connections.note: This concerns the city’s earlier commercial history rather than dating the beginning of the imperial expansion block; no political merger is implied.

connections.label: Asante annexation
connections.summary: Britain annexed Asante and established colonial government under an official responsible to the Gold Coast governor.
connections.note: Ashanti had a separate colonial legal status, and the Asante monarchy and communities continued; this was not annexation to the Gold Coast Colony itself.

connections.label: Ghana independent
connections.summary: The Gold Coast, Ashanti, Northern Territories and British Togoland became independent as Ghana.
connections.note: The four territories had different legal histories; modern Ghana is geographically and politically distinct from medieval Ghana/Wagadu.

connections.label: Archaeological heritage, not succession
connections.summary: Nok terracottas discovered in central Nigeria became part of the archaeological and museum heritage of modern Nigeria.
connections.note: This is a heritage and geographical link only: there is no established direct dynastic succession from Nok culture to the Nigerian state or to a named later kingdom. The discovery began before independence.

connections.label: One jurisdiction within the wider era
connections.summary: Colonial Nigeria is one specific British jurisdiction within the atlas’s broader African colonial-period overview.
connections.note: This is a period-to-example relationship, not a merger or a claim that all Africa had the same rulers or independence date.

continuations.label: West Africa: later realms, colonial borders & independence
West Africa: several kinds of connection
Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states

connectionMaps.title: Kongo, Atlantic contacts and southern African states

connections.label: Diplomacy and Christian exchange
connections.summary: Portuguese contact with Kongo led to diplomacy and religious and artistic exchanges between their rulers and communities.
connections.note: Early contact did not mean immediate Portuguese conquest or an equal relationship throughout later centuries; the slave trade and colonial warfare transformed the relationship.

connections.label: Colonial expansion in the Kongo region
connections.summary: Portuguese colonial expansion absorbed the southern Kongo region into Angola as Kongo political authority weakened.
connections.note: This shows only the Angolan branch: Kongo communities also live in both modern Congos, and the colonial territory was not simply the old kingdom renamed. No claim is made that all Kongo lands passed to Portugal.

connections.label: Angola independent
connections.summary: Portuguese rule ended as Angola became independent amid fighting between rival nationalist movements.
connections.note: This was not a peaceful agreed merger or the restoration of Kongo; independence was followed by civil war.

connections.label: Mbanza Kongo: living heritage
connections.summary: The former Kongo capital, Mbanza Kongo, survives as a cultural and spiritual heritage site in present-day Angola.
connections.note: A heritage link is not a claim that Angola alone inherits Kongo peoples, culture or territory.

connections.label: British occupation of the Cape
connections.summary: Britain occupied the Cape during wars with European rivals and retained control after its second occupation.
connections.note: The Cape settlement began under Dutch rule in 1652, and colonial expansion involved African dispossession and resistance.

connections.label: Four colonies form the Union
connections.summary: The Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies joined in the Union of South Africa.
connections.note: The Union was a self-governing British dominion dominated by white political power and excluded most South Africans; this was not universal democratic unification.

connections.label: Transition to universal suffrage
connections.summary: South Africa held its first national democratic election based on universal adult suffrage under an interim constitution.
connections.note: This was a constitutional and political transformation within the state; earlier segregation and apartheid are not equivalent to the later democratic order.

connections.label: Different paths out of colonial rule
connections.summary: Ghana, Kenya and Angola illustrate separate decolonisation processes in different years and colonial systems.
connections.note: The starting box is a broad era, not a state that split into these three countries; these are examples, not an exhaustive list of African independence movements.

continuations.label: Horn of Africa and the Indian Ocean coast
Sahel, Yoruba cities and the Gold Coast
Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers

connectionMaps.title: Mesoamerica & the Caribbean

connections.label: Ancient objects reused
connections.summary: Mexica offerings included an Olmec mask made roughly two millennia earlier.
connections.note: A documented reuse of ancient art, not evidence of a continuous Olmec–Aztec empire.

connections.label: Exchange & artistic connections
connections.summary: Teotihuacan interacted with Maya capitals including Tikal and Copán, with objects and artistic forms crossing regional boundaries.
connections.note: Different cities maintained different relationships; this is not a claim that all Maya lands belonged to Teotihuacan.

connections.label: Communities continue
connections.summary: Maya communities continued long after the Classic-period transformation of their cities.
connections.note: A cultural continuation, not a new state founded in 900 CE.

connections.label: Conquest of Tenochtitlan
connections.summary: Spanish forces and Indigenous allies conquered Tenochtitlan, followed by the development of New Spain.
connections.note: The colonial administration was established in stages; conquest did not end Nahua peoples or all Indigenous resistance.

connections.label: Mexican independence
connections.summary: Mexican independence ended Spanish rule in the core mainland territory represented by this New Spain entry.
connections.note: New Spain extended beyond modern Mexico; later empires, republics and territorial changes followed.

connections.label: French colony
connections.summary: French colonial rule developed in western Hispaniola as Saint-Domingue.
connections.note: This was not all of Hispaniola; the French monarchy later fell while colonial rule continued.

connections.label: Revolution & independence
connections.summary: A revolution against enslavement and French colonial power culminated in Haitian independence in 1804.
connections.note: The conflict involved shifting alliances and foreign intervention; later occupations and political changes are not excluded.

connectionMaps.description: Artistic exchange, living Maya communities, conquest in central Mexico and Haiti’s anti-slavery revolution. Separate branches do not imply one regional empire.

connectionMaps.title: Andes & Río de la Plata

connections.label: Artistic interaction
connections.summary: Wari artists interacted with Nasca traditions and developed new artistic forms.
connections.note: Interaction and influence do not mean that every Nasca community was replaced by one Wari government.

connections.label: Shared visual traditions
connections.summary: Wari art developed in dialogue with Tiwanaku religious imagery and visual traditions.
connections.note: These were distinct, contemporary powers; the arrow represents cultural interaction, not dynastic succession.

connections.label: North-coast artistic heritage
connections.summary: Chimú artists inherited and reworked earlier Moche cultural and artistic traditions.
connections.note: This is a long artistic relationship across intervening regional developments, not an immediate political handover.

connections.label: Earlier roads & practices
connections.dates: Earlier traditions · adapted by the 15th century
connections.summary: Inca rulers adapted road-building and other practices developed by earlier Wari and Tiwanaku societies.
connections.note: Several centuries and many local histories separate these periods; this is inheritance of practices, not direct state succession.

connections.label: Inca expansion
connections.summary: Inca expansion incorporated the Chimú kingdom into a much larger imperial system.
connections.note: Incorporation did not erase north-coast communities or their craft traditions.

connections.label: Spanish invasion
connections.summary: Spanish invaders exploited the Inca road system during conquest and imposed a new colonial order.
connections.note: The capture of Atahualpa did not instantly conquer the entire Andes; resistance and Indigenous communities continued.

connections.label: Living Andean traditions
connections.summary: Quechua-speaking communities have maintained and transformed traditions associated with the Inca world.
connections.note: Cultural continuation is not continuous imperial sovereignty or a claim that all Quechua speakers share one identity.

connections.label: Peruvian independence
connections.summary: San Martín proclaimed Peruvian independence in Lima in July 1821.
connections.note: A declaration did not end the war immediately or settle every territory.

connections.label: New viceroyalty
connections.summary: The Río de la Plata viceroyalty was created from territories previously administered within the Viceroyalty of Peru.
connections.note: The plotted colonial Argentina frame begins earlier; this arrow specifically concerns the 1776 administrative reorganisation.

connections.label: United Provinces declare independence
connections.summary: The Congress of Tucumán declared the independence of the United Provinces in South America on 9 July 1816.
connections.note: Argentina later developed through conflicts and constitutional changes; the whole former viceroyalty did not become Argentina.

connectionMaps.description: Andean cultural interactions, Spanish conquest, colonial reorganisation and selected independence histories. Caral is shown without an unsupported succession arrow.

connectionMaps.title: North American communities & changing borders

connections.label: Long-distance exchange
connections.summary: Caddo exchange routes linked their communities with distant centres including Cahokia.
connections.note: Trade connections do not imply shared political government or direct descent from Cahokia.

connections.label: Migration & descendants
connections.summary: People leaving the Chaco region joined communities in several directions, contributing to multiple present-day Pueblo populations.
connections.note: Exact migration routes vary; this does not identify one exclusive heir to Chaco.

connections.label: Colonisation & resistance
connections.summary: Spanish colonisation imposed demands on Pueblo communities, which organised a major revolt in 1680.
connections.note: Pueblo peoples persisted; Spanish control was interrupted and reconquest was gradual and contested.

connections.label: Mexico gains independence
connections.summary: New Mexico became part of independent Mexico after Spanish colonial rule ended.
connections.note: A change in state jurisdiction did not end Pueblo communities or their own institutions.

connections.label: War & territorial cession
connections.summary: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the U.S.–Mexican War and transferred extensive northern territory to the United States.
connections.note: Mexico continued as an independent state; Indigenous nations were not extinguished by this interstate boundary change.

connections.label: Land cession & forced removal
connections.summary: A Caddo removal treaty with the United States was followed by dispersal and repeated forced removals.
connections.note: This links communities to the state that dispossessed them, not a claim that they ceased to exist or became its predecessor.

connectionMaps.description: Caddo exchange networks, Chaco’s descendant communities and later colonial and interstate boundary changes. Indigenous histories continue.

connectionMaps.title: Pacific voyaging, communities & modern states

connections.label: Settlement before Tuʻi Tonga
connections.dates: Settlement c. 1100–800 BCE · later chiefly societies
connections.summary: Lapita-associated voyagers settled Tonga long before the Tuʻi Tonga chiefly line developed.
connections.note: A settlement and cultural background link, not a claim that the Tuʻi Tonga polity existed in the Bronze Age.

connections.label: Lapita settlement
connections.summary: Lapita-associated voyagers settled Fiji, forming part of its long and changing island histories.
connections.note: Material-culture associations do not make all Pacific peoples one ethnicity or state.

connections.label: Polynesian cultural development
connections.dates: Over many centuries · eastward voyages c. 1000 CE
connections.summary: Polynesian cultures emerged among western island communities before voyages expanded into East Polynesia.
connections.note: This compresses multiple stages through Fiji, Tonga and Samoa; it does not draw a direct Lapita-era voyage to every eastern island.

connections.label: Polynesian settlement
connections.summary: East Polynesian voyagers settled Rapa Nui, where distinctive monumental traditions developed.
connections.note: Dates remain approximate; this does not imply political rule from Tonga.

connections.label: Voyages to Aotearoa
connections.summary: Migrants from East Polynesian islands became the ancestors of Māori communities in Aotearoa.
connections.note: Many voyages and traditions are involved, rather than a single great fleet or an overseas empire.

connections.label: Kingdom consolidation
connections.summary: George Tupou I united the Tongan islands before the 1875 constitution established modern constitutional institutions.
connections.note: A transformation of chiefly and state authority, not an unchanged Tuʻi Tonga empire persisting to the present.

connections.label: Cession & British rule
connections.summary: The 1874 cession established British colonial rule in Fiji.
connections.note: The islands already contained Indigenous societies; colonial administration did not originate or replace their culture.

connections.label: Fijian independence
connections.summary: Fiji became independent from Britain in 1970.
connections.note: Later constitutional changes and coups are included in the broad modern-state entry.

connections.label: Chiefly traditions continue
connections.summary: Nan Madol remains connected to Pohnpei ceremonial traditions and the authority of the Nahnmwarki.
connections.note: Continuing institutions and heritage are distinct from an uninterrupted Saudeleur state.

connections.label: State in a federation
connections.summary: Pohnpei joined the constitutional federation that became the Federated States of Micronesia.
connections.note: The modern federation also includes Chuuk, Kosrae and Yap; centuries of changing colonial administrations lie between Nan Madol and this constitutional transition.

connections.label: A living culture
connections.summary: Rapa Nui people maintain a living relationship with their island and cultural heritage.
connections.note: The end of the selected monumental-phase bar is not the end of Rapa Nui society.

connections.label: 1888 agreement with Chile
connections.summary: The Agreement of Wills formalised Rapa Nui’s incorporation into the Republic of Chile.
connections.note: This state relationship did not end Rapa Nui identity or local titles and authority; its meanings and consequences remain contested.

connectionMaps.description: Voyaging and cultural connections alongside selected modern constitutional transitions. These are not branches of a single Pacific empire.

connectionMaps.title: Australia & Aotearoa New Zealand

connections.label: First Fleet & colonies
connections.summary: Britain established a convict settlement at Sydney Cove in 1788, followed by expanding and separate colonies.
connections.note: The continent already belonged to many Indigenous nations; British control developed unevenly.

connections.label: Colonisation & dispossession
connections.summary: British settlement disrupted and dispossessed Aboriginal communities while their cultures and resistance continued.
connections.note: The direction marks an encounter with an imposed colonial order, not cultural replacement or extinction.

connections.label: Six colonies federate
connections.summary: Six British colonies united in the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.
connections.note: Federation did not itself complete constitutional independence or end Indigenous histories.

connections.label: British colonial administration
connections.summary: The British Crown proclaimed sovereignty in 1840 and established New Zealand as a separate colony in 1841.
connections.note: A proclamation of sovereignty is not equivalent to universal Māori consent or immediate control of all territory.

connections.label: Te Tiriti / Treaty of Waitangi
connections.summary: Māori rangatira and the Crown signed a treaty whose Māori and English texts differ in meaning.
connections.note: This is a treaty relationship with disputed sovereignty and obligations, not a merger that ended Māori peoples or authority.

connections.label: Dominion & later autonomy
connections.summary: New Zealand gained Dominion status in 1907, adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947 and removed remaining British legislative authority in 1986.
connections.note: These were different stages, not one complete independence event in 1907.

connectionMaps.description: Continuing Indigenous histories, British colonisation, Australian federation and New Zealand’s treaty and constitutional transitions.

connectionMaps.title: China · early cultures and dynasties

connections.label: Jade traditions endure
connections.summary: Liangzhu jade traditions influenced later Bronze Age centres, including late Shang Anyang.
connections.note: This cultural legacy crosses a substantial chronological gap; it is not a claim of direct dynastic succession or a Liangzhu–Xia state lineage.

connections.label: Traditional sequence
connections.summary: Later histories place Xia before Shang in a dynastic sequence.
connections.note: Xia remains unconfirmed in contemporary inscriptions; this dashed link records historiography, not a securely attested conquest or identification of Erlitou.

connections.label: Zhou conquest
connections.summary: Zhou forces overthrew the Shang ruling house.
connections.note: The conventional date does not imply that Shang populations and cultural practices disappeared.

connections.label: Qin consolidation
connections.summary: Qin ended the Zhou royal house and later conquered the other Warring States before proclaiming an empire.
connections.note: Zhou kingship ended in 256 BCE; imperial unification followed in 221 BCE, so the two plotted period boundaries do not mark a single instantaneous transfer.

connections.label: Rebellion and Han rule
connections.summary: After Qin collapse and civil war, Liu Bang established Han rule and took the imperial title in 202 BCE.
connections.note: Han dates conventionally begin with Liu Bang’s kingdom in 206 BCE; this is a change of regime, not uninterrupted Qin government.

connections.label: Han breaks apart
connections.summary: The end of Han rule gave way to competing kingdoms and subsequent northern and southern dynasties.
connections.note: The Age of Division is a period containing many governments, including a brief Western Jin reunification, rather than a successor state.

connections.label: Sui reunification
connections.summary: Sui replaced Northern Zhou in 581 and conquered the southern Chen in 589.
connections.note: Northern and southern political consolidation occurred in stages; the period and dynasty intentionally overlap.

connections.label: Tang takes power
connections.summary: Li Yuan established the Tang dynasty amid the collapse of Sui authority.
connections.note: Early Tang consolidation continued after the dynastic proclamation.

connections.label: Competing realms
connections.summary: Tang collapse left successive northern dynasties and concurrent southern kingdoms.
connections.note: This umbrella period does not represent one united government or just five rulers of all China.

connections.label: Song consolidation
connections.summary: The Song foundation in 960 was followed by campaigns against several remaining independent kingdoms.
connections.note: Other states including Liao continued outside Song rule; 960 did not reunify all territory in modern China.

connectionMaps.note: Archaeological influence, later tradition and political change are distinct links. Continue from Song in the existing Mongols and China map for Yuan, Ming, Qing, ROC, PRC and Taiwan-era histories.

continuations.label: Later China: Mongol conquest and modern states
Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connectionMaps.title: Japan · cultures, courts and shogunates

connections.label: Agriculture and migration
connections.summary: Wet-rice farming and continental exchanges transformed communities while some Jōmon practices continued.
connections.note: These are overlapping regional archaeological classifications, not two empires or the replacement of an entire people; the transition has no single nationwide date.

connections.label: Regional state formation
connections.summary: Growing regional powers and monumental tomb building accompanied the emergence of Yamato political dominance.
connections.note: This is a long social and political process; the Kofun-period boundary is not an exact founding date for Japan or one securely identified conquest.

connections.label: Court moves to Nara
connections.summary: The court moved its capital from the Asuka region to Nara.
connections.note: A change of capital and historical period within developing court institutions, not a new people replacing the Yamato population.

connections.label: Capital at Heian
connections.summary: The imperial capital moved to Heian-kyō, present-day Kyoto.
connections.note: The court first moved through the Nagaoka capital, 784–794; the label condenses that transition.

connections.label: Embassies and statecraft
connections.summary: Court missions and imported models connected Tang China with Japan’s Nara court.
connections.note: Japanese missions to Tang China began earlier, in 630; this edge selects exchanges during the Nara period (710–794). Diplomatic and cultural exchange did not make Japan a province of Tang China.

connections.label: Warrior government
connections.summary: Minamoto victory in 1185 established a military regime at Kamakura, with Yoritomo named shogun in 1192.
connections.note: The imperial court continued; this marks a shift in political power rather than the end of the imperial institution.

connections.label: Failed invasions · 1274 & 1281
connections.summary: Mongol-led Yuan expeditions attacked Japan but failed to establish control.
connections.note: This is a conflict link, not successful conquest. Goryeo and other forces participated; Japan was not incorporated into Yuan rule.

connections.label: Shogunate overthrown
connections.summary: Go-Daigo and his supporters overthrew the Kamakura shogunate.
connections.note: The imperial revival was brief, while conflict over rival courts continued after it ended.

connections.label: Ashikaga ascendancy
connections.summary: Ashikaga Takauji displaced Go-Daigo in Kyoto and subsequently became shogun.
connections.note: Northern and Southern courts competed until 1392; this is not a peaceful complete transfer of national control.

connections.label: Nobunaga takes Kyoto
connections.summary: Nobunaga entered Kyoto and later removed the last Ashikaga shogun.
connections.note: Regional wars and Toyotomi consolidation followed; the Sengoku conflicts overlap these named periods.

connections.label: Tokugawa government
connections.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu’s ascendancy led to a shogunate based in Edo.
connections.note: The imperial court and regional domains continued, and Toyotomi resistance was not eliminated until 1615.

connections.label: Meiji Restoration
connections.summary: The Tokugawa shogunate fell and a new government claimed to restore imperial authority.
connections.note: Modern Japan includes later imperial, wartime, occupation and constitutional phases; 1868 is not Japan’s founding.

connectionMaps.note: Archaeological periods are not states, and courts and shogunates could coexist. Cross-map Japanese expansion and Korea appear in Korea’s map.

continuations.label: Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connectionMaps.title: Korea · dynasties, colonisation and division

connections.label: Mongol invasions
connections.summary: Mongol invasions devastated Goryeo before negotiated submission and later close dynastic ties.
connections.note: Goryeo retained its royal house; invasion and subordinate relations did not simply turn it into a replacement Chinese dynasty.

connections.label: Court and marriage ties
connections.summary: Goryeo and Yuan courts developed close political relations, including royal intermarriage.
connections.note: These unequal ties coexisted with Goryeo institutions; later Goryeo rulers contested Yuan influence.

connections.label: New royal dynasty
connections.summary: Yi Seonggye deposed the last Goryeo ruler and founded Joseon.
connections.note: A change of ruling house and political institutions within Korean history, not the origin of Korean people.

connections.label: Empire proclaimed
connections.summary: Gojong adopted the imperial title and renamed the state the Korean Empire.
connections.note: The timeline’s broad Joseon block extends to 1910 by dynastic convention; this node distinguishes the state-name change within that royal house.

connections.label: Japanese annexation
connections.summary: Japan annexed Korea after extending control through an imposed protectorate.
connections.note: Japan’s own government continued; the two source nodes identify the colonising state and the annexed Korean monarchy, not two equal partners in a union.

connections.label: Liberation and occupations
connections.summary: Japanese surrender ended colonial rule and Soviet and U.S. forces occupied zones divided at the 38th parallel.
connections.note: The military division was imposed amid liberation and did not immediately create the two states established in 1948.

connections.label: Republic established
connections.summary: The Republic of Korea was established in the southern zone.
connections.note: This followed a contested state-building process; the zone-to-state link does not imply unanimous consent or settled all-Korea sovereignty.

connections.label: DPRK established
connections.summary: The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was established in the northern zone.
connections.note: Both new governments claimed to represent Korea; this map describes administration without adjudicating those competing claims.

connections.label: War and armistice
connections.summary: North Korean invasion opened a war involving both Korean states and international forces, ending in an armistice.
connections.note: A conflict link, not state succession; the armistice suspended fighting and did not itself provide a final peace settlement.

connectionMaps.note: This map follows the histories already in the atlas and does not claim to start Korean history with Goryeo. Division in 1945 and state establishment in 1948 are separate events.

continuations.label: Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connectionMaps.title: Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connections.label: Buddhist journeys
connections.summary: The Tang-era monk Yijing studied and translated Buddhist texts at Srivijaya while travelling between China and India.
connections.note: A scholarly and maritime connection, not Chinese annexation or a single route followed by every traveller.

connections.label: Chola naval raid
connections.summary: Chola forces raided Srivijaya’s maritime realm.
connections.note: A raid and episode of warfare, not proof that Chola permanently replaced Srivijaya across its trading network.

connections.label: Mongol expedition repelled
connections.summary: A Yuan expedition into Java was defeated during the conflicts surrounding Majapahit’s foundation.
connections.note: The invaders did not establish lasting Yuan rule; the state’s foundation involved local struggles beyond this selected encounter.

connections.label: Literary legacy
connections.summary: Modern Indonesia adopted its national motto from the Majapahit-era poem Kakawin Sutasoma.
connections.note: A documented modern reception of a literary phrase, not direct political succession, unchanged borders or descent of all Indonesians from one empire.

connections.label: Company to colonial state
connections.summary: The Dutch government took over VOC possessions after the company’s dissolution.
connections.note: Expansion of colonial control continued over the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries; many local states had independent histories beyond the VOC’s reach.

connections.label: Japanese occupation
connections.summary: Japanese conquest displaced Dutch colonial administration in the East Indies.
connections.note: This represents wartime military rule rather than a voluntary transfer or liberation into an independent state.

connections.label: Independence proclaimed
connections.summary: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence after Japan’s surrender.
connections.note: Dutch attempts to restore colonial control led to a further revolution and war; independence was not uncontested or fully recognised on proclamation day.

connections.label: Sovereignty transferred
connections.summary: Dutch recognition and transfer of sovereignty in 1949 were followed by a unitary Indonesian republic in 1950.
connections.note: Territorial integration remained incomplete, notably in western New Guinea; this is not a claim that all present borders were settled in 1949.

connectionMaps.note: Separate precolonial encounters and cultural reception are shown alongside the colonial-to-independent state sequence. There is no asserted Srivijaya→Majapahit→Indonesia governmental lineage.

connectionMaps.title: Cambodia and Vietnam · courts, colonies and modern states

connections.label: Courts move south
connections.summary: Cambodian royal centres shifted southward as Angkor’s imperial power contracted.
connections.note: 1431 is a conventional political marker; Angkor was not wholly abandoned and Khmer people and culture continued.

connections.label: French protectorate
connections.summary: France established a protectorate over the Cambodian kingdom.
connections.note: The monarchy continued under colonial restriction; this is not a disappearance or replacement of Cambodian society.

connections.label: Colonial federation
connections.summary: Cambodia’s protectorate was incorporated into the French Indochinese federation.
connections.note: The protectorate and federation overlapped as different administrative levels, rather than one ending when the other began.

connections.label: Independence restored
connections.summary: Cambodia regained independence from France under the monarchy.
connections.note: The colonial federation’s final collapse in 1954 is a separate regional milestone.

connections.label: Coup and republic
connections.summary: Sihanouk’s removal was followed by the proclamation of the Khmer Republic.
connections.note: This regime change unfolded within civil war and international intervention, not a consensual national union.

connections.label: Khmer Rouge victory
connections.summary: Khmer Rouge forces captured Phnom Penh and imposed a new revolutionary regime.
connections.note: The takeover began the mass coercion and killings of Khmer Rouge rule; Democratic Kampuchea’s formal state constitution followed in 1976.

connections.label: Regime overthrown
connections.summary: Vietnamese invasion and Cambodian allied forces overthrew the Khmer Rouge government in Phnom Penh.
connections.note: Khmer Rouge forces continued fighting, and diplomatic representation remained contested; January 1979 did not bring immediate peace.

connections.label: Peace process and monarchy
connections.summary: The Paris peace process and UN transition led to elections and restoration of a constitutional monarchy in 1993.
connections.note: This condenses the 1989 State of Cambodia renaming and the multi-party transitional settlement; conflict did not cease instantly.

connections.label: French colonial expansion
connections.summary: French conquest and protectorate arrangements subordinated Vietnamese territories before federation in Indochina.
connections.note: Nguyễn monarchs remained at Huế until 1945 under colonial constraint; this edge does not imply the dynasty ended in 1887.

connections.label: Republic proclaimed
connections.summary: The Democratic Republic of Vietnam declared independence after the collapse of wartime Japanese control.
connections.note: French efforts to restore colonial authority led to further war; the proclamation did not bring immediate agreed sovereignty.

connections.label: Regroupment zones
connections.summary: French defeat and the Geneva settlement left rival northern and southern administrations divided near the 17th parallel.
connections.note: These were provisional military regroupment zones, not an agreed permanent international frontier; DRV dated from 1945, State of Vietnam from 1949, and the southern Republic from 1955.

connections.label: Victory and reunification
connections.summary: Northern victory in 1975 was followed by formal reunification as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976.
connections.note: A separate provisional revolutionary government administered the South in 1975–1976; the 1976 state was not founded through a peaceful voluntary merger of the two wartime governments.

connectionMaps.note: Two connected regional strands, with colonial and modern regime changes distinguished from enduring Khmer and Vietnamese communities. Ancient Vietnamese dynasties not already in the timeline are outside this selected expansion.

connectionMaps.title: Mongolia · after the Yuan

connections.label: Yuan court retreats
connections.summary: Yuan rulers withdrew to Mongolia after losing their main Chinese realm.
connections.note: Ming replacement in China did not end the Yuan ruling line or Mongol political histories; this is a different branch from Ming succession.

connections.label: Regional Mongol powers
connections.summary: Post-Yuan Mongol politics developed into competing confederations and principalities, including the Khalkha north of the Gobi.
connections.note: Khalkha were one regional grouping among Oirat, Chahar and others; this is not a single clean division in 1635 or a claim that Khalkha alone inherited the Yuan.

connections.label: Khalkha submit to Qing
connections.summary: Khalkha princes entered Qing rule in 1691.
connections.note: Mongol groups entered Qing rule at different dates; 1691 applies to this Khalkha branch, not all Mongolia.

connections.label: Independence declared
connections.summary: Outer Mongolian leaders declared independence under the Bogd Khan as Qing authority collapsed.
connections.note: Recognition and autonomy remained contested, and Chinese forces reoccupied the territory in 1919.

connections.label: Chinese reoccupation
connections.summary: Chinese forces reimposed control before being expelled during the upheavals of 1921.
connections.note: This is a temporary occupation episode within the interrupted khanate frame, not permanent annexation or a direct line into today’s PRC.

connections.label: Republic proclaimed
connections.summary: After the 1921 revolution and the Bogd Khan’s death, a people’s republic was proclaimed.
connections.note: Soviet influence was strong, but Mongolia did not become one of the USSR’s constituent republics.

connections.label: Democratic transition
connections.summary: A peaceful democratic movement led to multi-party change and a new constitutional era.
connections.note: 1990 marks the political revolution and 1992 the new constitution; Mongolian state and social histories continued across that change.

connectionMaps.note: A selected Outer Mongolian branch from the Yuan, distinct from the Chinese dynastic sequence and from other Mongol successor states. Present-day Mongolia was never a Soviet constituent republic.

continuations.label: Eastern Chagatai · Moghulistan, Tarim and Qing conquest

connectionMaps.title: Aegean networks, Greek worlds & modern independence

connections.label: Bronze Age trade networks
connections.summary: Aegean communities exchanged objects, materials and diplomatic gifts with Egypt and West Asian courts.
connections.note: The Aegean entry is a regional cultural frame, not a united empire or the origin of Egyptian civilization.

connections.label: Crete–mainland exchange
connections.summary: Minoan Cretan art and exchange strongly influenced emerging Mycenaean court cultures.
connections.note: Interaction did not mean that all Minoans became Mycenaeans or that either label describes one state.

connections.label: Palace collapse & local change
connections.summary: The disintegration of Mycenaean palace systems was followed by regional early Iron Age societies.
connections.note: A gradual and uneven archaeological transition; people and practices persisted and no single invasion is asserted as its cause.

connections.label: Cities, writing & wider trade
connections.summary: City-states, alphabetic writing and wider overseas networks developed during the Geometric and early Archaic centuries.
connections.note: The period labels overlap in scholarly usage; this is cultural and institutional change, not a succession between two kingdoms.

connections.label: Archaic → Classical convention
connections.summary: The Persian Wars mark the conventional transition from Archaic to Classical Greek periodisation.
connections.note: Greek city-states remained politically distinct and neither period boundary marks the origin or disappearance of Greek people.

connections.label: Persian–Greek wars
connections.summary: Achaemenid campaigns and Greek resistance reshaped relations among Persian rulers and Greek city-states.
connections.note: The node groups many city-states, which pursued different alliances; this was not a war between two modern nation-states.

connections.label: Macedonian predominance
connections.summary: Macedonian royal power under Philip II provided the military and political base for Alexander’s conquests.
connections.note: Macedonia was one kingdom in the wider Greek world; the arrow does not turn every Greek city into a direct predecessor of his empire.

connections.label: Successor kingdoms emerge
connections.summary: Wars among Alexander’s successors produced multiple Hellenistic kingdoms and leagues.
connections.note: Hellenistic kingdoms is an umbrella period; it includes several dynasties and independent city alliances, not a single successor empire.

connections.label: Roman expansion in Greek East
connections.summary: Rome progressively defeated or annexed Hellenistic powers, with Ptolemaic Egypt annexed in 30 BCE.
connections.note: Different states fell at different dates; Hellenistic cultures and artistic production continued under Roman government.

connections.label: War & independence recognition
connections.summary: The Greek war of independence led to international recognition of an independent Greek state in 1830 and subsequent settlement in 1832.
connections.note: The initial state comprised only part of present-day Greece; earlier Byzantine and ancient Greek histories were not one continuous sovereign state.

continuations.label: Iron Age communities, Rome & post-Roman Britain
Nile Valley: Egypt, Nubia and changing rulers

connectionMaps.title: Iron Age communities, Rome & post-Roman Britain

connections.label: Central European material networks
connections.summary: Hallstatt-period communities participated in the changing Iron Age networks represented by the wider central European frame.
