connections.note: Hallstatt is an archaeological label; it cannot be equated with every Celtic or Germanic-speaking population or with a single ethnic homeland.

connections.label: Noricum enters Roman rule
connections.summary: The Norican kingdom was incorporated into Roman rule around 15 BCE.
connections.note: The transition was largely peaceful in the museum account; formal provincial administration developed later, and this did not erase local communities.

connections.label: Rhine–Danube frontier exchange
connections.summary: Roman goods, diplomacy and military encounters connected imperial provinces with communities beyond the Rhine and Danube.
connections.note: Some regions were conquered and others remained outside Roman control; the arrow does not annex every society in the broad cultural frame.

connections.label: Claudius invades Britain
connections.summary: Roman armies invaded in 43 CE and progressively conquered much of present-day England and Wales.
connections.note: Conquest involved local allies and resistance and did not encompass the whole island; Iron Age communities did not disappear in 43.

connections.label: Resistance & Roman expansion
connections.summary: Roman expansion into western Iberia met prolonged resistance before imperial control consolidated.
connections.note: The cultural block’s 139 BCE endpoint follows Viriathus’ death, not the end of Lusitanian communities or the completion of conquest.

connections.label: Long conquest of Hispania
connections.summary: Roman expansion gradually incorporated Iberian and Celtiberian communities across many separate campaigns.
connections.note: The last campaigns occurred under Augustus after the Republic’s conventional endpoint; languages, settlements and identities did not abruptly vanish.

connections.label: Carthaginian possessions lost
connections.summary: Rome displaced Carthaginian power in Iberia during the Second Punic War.
connections.note: The struggle did not immediately bring the entire peninsula under Roman control or end Indigenous resistance.

connections.label: Alésia & Roman conquest
connections.summary: Caesar’s victory over Vercingetorix and his allies at Alésia was a major stage in the conquest of Gaul.
connections.note: This is a selected campaign episode, not the disappearance of Gallic people or an instant conquest of every region.

connections.label: Rome among Italian communities
connections.summary: Early Rome developed within the culturally and linguistically diverse Italian peninsula.
connections.note: Italic peoples is a collective label including Latins; it does not include every early Italian culture, and Rome was not their united kingdom.

connections.label: Monarchy → republic
connections.summary: Roman tradition dates the replacement of royal rule by republican government to 509 BCE.
connections.note: Early Roman chronology combines archaeology and much later literary accounts; 753 BCE is a traditional foundation date, not a securely documented founding event.

connections.label: Augustan principate
connections.summary: Augustus’ settlement marks the conventional transition to imperial government within the Roman state.
connections.note: The western timeline entry overlaps the shared Roman Empire frame used in other maps; it is not a separate state founded alongside it in 27 BCE.

connections.label: Roman government ends in Britain
connections.summary: Central Roman government in Britain ended and local authorities and kingdoms developed.
connections.note: The empire continued elsewhere; Sub-Roman Britain is a regional frame, not a new united British kingdom or a total population replacement.

connections.label: Settlement, conflict & coexistence
connections.summary: Migrants from continental northern Europe and existing British communities interacted as several Anglo-Saxon kingdoms formed.
connections.note: This overlaps the Sub-Roman frame, includes conflict and coexistence, and does not describe the whole island becoming Anglo-Saxon.

connections.label: English kingdom consolidates
connections.summary: Kings of Wessex and their successors consolidated territories into a kingdom of England during the tenth century.
connections.note: A protracted process involving Mercian, Northumbrian, Scandinavian and other territories, rather than a voluntary merger of all Britain; British kingdoms continued elsewhere.

continuations.label: Aegean networks, Greek worlds & modern independence

connections.label: Suevic kingdom in former provinces
connections.summary: Suevic rulers established a kingdom in northwestern Iberian lands formerly under Roman authority.
connections.note: Changing rule over a selected region, not succession to the whole Roman Empire or disappearance of its provincial population.

connections.label: Suevic realm incorporated
connections.summary: Visigothic rule incorporated the Suevic kingdom in 585.
connections.note: This ended a separate government, not its population or all local religious institutions.

connections.label: Umayyad conquest
connections.summary: Arab and Berber armies defeated Visigothic royal forces and conquered most of Iberia.
connections.note: Al-Andalus includes many later governments, while northern Christian realms and frontier zones followed different histories.

connections.label: Northern frontier kingdoms
connections.summary: The Asturian monarchy developed in the north while Umayyad rulers governed much of Iberia.
connections.note: A frontier relationship with warfare, settlement and exchange; Asturias was not a complete successor to al-Andalus or all Visigothic territory.

connections.label: Royal centre moves to León
connections.summary: The royal centre shifted from Oviedo to León and the monarchy became known as the kingdom of León.
connections.note: Asturian and Leonese labels overlap; this was a change of political centre within a developing monarchy, not replacement of one people by another.

connections.label: Portucale within northern expansion
connections.summary: The recovery of Porto formed the setting for the first Portucalense county under the northern Christian monarchy.
connections.note: A regional county within changing royal authority; its exact endpoints vary, and it was not an independent kingdom of Portugal.

connections.label: County reconstituted
connections.summary: A new Portucalense county was assigned to Henry of Burgundy in 1096.
connections.note: Nuno Mendes’s defeat in 1071 ended the first comital line. Royal administration and later reorganisation preceded Henry’s county; these entries do not indicate an unbroken independent state.

connections.label: Afonso adopts kingship
connections.summary: Afonso Henriques adopted royal status after 1139, followed by Leonese recognition in 1143 and papal recognition in 1179.
connections.note: Kingship, recognition and territorial consolidation were separate stages; the kingdom’s borders and institutions continued to change.

connections.label: Castile–León dynastic union
connections.summary: Ferdinand III united the crowns of Castile and León in 1230.
connections.note: León retained a recognised royal identity within the composite crown; dynastic union did not instantly homogenise its institutions or population.

connections.label: Granada surrendered
connections.summary: Ferdinand and Isabella’s forces took Granada, the last Muslim-ruled Iberian kingdom, in 1492.
connections.note: This ended the Nasrid government, not Muslim people or culture; conversion, persecution, expulsions and continuing communities belong to later histories.

continuations.label: Iron Age communities, Rome & post-Roman Britain

connections.label: Movement into Roman territories
connections.summary: Germanic-speaking groups were among the many populations that migrated, fought and settled within and beyond the Roman frontier.
connections.note: Migration Period is a broad historical frame, not a tribe or successor state; it also involves Huns, Slavs and others.

connections.label: Frankish kings consolidate Gaul
connections.summary: Clovis and later Frankish rulers consolidated kingdoms in former Roman Gaul.
connections.note: The Franks were one set of Germanic-speaking groups; the broad cultural label did not turn into a single Frankish nation.

connections.label: Post-imperial Alpine authorities
connections.summary: The end of western imperial rule left changing authorities in the eastern Alpine provinces.
connections.note: The selected regional frame includes Ostrogothic influence and local continuity; it was never one kingdom called Alpine kingdoms.

connections.label: Bavarian dukes attested
connections.summary: Agilolfing dukes are attested in the Bavarian region during the sixth century.
connections.note: Bavarian political formation was gradual; no secure single founding event or direct succession from every post-Roman Alpine authority is asserted.

connections.label: Tassilo deposed
connections.summary: Charlemagne deposed Duke Tassilo III and incorporated Bavaria under direct Carolingian authority.
connections.note: Bavaria remained a recognisable region and later duchy; the act did not end Bavarian communities.

connections.label: Charlemagne crowned emperor
connections.summary: Charlemagne received the imperial title in Rome in 800 while ruling the Frankish realm.
connections.note: The imperial-period block overlaps the broader Frankish entry; Carolingian kingship began earlier and the coronation did not absorb the Byzantine Empire.

connections.label: Babenberg frontier appointment
connections.summary: The emperor assigned the eastern march to Liutpold of the Babenberg family in 976.
connections.note: The march was a subordinate frontier jurisdiction associated with Bavaria, not an independent state replacing the empire.

connections.label: Austria raised to a duchy
connections.summary: The Privilegium minus raised Austria to a duchy and separated its ducal authority from Bavaria.
connections.note: It remained within the Holy Roman Empire; this was a legal and dynastic change rather than the birth of the modern republic.

connections.label: Archducal privileges confirmed
connections.summary: Emperor Frederick III confirmed privileges that recognised the Austrian archducal title.
connections.note: The claims originated in Rudolf IV’s fourteenth-century forgery; the Habsburg dynasty had already ruled Austria since the late thirteenth century.

connections.label: Austrian imperial title created
connections.summary: Francis adopted the hereditary title Emperor of Austria over the Habsburg lands in 1804.
connections.note: The new empire overlapped the Holy Roman Empire until the latter’s dissolution in 1806; its constituent lands were not all identical with the Austrian archduchy.

connections.label: Eastern Roman reconquest
connections.summary: Justinian’s armies defeated the Ostrogothic kingdom through a prolonged war in Italy.
connections.note: Campaign endpoints differ by definition; reconquest damaged the peninsula and did not produce lasting control of all Italy.

connections.label: Lombard invasion
connections.summary: Lombards conquered substantial parts of Italy while the Eastern Romans retained other territories.
connections.note: Italy remained divided; this was not a complete transfer of Byzantine Italy or a conquest of the Byzantine Empire.

connections.label: Charlemagne takes Lombard crown
connections.summary: Charlemagne conquered the northern Lombard kingdom and assumed its royal title.
connections.note: Southern Lombard principalities survived, and the imperial title represented by the Carolingian-period node followed in 800.

connections.label: Communal autonomy expands
connections.summary: Northern and central Italian communes asserted autonomy against imperial authority, later recognised in the Peace of Constance.
connections.note: The Italian-states entry is a broader regional frame including varied governments; not all gained autonomy together or broke every legal tie with the empire.

connections.label: Communes & southern monarchy coexist
connections.summary: Independent communes, papal lands and the southern Sicilian monarchy formed contrasting centres of power in medieval Italy.
connections.note: This is a contemporary regional relationship, not a claim that northern communes merged to create the Sicilian kingdom or shared one ruler.

connections.label: Naples–Sicily legal union
connections.summary: The Bourbon ruler formally combined the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
connections.note: The Sicily timeline entry groups the crowns’ changing history after the 1282 division; their shared monarch did not make them one unchanged state before 1816.

connections.label: Southern annexation & Italian kingdom
connections.summary: Garibaldi’s campaigns and Sardinian intervention brought the Two Sicilies into the new Kingdom of Italy.
connections.note: Unification also involved other states; Venetia joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870, and Italy became a republic in 1946.

connections.label: Christianisation & court connections
connections.summary: Volodymyr’s adoption of Christianity strengthened ecclesiastical and artistic connections between Rus’ and Byzantium.
connections.note: A religious and diplomatic relationship, not incorporation into the Byzantine state or the beginning of all Rus’ settlement.

connections.label: Regional principalities consolidate
connections.summary: Political authority became increasingly dispersed among competing Rus’ principalities.
connections.note: A gradual and overlapping development, not one dated partition into the modern nations of Ukraine, Russia and Belarus.

connections.label: Mongol invasion & tributary power
connections.summary: Mongol conquest, including the sack of Kyiv in 1240, subjected many Rus’ principalities to tribute under the Jochid realm.
connections.note: Rulers, cities and communities survived; not every Rus’ territory experienced identical control, and the Horde was not a renamed Rus’.

connections.label: Moscow expands among principalities
connections.summary: Moscow developed within northeastern Rus’ and expanded amid competition with other principalities under Horde supremacy.
connections.note: One regional path only; Moscow did not inherit every Rus’ land, and the shared medieval history is not exclusive ancestry or a modern territorial entitlement.

connections.label: Western Rus’ lands incorporated
connections.summary: Lithuanian expansion incorporated extensive western and southern Rus’ territories through changing military and dynastic relationships.
connections.note: Ruthenian legal and cultural traditions continued; these lands were not all incorporated at once, and Lithuania did not inherit the whole Kyivan realm.

continuations.label: Golden Horde, Muscovy & Soviet successor states

connectionMaps.title: Soviet dissolution · Russia and eastern Europe

connections.label: 1991 · four independent states
connections.summary: The Soviet breakup left Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova as independent states.
connections.note: One geographic subset of the same union-wide breakup; the regional grouping is a viewing aid, not an intervening state. No present-day territorial claims are inferred.

continuations.label: Earlier: Russian and Soviet state histories

connections.label: 1990–91 · independence restored
connections.summary: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania restored independence during the Soviet crisis.
connections.note: Soviet forces occupied and annexed these states in 1940. Lithuania proclaimed restoration in 1990; full independence and wider recognition followed in 1991. These are three of the fifteen final union republics.

continuations.label: Golden Horde, Muscovy & Soviet successor states

connections.label: 1991 · three independent states
connections.summary: Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia became independent as Soviet authority broke down.
connections.note: One geographic subset of the same union-wide breakup; the regional grouping is a viewing aid, not an intervening state. No present-day territorial claims are inferred.

continuations.label: Central Asia · khanates, Russian expansion and Soviet rule
Golden Horde, Muscovy & Soviet successor states

connectionMaps.title: Soviet dissolution · five Central Asian states

connections.label: 1991 · five independent states
connections.summary: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan became independent in 1991.
connections.note: One geographic subset of the same union-wide breakup; the regional grouping is a viewing aid, not an intervening state. No present-day territorial claims are inferred.

continuations.label: Earlier: khanates, Russian expansion and Soviet rule
Golden Horde, Muscovy & Soviet successor states

connectionMaps.title: Central Asia · khanates, Russian expansion and Soviet rule

connections.label: 1400s · eastern steppe powers
connections.summary: Abu’l-Khayr consolidated an Uzbek realm in the eastern Jochid steppe.
connections.note: One regional formation within post-Horde politics; other khanates and communities followed separate paths.

connections.label: 1460s · Kazakh khanate emerges
connections.summary: Kerei and Janibek left Abu’l-Khayr’s political orbit and founded a separate khanate.
connections.note: The conventional 1465 date marks consolidation, not the beginning of Kazakh people or all later territory.

connections.label: 1460s · refuge in Moghulistan
connections.summary: Kerei, Janibek and their followers settled in Moghulistan before consolidating their khanate.
connections.note: A political refuge and regional relationship, not the entire Moghulistan realm becoming Kazakhstan.

connections.label: 1500s · a Jochid dynastic link
connections.summary: Abu’l-Khayr’s grandson Muhammad Shaybani led conquests in Transoxiana.
connections.note: Dynastic connection and military expansion, not a simple renaming or migration of an entire state.

connections.label: 1500–12 · Uzbek conquests
connections.summary: Shaybani and subsequent Uzbek rulers defeated Timurid claimants and consolidated Transoxiana.
connections.note: Different cities changed hands repeatedly; Timurid dynastic histories continued in the Mughal realm.

connections.label: 1785 · Manghit emirate
connections.summary: Shah Murad’s rule marks the conventional emirate frame after Manghit consolidation.
connections.note: A change in ruling arrangements within Bukhara, not the creation of a new population.

connections.label: 1500s–1800s · neighbours and rivals
connections.summary: Bukhara and Khwarazm maintained separate ruling houses and competing regional interests.
connections.note: Contact does not imply that Khiva broke away from Bukhara or that either matches one modern nation.

connections.label: 1700s · Fergana consolidation
connections.summary: Fergana’s growing autonomy developed into the Kokand khanate.
connections.note: Separation and consolidation occurred in stages; the conventional 1709 foundation is not a sudden border-wide transfer.

connections.label: 1700s–1800s · Russian encroachment
connections.summary: Russian authority expanded through the Kazakh steppe by unequal agreements, administrative changes and conquest.
connections.note: Different zhuzes and regions were incorporated at different times, amid resistance.

connections.label: 1860s–76 · conquest and annexation
connections.summary: Russian forces took Kokandian territories and abolished the remaining khanate in 1876.
connections.note: Kokand’s dissolution did not end Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Tajik or other regional communities.

connections.label: 1868 · Russian domination
connections.summary: Bukhara came under Russian domination while retaining its emir’s government.
connections.note: This was unequal subordination and territorial loss, not immediate annexation of the whole emirate.

connections.label: 1873 · Khivan protectorate
connections.summary: Russian conquest reduced Khiva to a protectorate and annexed part of its territory.
connections.note: The khan’s restricted government survived until 1920.

connections.label: 1920 · khanate governments fall
connections.summary: Red Army campaigns and local revolutionary movements overthrew the Khivan khan and Bukharan emir.
connections.note: New Khorezm and Bukharan republics preceded later Soviet territorial reorganisation; armed resistance continued.

connections.label: 1924–36 · five union republics
connections.summary: Soviet reorganisation established Uzbek and Turkmen republics, followed by Tajik, Kazakh and Kyrgyz union republics.
connections.note: Tajikistan had an earlier autonomous status within Uzbekistan; Kazakh and Kyrgyz republics attained union status in 1936. This did not invent the region’s peoples.

connections.label: 1917 onward · revolution and war
connections.summary: Revolution broke imperial authority, followed by competing autonomy projects, civil war and Soviet consolidation.
connections.note: A regional overview of contested transitions, not the entire empire becoming one Soviet administration at once.

connectionMaps.title: Eastern Chagatai · Moghulistan, Tarim and Qing conquest

connections.label: 1340s · eastern khanate
connections.summary: Moghulistan emerged as the eastern Chagataid political realm while western power fragmented.
connections.note: Timur’s later western conquests did not eliminate the eastern Chagataid realm.

connections.label: 1500s · regional Chagataid branches
connections.summary: Chagataid rulers maintained distinct centres in the Tarim Basin and Turpan.
connections.note: Selected related branches after prolonged division and warfare; their territories did not comprise all former Moghulistan.

connections.label: 1670s · Khoja and Dzungar intervention
connections.summary: Afaq Khoja gained power in Kashgaria with Dzungar support, displacing Chagataid authority.
connections.note: Dating varies around 1678–1680; rival lineages and nominal princes continued to complicate local rule.

connections.label: 1670s–1750s · Dzungar supremacy
connections.summary: Dzungar khans imposed tribute and hostages on the Tarim Khoja governments.
connections.note: Overlordship and intervention, not the formation of the Dzungar state from the Chagataid dynasty.

connections.label: 1720s–50s · Qing alliance and rule
connections.summary: Turpan leaders sought Qing support against Dzungar power as Qing troops entered the oasis.
connections.note: Alliance, warfare, forced movement and later return unfolded over decades; Turpan was not simply annexed once in 1720.

connections.label: 1750s · Dzungar state destroyed
connections.summary: Qing campaigns destroyed the Dzungar state and incorporated its territories.
connections.note: The conquest brought catastrophic loss of life and displacement; surviving Oirat communities did not disappear.

connections.label: 1759 · Kashgaria conquered
connections.summary: Qing forces ended the Khojas’ government in Kashgaria.
connections.note: Resistance and Khoja political claims continued later; conquest did not end the region’s Muslim or Turkic communities.

continuations.label: Continue: Qing → republican and present-day Chinese frames
Kazakh and western Central Asian branches
Western Chagatai → Timurid and Iranian histories

connections.label: Urban culture
connections.summary: Uruk was a major center within the wider Sumerian urban landscape.
connections.note: This is cultural overlap, not one state succeeding another.

connections.label: Later city-state period
connections.summary: The Uruk urban phase preceded the Early Dynastic landscape of competing cities.
connections.note: Archaeological periods overlap locally; Uruk itself continued to exist.

connections.label: Sargon’s conquests
connections.summary: Sargon brought numerous Mesopotamian city-states under Akkadian imperial rule.
connections.note: Conquest did not erase Sumerian cities or language.

connections.label: Scribal inheritance
connections.summary: Old Babylonian scribes copied and transmitted Sumerian literature.
connections.note: A cultural relationship spanning intervening dynasties, not immediate political succession.

connections.label: Sack of Babylon
connections.summary: A Hittite raid ended Babylon’s first dynasty.
connections.note: The attackers withdrew; this was not permanent Hittite rule of Babylonia.

connections.label: Kassite consolidation
connections.summary: Kassite rulers gradually consolidated Babylonia after the first dynasty’s collapse.
connections.note: The transition is obscure and included rival southern rulers.

connections.label: Assyrian occupation
connections.summary: Tukulti-Ninurta I conquered Babylon during Kassite rule.
connections.note: The Kassite dynasty survived this intervention.

connections.label: Elamite campaigns
connections.summary: Elamite attacks brought the Kassite dynasty to an end.
connections.note: Subsequent Babylonian dynasties, not lasting Elamite annexation, followed.

connections.label: Renewed expansion
connections.summary: Later Assyrian kings renewed expansion after a period of contraction.
connections.note: Middle and Neo-Assyrian are modern period labels, not a single dated founding event.

connections.label: Fall of Nineveh
connections.summary: Babylonian and Median forces destroyed the Assyrian capital of Nineveh.
connections.note: Assyrian resistance continued after 612; neither the people nor their culture vanished.

connections.label: Iranian languages
connections.summary: The Medes were among the Iranian-speaking groups recorded in western Iran.
connections.note: A linguistic category is not a unified ancestral empire.

connections.label: Cyrus defeats Astyages
connections.summary: Cyrus overthrew the Median ruler and incorporated Media into his growing empire.
connections.note: The extent and organization of an earlier Median empire remain debated.

connections.label: Capture of Babylon
connections.summary: Cyrus captured Babylon and incorporated Babylonia into Achaemenid rule.
connections.note: Local institutions and traditions continued under new imperial government.

connections.label: Susa & administration
connections.summary: Susa and Elamite administrative traditions became important within Achaemenid government.
connections.note: Elam’s diverse earlier kingdoms are not one dynasty directly replaced on a single date.

connections.label: Regional successor states
connections.summary: Independent southeastern states preserved some Hittite dynastic and cultural traditions after the empire fell.
connections.note: These included Luwian and Aramaean polities, not a single restored Hittite empire.

connections.label: Assyrian expansion
connections.summary: Assyrian expansion progressively absorbed Syro-Hittite kingdoms.
connections.note: Different kingdoms were conquered at different times.

connections.label: Fall of Croesus
connections.summary: Cyrus defeated Lydia and brought western Anatolia under Persian rule.
connections.note: The conventional dating varies slightly across chronologies.

connections.label: Artistic exchange
connections.summary: Samaria’s ivories show exchanges with Phoenician and Syrian neighbors.
connections.note: Shared artistic forms do not prove a shared political identity.

connections.label: Capture of Samaria
connections.summary: Assyrian conquest ended the northern kingdom and deported part of its population.
connections.note: People remained in the region; this was not the disappearance of all Israelites.

connections.label: Jerusalem destroyed
connections.summary: Babylonian forces destroyed Jerusalem’s temple and deported part of Judah’s population.
connections.note: The exiles were not all inhabitants, and Jewish history continued in several places.

connections.label: Persian imperial rule
connections.summary: Phoenician cities came under Achaemenid rule while maintaining important maritime roles.
connections.note: Their earlier city-state independence was already constrained by several empires.

connections.label: Hasmonean autonomy
connections.summary: Hasmonean rulers gained autonomy amid Seleucid conflict and declining control of Judea.
connections.note: The revolt and independence were processes involving competing local factions.

connections.label: Roman-backed Herod
connections.summary: Herod captured Jerusalem with Roman support and displaced the last Hasmonean ruler.
connections.note: Roman involvement in Judea had begun earlier; Herod ruled as a client king.

connections.label: Roman patronage
connections.summary: Roman political and military support enabled Herod’s kingship.
connections.note: This relationship concerns Roman patronage, not an equal alliance.

continuations.label: Aegean networks, Greek worlds & modern independence

connections.label: Seljuqs take Baghdad
connections.summary: Seljuq rulers took Baghdad and exercised military power alongside the Abbasid caliphate.
connections.note: The caliphate continued; the Seljuqs did not become a replacement caliphate.

connections.label: Battle of Manzikert
connections.summary: Seljuq forces defeated the Byzantine army at Manzikert, accelerating changes across Anatolia.
connections.note: Byzantium survived; settlement and political transformation took decades.

connections.label: Anatolian branch
connections.summary: A Seljuq branch established the Sultanate of Rûm in Anatolia.
connections.note: Related dynastic branches overlapped rather than splitting in a single treaty.

connections.label: Köse Dağ & overlordship
connections.summary: Mongol victory at Köse Dağ reduced the Sultanate of Rûm to dependent status.
connections.note: The Ilkhanate was established later; the 1243 attackers were a Mongol imperial army.

connections.label: Regional principalities
connections.summary: Declining Seljuq authority accompanied the growth of rival Anatolian principalities.
connections.note: Not every beylik originated in the same way or at the same time.

connections.label: Ottoman expansion
connections.summary: The Ottoman principality grew among these rivals and progressively absorbed many of them.
connections.note: The Ottomans were one beylik among several, not the automatic successor to all Seljuq lands.

connections.label: Regional dynastic context
connections.summary: The Ilkhanate and later regional dynasties form parts of this broad Iran–Iraq period.
connections.note: This umbrella entry is not a separate successor state.

connections.label: Timur’s campaigns
connections.summary: Timur conquered much of Iran and Iraq amid competing regional dynasties.
connections.note: The umbrella period includes multiple polities and overlapping zones of rule.

connections.label: Pahlavi dynasty
connections.summary: The Pahlavi dynasty replaced Qajar rule in Iran.
connections.note: The endpoint groups Pahlavi and later republican eras; the dedicated Iran map distinguishes 1979.

continuations.label: From the Ilkhanate to modern Iran

connections.label: British wartime occupation
connections.summary: British conquest of Ottoman Mesopotamia was followed by a mandate project and treaty arrangements.
connections.note: Postwar borders and institutions were contested, including during the Iraqi revolt of 1920.

connections.label: Faisal’s monarchy
connections.summary: Faisal became king in 1921 while British supervision continued until formal independence in 1932.
connections.note: The monarchy overlapped with British control rather than beginning after it ended.

connections.label: Republican coup
connections.summary: Army officers overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and proclaimed a republican government.
connections.note: Later republican regimes are grouped by the timeline, not treated as one unchanged government.

connections.label: French mandate rule
connections.summary: After Ottoman defeat and contested postwar settlement, Syria and Lebanon came under French mandate rule.
connections.note: This schematic omits the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria and several mandate subdivisions.

connections.label: Independence & withdrawal
connections.summary: Syria and Lebanon achieved independence through separate processes, completed by French troop withdrawal.
connections.note: Lebanon commemorates 1943; Syria commemorates the 1946 evacuation.

connections.label: Territorial consolidation
connections.summary: Ibn Saud’s expansion included taking al-Ahsa from Ottoman forces before later consolidating his dominions.
connections.note: Not all Saudi territories had been directly administered by the Ottomans.

connections.label: Kingdom proclaimed
connections.summary: The consolidated dominions were proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
connections.note: The proclamation followed years of conquest and administration; it was not a union of all Arabian states.

connections.label: British administration
connections.summary: British military conquest was followed by League of Nations mandate administration in Palestine.
connections.note: The population’s political rights and future were contested; this was not a consensual union.

connections.label: Separate administrations
connections.summary: Transjordan developed under a separate Arab administration within the wider mandate framework.
connections.note: The map’s Palestine node denotes territory west of the Jordan, not a claim that the emirate was carved from an already independent state.

connections.label: Independent kingdom
connections.summary: British recognition of Transjordan’s independence ended the mandate relationship there.
connections.note: Recognition, treaty effect, and the kingdom’s proclamation had different dates within 1946.

connections.label: Israel proclaimed
connections.summary: Israel was proclaimed as British rule ended, amid war in the former mandate territory.
connections.note: The 1947 UN partition proposal did not produce two functioning states as envisaged.

connections.label: Displacement & organizing
connections.summary: War, Palestinian displacement, and continuing national mobilization preceded the PLO’s establishment.
connections.note: A contextual political history link, not a transfer of British governmental authority to the PLO.

connections.label: Palestine proclaimed
connections.summary: The Palestine National Council proclaimed the State of Palestine, acknowledged by the UN General Assembly.
connections.note: Declaration and diplomatic recognition did not establish full territorial sovereignty or end occupation.

connections.label: Mutual recognition & Oslo
connections.summary: Israel and the PLO exchanged recognition and signed interim self-government arrangements.
connections.note: The accords did not settle final borders or create a sovereign Palestinian state.

connections.label: Long-distance trade
connections.summary: Indus and Mesopotamian societies participated in long-distance exchange networks.
connections.note: Trade links do not establish political union or population identity.

connections.label: Overlapping transformations
connections.summary: Late Harappan communities overlapped with changing Indo-Gangetic cultural landscapes.
connections.note: This is not a conquest or simple Harappan-to-Vedic state succession; language and identity remain research questions.

connections.label: Later regional states
connections.summary: Later Vedic textual traditions developed alongside the emergence of regional states in northern South Asia.
connections.note: Culture, texts, and states have different chronologies; there was no single Vedic empire.

connections.label: Magadhan consolidation
connections.summary: The Magadhan political core of the mahājanapadas was incorporated into the Mauryan imperial project.
connections.note: Not every mahājanapada survived until, or was conquered by, the Mauryas in the same way.

connections.label: Treaty & frontier
connections.summary: Chandragupta Maurya and Seleucus established a negotiated frontier after conflict.
connections.note: A selected interstate encounter, not the descent of one empire from the other.

connections.label: Regional dynasties
connections.summary: After Mauryan power ended, numerous regional dynasties governed different parts of South Asia.
connections.note: The endpoint is a modern grouping, not one successor kingdom.

connections.label: Northwestern imperial setting
connections.summary: Kushan power formed one important part of the diverse post-Mauryan political landscape.
connections.note: An umbrella-to-member context link, not a single dynasty changing its name.

connections.label: Changing northern powers
connections.summary: As Kushan power contracted, Gupta rulers consolidated parts of northern India.
connections.note: Regional successors and intervening rulers existed; there was no wholesale handover of all Kushan lands.

connections.label: Regional rule expands
connections.summary: Gupta power fragmented as invasions and regional autonomy reshaped northern India.
connections.note: The post-Gupta label groups different kingdoms rather than one political successor.

connections.label: Harsha’s northern realm
connections.summary: Harsha’s kingdom was one major polity within the wider post-Gupta landscape.
connections.note: It did not reunite all former Gupta territories or govern all South Asia.

connections.label: Diplomatic missions
connections.summary: Harsha exchanged diplomatic missions with Tang China.
connections.note: Diplomatic contact is not territorial continuity.

connections.label: Regional courts
connections.summary: Following Harsha’s death, northern power again rested with multiple regional courts.
connections.note: Many kingdoms already existed beyond his control; this umbrella spans the wider subcontinent.

connections.label: Southern imperial center
connections.summary: The Cholas rose within a competitive southern landscape of regional dynasties.
connections.note: They were not the sole successors to northern post-Gupta kingdoms.

connections.label: Maritime raids
connections.summary: Chola naval forces attacked Srivijayan ports and centers in Southeast Asia.
connections.note: A campaign did not create permanent Chola rule over the whole Srivijayan maritime world.

connections.label: Northern sultanate expands
connections.summary: Conquest and consolidation established Delhi sultanate rule across parts of northern India.
connections.note: Many regional kingdoms survived; this was not the end of all pre-existing South Asian states.

connections.label: Deccan political setting
connections.summary: Vijayanagara emerged amid Delhi’s southern campaigns and a changing Deccan political landscape.
connections.note: This is regional context, not a claim that Vijayanagara was simply a renamed Delhi province.

connections.label: Babur’s victory
connections.summary: Babur defeated the Lodi ruler at Panipat and established Mughal rule in northern India.
connections.note: Mughal consolidation was prolonged and interrupted by Sur rule.

connections.label: Battle of Talikota
connections.summary: A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara and devastated its capital.
connections.note: The Vijayanagara dynasty continued from other capitals after 1565.

connections.label: Mughal annexations
connections.summary: Mughal campaigns absorbed major Deccan sultanates, culminating in the late 1680s.
connections.note: Different sultanates ended at different dates; this is a grouped regional account.

continuations.label: Maritime Southeast Asia · encounters and independence

connections.label: Durrani state emerges
connections.summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani established a realm after Nader Shah’s death.
connections.note: Afsharid fragmentation produced several regional powers.

connections.label: Dost Mohammad in Kabul
connections.summary: Dost Mohammad consolidated Barakzai rule in Kabul after Durrani fragmentation.
connections.note: Regional rivals and later Durrani restoration complicate a simple dynasty-to-dynasty chain.

connections.label: First Anglo-Afghan War
connections.summary: British forces deposed Dost Mohammad and restored a Durrani ruler, then withdrew.
connections.note: Dost Mohammad subsequently returned to power.

connections.label: Foreign-policy independence
connections.summary: The Treaty of Rawalpindi recognized Afghanistan’s full foreign-policy independence after war.
connections.note: Afghanistan had not been an annexed province of British India.

connections.label: Monarchy overthrown
connections.summary: Daoud overthrew the monarchy and proclaimed a republic.
connections.note: The endpoint groups subsequent governments; it is not one unchanged republican regime.

connectionNodes.title: Kingdom of Ireland
connectionNodes.note: A kingdom sharing a monarch with England and later Great Britain. The map’s union event concerns 1801, not the origin of Ireland.

connectionNodes.title: Irish Free State
connectionNodes.note: Created as a dominion in 1922. Northern Ireland remained in the UK. A new constitution followed in 1937; the later Republic of Ireland is a further constitutional development.

connectionNodes.title: British northern colonies · pre-Confederation
connectionNodes.note: This collective frame includes British Canada after 1763 and the colonies usually grouped as British North America after 1783. It was not one sovereign state. Confederation initially joined only some colonies; other territories entered Canada later.

connectionNodes.title: Roman Empire · shared imperial frame
connectionNodes.note: This node provides a common imperial frame before the 395 division. Earlier partitions and reunifications occurred; the eastern state continued as Roman, rather than becoming a new people.

connectionNodes.title: Middle Francia
connectionNodes.location: Central strip of the former Carolingian realm
connectionNodes.note: Lothair I’s realm after Verdun included lands from the Low Countries to Italy. Further partitions followed in 855.

connectionNodes.title: Golden Horde
connectionNodes.note: A regional Mongol realm developing from the Jochid appanage. Its formation was gradual, and later successor khanates had separate histories.

connectionNodes.title: Chagatai Khanate
connectionNodes.note: The early khanate later divided into western and eastern political formations. This map does not date the end of all Chagataid lineages.

connectionNodes.title: Saadi Morocco
connectionNodes.note: A dynastic frame for the Moroccan force behind the 1591 invasion. It was not a successor state encompassing all Songhai territory.

connectionNodes.title: Crown of Castile
connectionNodes.note: Its institutions remained distinct after the dynastic union with Aragon. Later centralisation occurred in stages.

connectionNodes.title: Crown of Aragon
connectionNodes.note: A composite crown whose territories retained distinct laws and institutions after the union of rulers with Castile.

connectionNodes.title: Gran Colombia
connectionNodes.note: A republic formed during independence struggles. Territorial liberation and integration occurred in stages; the union dissolved in 1830–1831.

connectionNodes.title: Republic of New Granada
connectionNodes.note: One successor to Gran Colombia. Later constitutional forms and the separation of Panama in 1903 are distinct developments.

connectionNodes.title: Venezuela · separate republic
connectionNodes.note: The map anchors this political frame in separation from Gran Colombia. Earlier independence declarations, changing regimes and territory have their own histories.

connectionNodes.title: Ecuador · separate republic
connectionNodes.note: Ecuador withdrew from Gran Colombia in 1830. This does not date the region’s peoples or settle later border disputes.

connectionNodes.title: Jalayirid Sultanate
connectionNodes.note: One of several powers following Ilkhanid fragmentation. Its territory changed and rulers returned after some conquests; it never inherited the whole Ilkhanate.

connectionNodes.title: Muzaffarid dynasty
connectionNodes.note: A regional dynasty whose origins predate 1335 and which expanded after Ilkhanid fragmentation. Timur ended its rule; this is only one of the regional powers shown.

connectionNodes.title: Qara Qoyunlu
connectionNodes.note: A Turkoman confederation with a history before and alongside Timurid rule. The map concerns expansion into selected Jalayirid and western Timurid territories.

connectionNodes.title: Aq Qoyunlu
connectionNodes.note: A Turkoman confederation whose major Iranian expansion followed victories in 1467–1469. Rival branches continued after the Safavids took Tabriz in 1501.

connectionNodes.title: Hotak occupation & Safavid claimants
connectionNodes.note: A selected crisis, not one unified dynasty: Hotak forces occupied Isfahan in 1722; Nader expelled them in 1729 and restored a Safavid claimant before taking the throne in 1736.

connectionNodes.title: Afsharid Khorasan
connectionNodes.note: After Nader’s death, Afsharid rulers survived in Khorasan while other powers ruled elsewhere. This overlaps with Zand rule and Qajar expansion.

connectionNodes.title: Zand Iran
connectionNodes.note: Karim Khan and later Zand rulers controlled much of Iran, while Khorasan remained outside their rule. Qajars defeated the last Zand ruler in 1794.

connectionNodes.title: Ireland · constitutional state
connectionNodes.note: The 1937 constitution replaced the Free State constitution and named the state Ireland. The Republic of Ireland description took effect in 1949. Northern Ireland remained in the UK.

connectionNodes.title: North German Confederation
connectionNodes.note: A Prussia-led federal state established after the 1866 war and dissolution of the older German Confederation. Southern states joined the enlarged empire in 1871; Austria was excluded.

connectionNodes.title: Granadine Confederation
connectionNodes.note: A federal constitutional framework after New Granada. Civil war and transitional names preceded the 1863 constitution.

connectionNodes.title: United States of Colombia
connectionNodes.note: The 1863 constitution established this federal framework after civil war. The name had been used earlier during the conflict. It was replaced by the centralising 1886 constitution.

connectionNodes.title: Colombia · 1886 and later eras
connectionNodes.note: The name Republic of Colombia was restored in the 1886 constitution. Modern Colombia has earlier state histories, later reforms including the 1991 constitution, and a changed border following Panama’s separation.

connectionNodes.title: Panama · independent republic
connectionNodes.note: Panama separated from Colombia in November 1903 amid US involvement and canal negotiations. This does not date the beginning of Panamanian communities or regional identities.

connectionNodes.title: Bamana, Massina & Toucouleur realms
connectionNodes.note: Several different states and communities occupied parts of regions formerly within Mali or Songhai. This collective frame does not imply one continuous state or identical boundaries.

connectionNodes.title: French Sudan / Sudanese Republic
connectionNodes.location: Present-day Mali and changing adjoining territories
connectionNodes.note: French conquest and colonial reorganisation occurred in stages and met resistance. This selected frame ends with the Mali Federation; colonial borders did not match medieval empires.

connectionNodes.title: Mali Federation
connectionNodes.note: A short-lived federation of Senegal and the Sudanese Republic, independent from France on 20 June 1960. It broke apart later that year.

connectionNodes.title: Mali · independent state
connectionNodes.note: The Sudanese Republic adopted the name Republic of Mali in September 1960 after the federation dissolved. It is not the medieval Mali Empire restored or the whole former Songhai realm.

connectionNodes.title: Senegal · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Senegal left the Mali Federation in August 1960. Its earlier histories and colonial borders differ from those of medieval Sahelian empires.

connectionNodes.title: Southern Nigerian colonial jurisdictions
connectionNodes.note: This selected frame begins with the invasion of Benin in 1897, before the Southern Nigeria Protectorate was established in 1900. Niger Coast, Lagos and Southern Nigeria administrations changed before 1914.

connectionNodes.title: Northern Nigeria Protectorate
connectionNodes.note: British rule expanded through conquest and agreements. The protectorate included only part of the wider Lake Chad region; Kanuri communities and institutions continued across colonial borders.

connectionNodes.title: Colonial Nigeria
connectionNodes.location: Present-day Nigeria and changing adjoining territories
connectionNodes.note: British administrators amalgamated northern and southern jurisdictions in 1914. This joined many peoples and political traditions, rather than being a merger only of Benin and Bornu.

connectionNodes.title: Khanate of Kazan
connectionNodes.note: One of several khanates formed in the fragmentation of the Golden Horde. Muscovite conquest in 1552 ended its government; Tatar communities and traditions continued.

connectionNodes.title: Great Horde
connectionNodes.note: A later Jochid political formation claiming the central Horde inheritance. It coexisted and competed with other khanates; it did not represent all post-Horde societies.

connectionNodes.title: Grand Principality of Moscow
connectionNodes.note: A separate principality that developed under Horde tributary supremacy and expanded over neighbouring principalities. Ending tribute did not mean the Golden Horde was renamed Russia.

connectionNodes.title: Tsardom of Russia
connectionNodes.location: Changing territories across northeastern Europe and northern Asia
connectionNodes.note: Ivan IV adopted the tsar’s title in 1547. Territorial conquest and state expansion continued; Peter’s imperial title in 1721 marks the next frame.

connectionNodes.title: Ukraine · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Ukraine declared independence in August 1991, confirmed by a December referendum. Its peoples and political histories predate Soviet rule; this node does not make contemporary territorial claims.

connectionNodes.title: Kazakhstan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Kazakhstan became independent in December 1991. Earlier Kazakh polities and societies are not represented as beginning with Soviet dissolution.

connectionNodes.title: Nobatia
connectionNodes.location: Lower Nubia; southern Egypt and northern Sudan
connectionNodes.note: Christianised in the sixth century; later governed with Makuria while retaining a distinctive regional administration. Exact dates and circumstances of union are uncertain.

connectionNodes.title: Makuria
connectionNodes.location: Middle Nile; capital at Old Dongola
connectionNodes.note: Christian Nubian kingdom with changing territorial reach and late fragmentation; its chronology is not the lifetime of all Nubian communities.

connectionNodes.title: Alodia / Alwa
connectionNodes.location: Blue and White Nile region; capital at Soba
connectionNodes.note: Christian Nubian kingdom distinct from Makuria. Late chronicles associate Soba’s destruction with 1504, while archaeology indicates much earlier decline in excavated areas; a precise end date is uncertain.

connectionNodes.title: Funj Sultanate of Sennar
connectionNodes.location: Middle Nile and Blue Nile; changing dominions
connectionNodes.note: A regional sultanate conventionally dated from 1504. It incorporated diverse communities and territories and was not a restored, unchanged Alodian monarchy or all of modern Sudan.

connectionNodes.title: Turco-Egyptian Sudan
connectionNodes.location: Sudanese territories ruled from Egypt; frontiers changed
connectionNodes.note: Muhammad Ali’s conquest began in 1820, ending Funj rule in 1821. Egyptian government expanded unevenly into other regions; this did not constitute simultaneous control of every part of today’s Sudan and South Sudan.

connectionNodes.title: Mahdist State
connectionNodes.note: The movement began in 1881 and captured Khartoum in 1885. Omdurman fell in 1898; the Khalifa was defeated and killed in 1899. The stages should not be collapsed into a single founding or ending day.

connectionNodes.title: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
connectionNodes.location: Territories of present-day Sudan and South Sudan, with changing boundaries
connectionNodes.note: The 1899 agreements established nominal joint British and Egyptian authority, with British officials dominant in administration. Colonial borders and institutions differed from those of preceding kingdoms.

connectionNodes.title: Sudan: independent eras
connectionNodes.note: An overview of successive governments and conflicts following independence, not one unchanged regime. South Sudan became independent in 2011; Sudan continued as a state. Ancient Nubian kingdoms were not coterminous with this modern country.

connectionNodes.title: South Sudan: independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence on 9 July 2011 followed a January referendum under the 2005 peace settlement. This date marks a modern state, not the beginning of the histories of its many peoples.

connectionNodes.title: Egypt: Tulunid, Abbasid and Ikhshidid governments
connectionNodes.location: Egypt and, at times, neighbouring lands
connectionNodes.note: An explicitly grouped transition frame: Tulunids 868–905, restored direct Abbasid government 905–935, and Ikhshidids 935–969; this is not one dynasty.

connectionNodes.title: Zagwe dynasty
connectionNodes.note: The dynasty’s origins and exact founding date remain uncertain. Christian traditions connect this period with Aksumite and later Ethiopian histories, without establishing an uninterrupted royal genealogy.

connectionNodes.title: Ethiopia: post-monarchical eras
connectionNodes.note: This groups the Derg, subsequent transitional government and later federal republic. These are different regimes and constitutional orders, not one government lasting from 1974.

connectionNodes.title: Eritrea: independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence followed a long war, military victory in 1991 and the 1993 referendum. The modern border is not a boundary inherited unchanged from Aksum.

connectionNodes.title: Omani and Zanzibar coastal rule
connectionNodes.location: Western Indian Ocean and selected East African coastal ports
connectionNodes.note: A regional frame for changing Omani and Zanzibar authority, not a single state covering every Swahili settlement. The independent Zanzibar sultanate dates from the nineteenth century.

connectionNodes.title: German East Africa
connectionNodes.location: Mainland Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi, with changing frontiers
connectionNodes.note: German claims began in 1885, and conquest and administrative control developed later. The territory was divided after World War I.

connectionNodes.title: Tanganyika under British administration
connectionNodes.note: British occupation was followed by a League of Nations mandate and UN trust territory; 1919 is a transition anchor rather than the date of all legal arrangements.

connectionNodes.title: Tanganyika: independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence in 1961 was followed by a republic in 1962 and union with Zanzibar in 1964.

connectionNodes.title: Zanzibar: independence and revolution
connectionNodes.note: Independence under the sultanate in December 1963 was followed by revolution in January 1964 and union in April; these were distinct political stages.

connectionNodes.title: United Republic of Tanzania
connectionNodes.note: Tanganyika and Zanzibar united on 26 April 1964; Zanzibar retained separate institutions within the union.

connectionNodes.title: British East Africa and colonial Kenya
connectionNodes.note: A changing colonial frame: protectorate, colony and a legally distinct coastal protectorate; it did not cover every area of British East Africa at all times.

connectionNodes.title: Gold Coast, Ashanti, Northern Territories and British Togoland
connectionNodes.note: Four different legal territories were administered in relation to the Gold Coast and were joined at independence. Ashanti was not simply annexed to the Gold Coast Colony in 1902.

connectionNodes.title: Portuguese Angola
connectionNodes.note: Portuguese settlement and claims began centuries before effective conquest of many inland regions. The colonial territory was not identical to the former Kingdom of Kongo.

connectionNodes.title: Angola: independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence on 11 November 1975 came amid conflict among nationalist movements and was followed by civil war. This node does not imply the restoration of the Kingdom of Kongo.

connectionNodes.title: Cape Colony
connectionNodes.note: Dutch settlement began in 1652; British occupation occurred in 1795 and again in 1806. The colony expanded through dispossession, warfare and changing agreements.

connectionNodes.title: Colony of Natal
connectionNodes.note: A British colony preceding the 1910 Union; its borders and political institutions did not represent all communities of the region.

connectionNodes.title: Transvaal Colony
connectionNodes.note: British colonial government after conquest of the South African Republic; this node does not date the beginning of societies in the region.

connectionNodes.title: Orange River Colony
connectionNodes.note: British colonial government following the South African War, before the 1910 Union.

connectionNodes.title: South Africa: democratic constitutional era
connectionNodes.note: The first national election based on universal adult suffrage was held in April 1994. This is a transition within South African state history, not a new population replacing an earlier one.

connectionNodes.title: Maya peoples · living communities
connectionNodes.note: Many distinct Maya peoples, languages and communities persist; this is not a single successor state or a civilisation that ended in 900 CE.

connectionNodes.title: Saint-Domingue · French colonial rule
connectionNodes.note: French colonial society depended on the enslavement of Africans; its overthrow followed a complex revolution, not a routine administrative transfer.

connectionNodes.title: Chimú kingdom / Chimor
connectionNodes.note: A regional kingdom centred on Chan Chan, with artistic traditions drawing on earlier north-coast cultures.

connectionNodes.title: Spanish colonial Peru
connectionNodes.note: Spanish rule developed through conquest and changing jurisdictions; large Indigenous communities and resistance continued.

connectionNodes.title: Peru · independent eras
connectionNodes.note: Independence was proclaimed in 1821; warfare and royalist resistance continued, including the decisive 1824 campaigns.

connectionNodes.title: Quechua-speaking communities
connectionNodes.note: Diverse living communities, not an unchanged Inca state; language, identity and local histories are not interchangeable.

connectionNodes.title: Caddo communities
connectionNodes.note: Distinct confederacies and communities persisted through dispossession and forced removal; historical trade partners are not automatically ancestors.

connectionNodes.title: Pueblo peoples · continuing communities
connectionNodes.note: Many distinct Pueblo nations share connections to Chaco; no single present-day Pueblo is its sole direct successor.

connectionNodes.title: Spanish colonial New Mexico
connectionNodes.location: Northern New Spain · Southwestern North America
connectionNodes.note: Spanish colonisation was contested; the Pueblo Revolt expelled colonists in 1680, followed by reconquest in the 1690s.

connectionNodes.title: East Polynesian voyaging networks
connectionNodes.note: Multiple migrations and connected island societies, not one empire or a single founding voyage.

connectionNodes.title: Kingdom of Tonga · modern eras
connectionNodes.note: Modern consolidation and constitutional government differed from earlier chiefly arrangements; British protection 1900–1970 limited external affairs without annexation.

connectionNodes.title: Fijian societies
connectionNodes.note: Long histories of distinct island communities precede the modern state and continued through colonial rule.

connectionNodes.title: British colonial Fiji
connectionNodes.note: The 1874 cession and colonial administration did not end Indigenous Fijian communities; later migration also shaped society.

connectionNodes.title: Pohnpei · continuing communities
connectionNodes.dates: Island traditions continue · state in FSM since 1979
connectionNodes.note: Nan Madol is associated with living chiefly traditions; modern constitutional statehood is distinct from Saudeleur rule.

connectionNodes.title: Federated States of Micronesia
connectionNodes.note: A federation of four island states with distinct earlier histories; independence developed through constitutional government and the Compact of Free Association.

connectionNodes.title: Rapa Nui people · continuing community
connectionNodes.location: Rapa Nui / Easter Island and diaspora
connectionNodes.note: Rapa Nui people and culture continue beyond the monumental phase; modern administration and Indigenous rights have their own contested history.

connectionNodes.title: Chile · independent state
connectionNodes.note: The 1888 agreement concerns Rapa Nui and Chile; it is not the founding of Chile or the disappearance of Rapa Nui authority.

connectionNodes.title: New Zealand · British colonial era
connectionNodes.note: British sovereignty was proclaimed in 1840; the separate colony followed in 1841, and Māori authority and treaty rights remained contested.

connectionNodes.title: Kenmu Restoration
connectionNodes.note: A brief attempt by Emperor Go-Daigo to restore direct imperial rule; the later Southern Court continued after the Ashikaga seized Kyoto.

connectionNodes.title: Azuchi–Momoyama · unification
connectionNodes.note: Selected political frame for Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Tokugawa consolidation. Art histories often extend the Momoyama period to 1615; it is not a single hereditary dynasty.

connectionNodes.title: Korean Empire
connectionNodes.note: Gojong proclaimed an empire in 1897 within the continuing Yi royal house. Japan imposed a protectorate in 1905 before annexation in 1910.

connectionNodes.title: Korea under Japanese rule
connectionNodes.note: Japanese colonial administration over Korea; Korean resistance, culture and independence movements continued. Colonial government did not represent voluntary political union.

connectionNodes.title: Northern Korea · Soviet occupation
connectionNodes.note: The northern occupation zone after Japanese surrender; local politics and competing projects developed within a Soviet military framework. This was not yet the DPRK at its creation in 1945.

connectionNodes.title: Southern Korea · U.S. military government
connectionNodes.wikiTitle: United States Army Military Government in Korea
connectionNodes.note: The southern occupation zone after Japanese surrender, preceding the Republic of Korea. Local political struggles and violence are not captured by a simple line of institutional succession.

wikipedia.title: United States Army Military Government in Korea

connectionNodes.title: Dutch East India Company · island Southeast Asia
connectionNodes.note: Selected VOC activity in the Indonesian archipelago, not the company’s full Asian reach or uniform control of every island. Local states remained independent or negotiated and fought with the company.

connectionNodes.title: Dutch East Indies
connectionNodes.note: Colonial administration succeeded VOC rule in stages, with British interregnum and later Japanese occupation. Dutch territorial claims were resisted and did not imply uniform control from 1800.

connectionNodes.title: Japanese occupation · East Indies
connectionNodes.wikiTitle: Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies
connectionNodes.note: Japanese military occupation displaced Dutch colonial government during the Second World War; it was not Indonesian independence.

wikipedia.title: Japanese occupation of the Dutch East Indies

connectionNodes.title: Cambodian kingdoms after Angkor
connectionNodes.note: Cambodian courts and capitals continued after Angkor’s political decline amid changing relations with Siam and Vietnam; neither Khmer society nor Angkor’s religious significance ended in 1431.

connectionNodes.title: French protectorate of Cambodia
connectionNodes.note: French colonial control coexisted with a Cambodian monarchy; Japanese wartime intervention and the brief 1945 independence episode interrupted the wider protectorate frame.

connectionNodes.title: Cambodia · independent kingdom
connectionNodes.note: Independent monarchy and Sihanouk-led political order before the 1970 coup; Sihanouk abdicated the throne in 1955 but remained a dominant political leader.

connectionNodes.title: Khmer Republic
connectionNodes.note: Lon Nol’s republican regime emerged after Sihanouk’s removal amid widening regional warfare and civil war.

connectionNodes.title: Khmer Rouge · Democratic Kampuchea
connectionNodes.note: Khmer Rouge rule began with the capture of Phnom Penh in April 1975; the formal Democratic Kampuchea constitution followed in 1976. Forced labour, persecution, mass deaths and genocide marked this regime.

connectionNodes.title: People’s Republic / State of Cambodia
connectionNodes.note: Vietnamese-backed government controlled most of Cambodia while war and international recognition disputes continued; renamed State of Cambodia in 1989, before the 1991 settlement and 1992–1993 UN transition.

connectionNodes.title: Cambodia · restored kingdom
connectionNodes.note: Constitutional monarchy restored after the Paris peace process, UN-sponsored elections and 1993 constitution. Restoration of the royal institution did not erase the preceding republics, wars or their effects.

connectionNodes.title: Nguyễn dynasty
connectionNodes.note: The last Vietnamese royal dynasty continued at Huế after France imposed colonial rule. Its dynastic lifespan must not be equated with uninterrupted sovereignty over modern Vietnam.

connectionNodes.title: French Indochina
connectionNodes.note: A colonial federation developed through conquests and protectorates over different territories, including Vietnam, Cambodia and later Laos; Japanese wartime control and independence movements interrupted the frame.

connectionNodes.title: Democratic Republic of Vietnam
connectionNodes.note: Independence proclaimed in 1945; the government controlled the northern regroupment zone after the 1954 agreements and later won the war. This was not a state first founded in 1954.

connectionNodes.title: Southern Vietnam · State and Republic
connectionNodes.note: Selected umbrella for the State of Vietnam from 1949 and the Republic proclaimed in 1955; administrative control and borders were contested throughout the wars.

connectionNodes.title: Northern Yuan and post-Yuan Mongol courts
connectionNodes.note: After losing the main Chinese realm, Yuan rulers retreated to Mongolia; successor courts and confederations competed with Oirat powers. Later regional Mongol histories extended beyond the Northern Yuan dynastic endpoint.

connectionNodes.title: Khalkha Mongol principalities
connectionNodes.location: Mongolian plateau north of the Gobi
connectionNodes.note: Selected regional political frame north of the Gobi, not the full lifespan of Khalkha people. This branch is not identical to all Mongols or every Northern Yuan successor polity.

connectionNodes.title: Bogd Khanate of Mongolia
connectionNodes.note: Independence declared in 1911, with contested autonomy and Chinese military reoccupation in 1919; the Bogd Khan returned in 1921 before the 1924 republic.

connectionNodes.title: Mongolian People’s Republic
connectionNodes.note: A Soviet-aligned socialist state, not a Soviet Union constituent republic. The democratic revolution began in 1990 before the constitutional state-name change in 1992.

connectionNodes.title: Mongolia · democratic constitutional era
connectionNodes.note: The peaceful democratic transition began in 1990 and a new constitution followed in 1992; this was a change of political system within a continuing state, not the origin of Mongolian people.

connectionNodes.title: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and settlement
connectionNodes.note: Several kingdoms formed amid migration, conflict and interaction with existing British communities; this was never one united state spanning the full frame.

connectionNodes.title: Rus’ principalities · regional realms
connectionNodes.note: An overlapping network of principalities, not a state created at one partition. Their later histories fed into several countries and cannot be assigned exclusively to modern Russia, Ukraine or Belarus.

connectionNodes.title: Grand Duchy of Lithuania
connectionNodes.note: A multiethnic polity that incorporated many western and southern Rus’ lands. It entered dynastic union with Poland and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth; this map selects its relationship with Rus’, not its entire history.

connectionNodes.title: Belarus · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Moldova · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Armenia · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Azerbaijan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Georgia · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Kyrgyzstan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Tajikistan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Turkmenistan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Uzbekistan · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Selected independent-state frame after Soviet dissolution; earlier regional histories and communities predate 1991.

connectionNodes.title: Estonia · restored independence
connectionNodes.note: Restored independence after Soviet occupation and annexation, rather than the beginning of the country’s history.

connectionNodes.title: Latvia · restored independence
connectionNodes.note: Restored independence after Soviet occupation and annexation, rather than the beginning of the country’s history.

connectionNodes.title: Lithuania · restored independence
connectionNodes.note: Restored independence after Soviet occupation and annexation, rather than the beginning of the country’s history.

connectionNodes.title: Abu’l-Khayr’s Uzbek steppe realm
connectionNodes.note: A post-Horde steppe realm; not the modern state of Uzbekistan or all Uzbek communities.

connectionNodes.title: Kazakh khanate and zhuzes
connectionNodes.note: Kerei and Janibek established a khanate after migration into Moghulistan. Later zhuzes had distinct, overlapping political paths.

connectionNodes.title: Bukhara and Transoxiana · khanate eras
connectionNodes.note: Shibanid, Janid and early Manghit arrangements are grouped; capitals, borders and the location of effective authority changed.

connectionNodes.title: Emirate of Bukhara
connectionNodes.location: Parts of present-day Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and neighbouring countries
connectionNodes.note: Manghit emirate; Russian domination after 1868 did not immediately abolish the emir’s government.

connectionNodes.title: Khwarazm / Khanate of Khiva
connectionNodes.note: Founded by a separate Jochid dynasty; not an offshoot of modern Uzbekistan or an ethnically uniform state.

connectionNodes.title: Khanate of Kokand
connectionNodes.note: A Fergana-based khanate whose expansion included diverse settled and nomadic communities.

connectionNodes.title: Russian rule in Central Asia
connectionNodes.note: A regional overview of annexed territories and unequal protectorates, not one uniform administration.

connectionNodes.title: Central Asia · revolution and early Soviet governments
connectionNodes.note: War, autonomous experiments, Soviet republics and resistance preceded the five union-republic framework.

connectionNodes.title: Moghulistan · eastern Chagataid realms
connectionNodes.location: Ili, Tian Shan and Tarim regions
connectionNodes.note: The eastern Chagataid political world continued after Timur’s rise in the west; rule later divided into regional branches.

connectionNodes.title: Yarkent Khanate
connectionNodes.note: One eastern Chagataid realm, with power increasingly contested by Khoja lineages and regional lords.

connectionNodes.title: Turpan · Chagataid and later oasis rule
connectionNodes.note: A selected regional frame; Chagataid rulers, local leaders and Dzungar overlords were distinct phases.

connectionNodes.title: Tarim Khoja governments under Dzungar supremacy
connectionNodes.note: Competing Sufi lineages ruled or influenced oasis governments; Dzungar khans demanded tribute and hostages.

connectionNodes.title: Dzungar Khanate
connectionNodes.location: Dzungaria and expanding Inner Asian territories
connectionNodes.note: An Oirat Mongol state, distinct from Chagataid realms. Qing conquest destroyed its government and devastated its population.

connectionNodes.title: Herodian Judea
connectionNodes.note: A Roman client kingdom; dates combine Herod’s kingdom and Archelaus’s reduced ethnarchy.

connectionNodes.title: Anatolian beyliks
connectionNodes.note: Many rival principalities emerged in a landscape of weakening Seljuq, Mongol, and Byzantine control.

connectionNodes.title: British occupation & mandate project in Iraq
connectionNodes.note: Wartime occupation, a mandate project, and treaty supervision overlapped with the monarchy established in 1921.

connectionNodes.title: French mandate: Syria & Lebanon
connectionNodes.wikiTitle: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon
connectionNodes.note: French rule created and reorganized several administrations, not one enduring national state.

wikipedia.title: Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon

connectionNodes.title: Lebanon · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence in 1943 and final French troop withdrawal in 1946 were separate milestones.

connectionNodes.title: Syria · independent state
connectionNodes.note: Independence involved wartime recognition and transfer of power followed by French withdrawal in 1946.

connectionNodes.title: Kingdom of Hejaz & Nejd
connectionNodes.note: Ibn Saud’s dominions followed conquest and consolidation of distinct regions; this was not all Arabia.

connectionNodes.title: British Mandate for Palestine
connectionNodes.location: Eastern Mediterranean · west of the Jordan River
connectionNodes.note: British administration followed Ottoman defeat; Transjordan was administered separately.

connectionNodes.title: Emirate of Transjordan
connectionNodes.note: An autonomous Arab administration within the mandate framework; its provisions differed from Palestine west of the Jordan.

connectionNodes.title: Jordan · independent kingdom
connectionNodes.note: Independent as Transjordan in 1946, later renamed Jordan; borders and territorial claims changed.

connectionNodes.title: Palestine Liberation Organization
connectionNodes.note: A national representative organization, not a country or an unchanged government.

connectionNodes.title: Deccan sultanates
connectionNodes.note: Five major sultanates succeeded Bahmanid fragmentation; their political relations changed repeatedly.

connectionNodes.title: Durrani Empire
connectionNodes.note: Durrani rule had regional continuations and a British-backed restoration after this principal phase.

connectionNodes.title: Afghanistan · Barakzai rule
connectionNodes.note: Emirs and kings ruled with interruptions; territory and foreign-policy independence changed.

connectionNodes.title: Afghanistan · later regimes
connectionNodes.note: Groups republican, communist, wartime, and Taliban governments; these are distinct regimes, including Taliban takeover in 2021.

topics.title: Roman Republican conquest and rule in Iberia
topics.shortTitle: Roman Republican conquest and rule in Iberia
topics.note: Roman intervention began in 218 BCE, but conquest lasted into the Augustan period. This is a regional phase of the Republic, not a second Roman state.
topics.wikiTitle: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

wikipedia.title: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

topics.title: Roman Republican conquest of Gaul
topics.note: The poster marks 58 BCE. Caesar’s wars ran through 50 BCE, while Roman rule in southern Gaul began earlier.

topics.title: Cycladic culture · Early Bronze Age
topics.note: Early Cycladic chronology is approximate and distinct from the Minoan and mainland Mycenaean sequences. Added explicitly to make the poster’s Aegean umbrella meaningful.

topics.title: Macedonian hegemony · Philip II and Alexander
topics.shortTitle: Macedonian hegemony · Philip II and Alexander
topics.note: 338 BCE marks Philip II’s victory at Chaeronea. Alexander’s Asian conquests began in 334 BCE; his death in 323 BCE initiated succession struggles, rather than instantly creating stable successor states.

topics.title: Roman expansion into Greece
topics.note: The destruction of Corinth in 146 BCE is a conventional marker; incorporation and provincial organisation occurred in stages. This is a regional phase of the Roman Republic.

topics.title: Anglo-Saxon England
topics.note: Approximate settlement and early English kingdom frame. It overlaps British polities, Scandinavian rule and the later unified kingdom, rather than replacing every inhabitant.

topics.title: House of Wessex · selected royal phase
topics.shortTitle: House of Wessex · selected royal phase
topics.note: 802 marks Ecgberht’s accession in Wessex; 829 was a temporary supremacy, not the founding of a united England. The selected dynasty frame includes interruptions by Danish rulers; unification is conventionally placed in 927.

topics.title: Norman dynasty in England
topics.note: The Norman conquest began in 1066. This selected royal period ends with Henry II’s accession in 1154 and does not mean England and Normandy always had identical institutions.

topics.title: Plantagenet kings of England
topics.note: A broad dynastic convention including Angevin, Lancaster and York branches. It does not describe a single stable government or peaceful succession.

topics.title: Tudor dynasty
topics.note: The Tudor royal period runs from Henry VII’s victory in 1485 to Elizabeth I’s death in 1603. Wales, Ireland and England had different relationships to royal government.

topics.title: Stuarts in England, Scotland and Great Britain
topics.shortTitle: Stuarts in England, Scotland and Great Britain
topics.note: The shared crowns began in 1603; England and Scotland remained separate kingdoms until 1707. Republican rule interrupted the monarchy in 1649–1660, and William III was of the House of Orange.

topics.title: Hanoverian monarchy in Britain
