topics.note: The British Hanoverian royal period runs 1714–1901, not to the poster’s 1917 boundary. Shared monarchy with Hanover ended in 1837 because succession laws differed.

topics.title: House of Windsor
topics.note: 1917 marks the adoption of the royal house name Windsor. It is a dynastic phase within the United Kingdom, not the state’s foundation.

topics.title: Iberian Union
topics.note: Portugal and the Spanish crowns shared Habsburg monarchs. Separate laws, institutions and overseas possessions persisted; this was not complete administrative fusion.

topics.title: Portuguese Restoration and Braganza monarchy
topics.note: 1640 began the restored Portuguese monarchy and the war for recognition, which Spain accepted in 1668. The restored kingdom continued beyond this war and was not newly founded again in 1807.

topics.title: Portugal · constitutional monarchy
topics.note: The Liberal Revolution of 1820 began the constitutional transition; the first constitution followed in 1822. Civil war and absolutist restoration interrupted constitutional government before 1834. The poster’s 1807 start belongs to the French invasions.

topics.title: First Portuguese Republic
topics.note: The First Republic began with the revolution of 5 October 1910 and ended in the military coup of 1926; it did not continue unbroken until Estado Novo in 1933.

topics.title: Portugal · Estado Novo dictatorship
topics.note: The authoritarian Estado Novo was institutionalised in 1933 and overthrown in the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974. A military dictatorship preceded it in 1926–1933.

topics.title: Portugal · democratic republic
topics.note: The democratic transition began in 1974 and the constitution took effect in 1976; the poster uses the constitutional date.

topics.title: Late medieval Iberian conquests and Granada
topics.shortTitle: Late medieval Iberian conquests and Granada
topics.note: 1238 marks the Nasrid foundation convention selected by the poster. Reconquista is a retrospective, contested umbrella rather than one continuous national war; Christian and Muslim rulers also allied across religious boundaries.

topics.title: Dynastic union of Castile and Aragon
topics.shortTitle: Dynastic union of Castile and Aragon
topics.note: 1479 marks the shared rule of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon after Ferdinand’s Aragonese accession. The crowns retained separate institutions; this was not instant state or territorial unification.

topics.title: Habsburg Spain
topics.note: A composite monarchy under the Spanish Habsburgs. Charles I’s accession in 1516 is the selected start; the crowns and territories retained distinct laws and institutions.

topics.title: Spain · early Bourbon monarchy and reforms
topics.shortTitle: Spain · early Bourbon monarchy and reforms
topics.note: A selected eighteenth-century reform frame under Bourbon rulers, with a major overseas dimension. The reforms were introduced in different territories at different times; not every reform began in 1700.

topics.title: Spain · constitutional struggles and regime changes
topics.shortTitle: Spain · constitutional struggles and regime changes
topics.note: Spain’s first national constitution dates to 1812, not 1808; the Bayonne Statute was imposed under Napoleonic influence. The period includes restored absolutism, constitutional monarchies, republics and dictatorship.

topics.title: Francoist Spain
topics.note: The regime emerged during the Civil War from 1936 and controlled the whole country after 1939. Franco died in 1975, followed by a democratic transition; the 1978 constitution is a separate milestone.

topics.title: Spain · parliamentary constitutional monarchy
topics.note: The democratic transition followed Franco’s death in 1975; the constitution was approved in 1978. This frame does not imply that Spain came into existence in 1978.

topics.title: France · Bourbon monarchy before the Revolution
topics.shortTitle: France · Bourbon monarchy before the Revolution
topics.note: Henry IV’s accession in 1589 begins the selected Bourbon royal frame. Bourbon restoration in 1814–1830 is a later phase, interrupted by Napoleon’s Hundred Days.

topics.title: First French Republic
topics.note: The monarchy was abolished in 1792. The republic included the Convention, Directory and Consulate before Napoleon’s imperial title in 1804.

topics.title: First French Empire
topics.note: Napoleon’s empire lasted 1804–1814 and returned during the Hundred Days in 1815. The poster’s long black band crosses countries with different occupation dates and incorrectly suggests uniform annexation.

topics.title: French invasions of Portugal
topics.note: Three French invasions occurred in 1807–1811. Portugal was not permanently annexed to the First French Empire; the royal court moved to Brazil and Anglo-Portuguese forces resisted.

topics.title: Spain under Napoleonic occupation and war
topics.shortTitle: Spain under Napoleonic occupation and war
topics.note: Joseph Bonaparte’s imposed monarchy and French occupation faced competing Spanish governments and armed resistance. The whole country was never securely governed as one French province.

topics.title: Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy
topics.note: A northern Italian kingdom under Napoleon, not the whole peninsula. Other areas were annexed to France, governed by allied states or remained outside his rule.

topics.title: Confederation of the Rhine
topics.note: A confederation of German states under Napoleon’s protection, not wholesale French annexation of Germany. The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806.

topics.title: France · changing regimes, 1815–1946
topics.note: The poster’s label is inaccurate: restored monarchies ruled in 1815–1848 and the Second Empire in 1852–1870. The period also includes the Second and Third Republics, occupation, Vichy and provisional government.

topics.title: Fourth and Fifth French republics
topics.note: The Fourth Republic lasted 1946–1958, followed by the Fifth Republic. This country phase is not a single unchanging constitution.

topics.title: Eastern Roman rule in Italy
topics.note: Justinian’s reconquest began in 535; Byzantine rule survived in changing parts of Italy until Bari fell in 1071. The poster’s 553–774 band is only a selected phase, not the full duration.

topics.title: Italy · regional states and foreign intervention
topics.shortTitle: Italy · regional states and foreign intervention
topics.note: 1494 marks the start of the Italian Wars, not the first division of Italy. Regional states and competing foreign powers continued through the early modern period, with major changes during the Napoleonic wars.

topics.title: Kingdom of Italy
topics.note: The kingdom was proclaimed in 1861; Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Fascist dictatorship developed within the monarchy; the republican referendum took place in 1946.

topics.title: Italian Republic
topics.note: The referendum of 2 June 1946 chose a republic; official confirmation followed in June, and the constitution took effect on 1 January 1948.

topics.title: Kingdom of Prussia
topics.note: The royal title was adopted in 1701. Prussia did not cease in 1871: it became the largest constituent kingdom of the German Empire and its monarchy ended in 1918.

topics.title: German Confederation
topics.note: A loose confederation established at Vienna in 1815 and dissolved in 1866; it was not a united Germany. The North German Confederation followed in 1867 before imperial unification in 1871.

topics.title: German Empire
topics.note: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 and its monarchy fell in 1918. The 1919 constitution belongs to the subsequent republic, not the continuation of imperial monarchy.

topics.title: Weimar Republic
topics.note: Republican government was proclaimed in November 1918; the Weimar constitution followed in 1919. Nazi dictatorship developed after Hitler’s appointment in January 1933.

topics.title: Nazi Germany
topics.note: Nazi rule lasted 1933–1945, with escalating dictatorship, aggressive war and genocide. Territorial extent changed; occupation zones followed military defeat.

topics.title: Germany · occupation and two German states
topics.shortTitle: Germany · occupation and two German states
topics.note: Allied occupation began in 1945; the Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic were founded separately in 1949. The poster’s 1945 label must not imply that both states already existed then.

topics.title: Germany · reunified Federal Republic
topics.note: The GDR acceded to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Federal Republic itself dates from 1949; modern German history did not begin in 1990.

topics.title: First Austrian Republic
topics.note: Republican Austria emerged in 1918; democratic parliamentary government was dismantled in 1933 and the authoritarian Federal State replaced the constitutional republic in 1934. Nazi annexation followed in 1938.

topics.title: Second Austrian Republic
topics.note: The republic was restored in 1945, not in 1955. Allied occupation ended under the 1955 State Treaty, followed by constitutional permanent neutrality.

topics.title: Austria · State Treaty and restored sovereignty
topics.shortTitle: Austria · State Treaty and restored sovereignty
topics.note: The 1955 State Treaty ended Allied occupation. The Second Republic had already been restored in 1945, and the neutrality law was a separate act of October 1955.

topics.title: Byzantine successor states after 1204
topics.note: After the Fourth Crusade, Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond were distinct successor powers. Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261; Trebizond survived until 1461. This was not one state ending uniformly in 1453.
topics.wikiTitle: Byzantine Empire under the Laskarid dynasty

topics.title: Empire of Nicaea
topics.note: Nicaea was one of several Byzantine successor states after 1204. Its rulers recovered Constantinople in 1261, rather than founding an unrelated empire.

topics.title: Despotate of Epirus
topics.note: An approximate successor-state frame; the conventional name is retrospective and political control changed. Ottoman conquest of the last Tocco-held territories in 1479 is a conventional endpoint.

topics.title: Empire of Trebizond
topics.note: The Komnenian empire on the Black Sea survived Constantinople’s fall in 1453 and was conquered by the Ottomans in 1461.

topics.title: Latin Empire of Constantinople
topics.note: The crusader-founded Latin Empire occupied Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade. It was distinct from the Byzantine successor states and ended there with the city’s recovery in 1261.

topics.title: Latin states in the Greek world
topics.shortTitle: Latin states in the Greek world
topics.note: A broad, non-unitary regional category for Latin and Venetian rule after the Fourth Crusade. Different territories had different durations; some Venetian Ionian possessions survived until 1797. The poster’s tiny band cannot represent one uniform state.

topics.title: Kingdom of Greece · first royal phase
topics.shortTitle: Kingdom of Greece · first royal phase
topics.note: The monarchy was established in 1832 after the independence struggle and international recognition. Borders expanded later; the Second Hellenic Republic replaced the monarchy in 1924.

topics.title: Second Hellenic Republic
topics.note: The republic lasted 1924–1935 and faced coups and instability. Monarchy was restored in 1935.

topics.title: Kingdom of Greece · restored monarchy
topics.note: The restored royal period included Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation, civil war and the 1967 military coup. The junta abolished the monarchy in 1973; democratic institutions returned in 1974.

topics.title: Third Hellenic Republic · democratic Greece
topics.note: The junta proclaimed a republic in 1973, but democratic transition began in July 1974; a free December 1974 referendum rejected monarchy and the constitution followed in June 1975.

topics.title: Restored Byzantine Empire · Palaiologan period
topics.note: Michael VIII recovered Constantinople in 1261. The restored empire occupied a reduced and changing territory and ended in Constantinople in 1453; some Byzantine successor territories survived later.
topics.wikiTitle: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty

wikipedia.title: Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty

topics.title: Egypt · Early Dynastic period
topics.note: Approximate dynastic chronology. Egypt had substantial predynastic societies before unification; this is not the beginning of Egyptian culture.

topics.title: Egypt · Old Kingdom
topics.note: Approximate traditional chronology; the pyramid-building era, not an uninterrupted ethnic or national founding.

topics.title: Egypt · First Intermediate period
topics.note: Regional dynasties overlapped. Alternative chronologies put the Middle Kingdom reunification around 2030 BCE.

topics.title: Egypt · Middle Kingdom
topics.note: Approximate Egyptian ministry periodization; other scholarly chronologies begin around 2030 BCE or use a narrower end date.

topics.title: Egypt · Second Intermediate period
topics.note: Regional courts, including Hyksos rule in the north and the Theban kingdom in the south, coexisted; not a single dynasty.

topics.title: Egypt · New Kingdom
topics.note: Approximate dynastic period, traditionally Dynasties 18–20.

topics.title: Egypt · Third Intermediate period
topics.note: Competing royal lines and regional powers overlapped; the poster’s 1070 is a rounded alternative.

topics.title: Egypt · Late Period
topics.note: The poster truncates this at the first Persian conquest 525 BCE. The full Late Period conventionally includes Persian and restored native dynasties through 332 BCE.

topics.title: Early Islamic caliphates · Rashidun and Umayyad
topics.shortTitle: Early Islamic caliphates · Rashidun and Umayyad
topics.note: The poster uses 633,641 and 651 for regional conquests. The Rashidun 632–661 and Umayyad 661–750 states are separate, already represented histories; Egypt conquered 639–642 and Sasanian defeat unfolded 633–651.

topics.title: Egypt · British occupation and protectorate
topics.note: Occupation began 1882; the formal protectorate lasted 1914–1922. British influence, treaty rights and forces persisted after limited independence 1922.
topics.wikiTitle: History of Egypt under the British

wikipedia.title: History of Egypt under the British

topics.title: Kingdom of Egypt
topics.note: Independence declared 1922 with important British reservations; monarchy abolished 1953.

topics.title: Egypt · republican eras
topics.note: Republic proclaimed 1953. The existing broad modern-Egypt entry begins 1922; this adds its republican phase explicitly.

topics.title: Neo-Sumerian revival · Ur III
topics.note: The poster’s 2154–1894 frame conflates several post-Akkadian dynasties. Ur III is 2112–2004 BCE; earlier Lagash II and later Isin-Larsa states are distinct.

topics.title: Iran · Pahlavi dynasty
topics.note: Reza Khan’s 1921 coup preceded the foundation of the Pahlavi monarchy 1925. Monarchy overthrown 1979.

topics.title: Iran · Islamic Republic era
topics.note: Revolution and Islamic Republic established 1979; the broader history of Iran and its society long predates this constitutional phase.
topics.wikiTitle: History of the Islamic Republic of Iran

wikipedia.title: History of the Islamic Republic of Iran

topics.title: Sengoku period
topics.note: Conventional broad Warring States frame from the Ōnin War; proposed end dates 1568,1573,1600 or 1615 depend on the event emphasized.1603 is the Tokugawa establishment, not a universally agreed period end.

topics.title: Japan · Meiji era
topics.note: Meiji is an imperial era within modern imperial Japan, not a separate state preceding the empire.

topics.title: Empire of Japan
topics.note: The poster starts 1912, which omits the Meiji imperial state. Broad constitutional-political frame 1868–1947; defeat 1945 and constitutional change 1947 are distinct endpoints.

topics.title: Japan · postwar constitutional era
topics.note: Current constitution effective 3 May 1947. Allied occupation began 1945 and ended 1952 for most of Japan;1947 is not independence or the creation of Japan.

topics.title: Indus · Early Harappan phase
topics.note: A regionalization period including Ravi/Hakra and Kot Diji phases; dates and material traditions vary by site. Complements the existing Mature Harappan band.
topics.wikiTitle: Periodisation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

wikipedia.title: Periodisation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

topics.title: Indus · Late Harappan traditions
topics.note: Urban decentralization and regional cultural continuities after the Mature phase; site chronologies vary. This does not imply the disappearance of people or traditions.
topics.wikiTitle: Periodisation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

wikipedia.title: Periodisation of the Indus Valley Civilisation

topics.title: Indigenous peoples of the present-day United States
topics.shortTitle: Indigenous peoples of the present-day United States
topics.note: The poster groups many peoples into one band. Indigenous histories long predate the United States and continue today. There is no single founding year or collective end at European settlement; archaeological societies and living nations have their own histories.
topics.wikiTitle: Native Americans in the United States
posterLabels: Indigenous Era · Native American Civilizations (Iroquois, Pueblo, etc.)

wikipedia.title: Native Americans in the United States

topics.title: Haudenosaunee / Iroquois Confederacy
topics.note: Haudenosaunee is the confederacy’s own name. Oral traditions and scholarly chronologies differ about its foundation; no disputed date is treated as settled. The Six Nations and their political and cultural traditions continue.

topics.title: Pueblo peoples · ancestral and living communities
topics.shortTitle: Pueblo peoples · ancestral and living communities
topics.note: Pueblo peoples include distinct contemporary communities with ancestral ties to sites such as Mesa Verde and Chaco. The abandonment of a settlement is not the disappearance of its people.

topics.title: Indigenous peoples in present-day Canada
topics.note: First Nations, Inuit and Métis are distinct groups, not one ancient state or a culture that ended at colonisation. Métis communities formed in particular colonial-era historical contexts; their identity should not be projected unchanged into antiquity.
posterLabels: Indigenous Era · Inuit, First Nations & Métis

topics.title: Inuit
topics.note: Inuit histories span different Arctic regions and communities. This cultural entry has no single founding year and does not date all earlier Arctic peoples as Inuit.

topics.title: First Nations
topics.note: First Nations is a collective term for many distinct Indigenous peoples in Canada; it does not include Inuit or Métis and is not the name of a single ancient state.

topics.title: Métis peoples
topics.dates: Distinct communities emerging in the colonial era · continuing
topics.note: Métis peoples and nationhood developed in specific historical communities, particularly in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The poster’s continuous ancient-to-colonial band must not be read as a date for Métis origins.

topics.title: Mesoamerican societies
topics.dates: Many archaeological periods and living peoples
topics.note: Olmec traditions, Maya societies, Teotihuacan and the Mexica-led Triple Alliance belong to different places and periods. The poster’s shared band is not one uninterrupted empire, and Indigenous societies continue after Spanish conquest.
posterLabels: Indigenous Era · Olmec, Maya, Aztec & Other Civilizations

topics.title: Indigenous peoples of Oceania
topics.note: Māori settlement of Aotearoa New Zealand dates to approximately the late thirteenth century; other Pacific populations have their own earlier and later settlement histories. This broad label is not a single state, people or shared founding date.
posterLabels: Indigenous Era · Māori & Other Indigenous Cultures

topics.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
topics.shortTitle: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
topics.note: Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct cultural groups comprising many communities. European colonisation and federation did not end their histories or identities.
posterLabels: Indigenous Era · Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultures

topics.title: Torres Strait Islander peoples
topics.dates: Living island cultures · no single founding year
topics.note: Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct island homelands, languages and histories. They are not simply another name for Aboriginal Australians.

topics.title: Canada · French and British colonial periods
topics.shortTitle: Canada · French and British colonial periods
topics.note: 1608 marks the founding of Quebec, not the first European presence or the beginning of the region’s history. French and British rule followed different territorial timelines; Canada’s Confederation in 1867 was a later partial union, not immediate full independence. See New France and British northern colonies for distinct frames.
posterLabels: Colonial Canada · French and British Colonial Settlements

topics.title: Bronze Age
topics.note: An archaeological period defined by particular technologies and social changes, with different dates in different regions. A single global date band cannot describe every society on this timeline.

topics.title: Early Bronze Age
topics.note: A regional subdivision of the Bronze Age, especially used in Near Eastern and European chronologies. It does not begin and end everywhere at the same date.

topics.title: Iron Age
topics.note: An archaeological period whose chronology varies regionally. Ironworking spread through different societies over a long period; it is not a global change occurring in one year.

topics.title: Classical Antiquity
topics.note: A conventional period focused on the ancient Mediterranean. Its boundaries are approximate and it should not be treated as the name for every contemporary society worldwide.

topics.title: The Middle Ages
topics.note: A conventional European period, often approximately the fifth to fifteenth centuries. Histories elsewhere use their own periodisations; the chart’s common date scale allows comparison without assigning all societies to a European age.

topics.title: The Modern Era
topics.note: A broad historical convention, often beginning around 1500 in European periodisation. The Modern era chart starts at 1450 to include major transitions; this is a viewing window rather than a single worldwide beginning.

topics.title: BCE / CE date axis
topics.note: BCE and CE use the same year numbering as BC and AD. There is no year zero. Approximate dates and scholarly disagreements are explained in individual entries; the chart uses one linear scale.

topics.title: Historical Landmark · legend
topics.note: Landmarks have their own construction, use and alteration histories. Their placement beside a political period in the reference poster is not evidence that the place originated in that period. Select Landmarks in the index for the dated entries.

topics.title: Landmark illustrations and symbols
topics.note: The poster’s decorative monument illustrations are not chronological evidence. In particular a later Japanese pagoda should not be read as a Jōmon-period building. This atlas separates monument histories from the surrounding political and archaeological periods.

topics.title: National flags · country labels
topics.note: The flags identify the modern countries in the poster’s bottom row. They do not represent ancient polities, imply continuous borders or establish direct descent from every earlier society. The country shortcuts in the index open the corresponding modern histories.

topics.title: Digital revolution
topics.note: A long worldwide transition involving electronics, computers and networks, not a single national invention or founding date. The transistor of 1947 is one precursor.

topics.title: Discovery and clinical use of insulin
topics.shortTitle: Discovery and clinical use of insulin
topics.note: The Toronto work involved Frederick Banting, Charles Best, J. J. R. Macleod and James Collip, alongside earlier international research; not the achievement of one person alone.

topics.title: Maize domestication
topics.location: Southwestern Mexico, followed by wider American cultivation
topics.note: A gradual Indigenous domestication process, not an invention by one later empire. Its beginning predates this timeline’s 3500 BCE start.

topics.title: Maya astronomy
topics.dates: Developed across Preclassic, Classic and Postclassic Maya histories
topics.note: No single invention date is justified. Maya observations, calendars and eclipse tables developed over centuries; surviving Dresden Codex astronomy reflects a later manuscript tradition.

topics.title: Tango
topics.location: Río de la Plata · Argentina and Uruguay
topics.note: Developed in Buenos Aires and Montevideo from multiple cultural traditions. It belongs to both Argentina and Uruguay, rather than one country alone.

topics.title: Wireless LAN innovations and Wi-Fi
topics.dates: 1992 · CSIRO WLAN breakthrough; Wi-Fi standards developed internationally
topics.location: Australia and international research and standards networks
topics.note: CSIRO’s Australian team made an important high-speed wireless LAN contribution. Wi-Fi as a whole involved many inventors, companies and IEEE standards; “Australia invented all Wi-Fi” overstates it.

topics.title: Newton’s laws of motion and universal gravitation
topics.shortTitle: Newton’s laws of motion and universal gravitation
topics.note: Newton formulated these in the Principia, building on earlier mathematical and physical work. This is not the first human awareness of motion or gravity.

topics.title: Watt’s separate condenser
topics.note: Watt greatly improved steam-engine efficiency; he did not invent the first steam engine. Newcomen and other predecessors must not disappear from the account.

topics.title: Evolution by natural selection
topics.dates: 1858 · Darwin–Wallace presentation; 1859 · On the Origin of Species
topics.location: Britain and research across multiple continents
topics.note: Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed explanations of natural selection and their work was jointly presented in 1858.

topics.title: Vasco da Gama’s sea voyage to India
topics.shortTitle: Vasco da Gama’s sea voyage to India
topics.location: Portugal, Africa and the Indian Ocean
topics.note: This opened a Portuguese Cape route to India, entering existing African, Arab, South Asian and other Indian Ocean trade networks. It was not the discovery of India or the first sea route there.
topics.wikiTitle: Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India

wikipedia.title: Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India

topics.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
topics.shortTitle: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
topics.note: This French revolutionary declaration is a particular document, not the beginning of all rights traditions. Its stated universality coexisted with exclusions in political and colonial practice.
topics.wikiTitle: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

wikipedia.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

topics.title: Development of the metric system
topics.note: The French metric reforms and modern SI are related but not identical. SI was established in 1960 and continues to develop.

topics.title: European Renaissance
topics.dates: c. 14th–17th centuries · dates vary by region
topics.note: A broad cultural and intellectual period with regional variation, drawing on classical, Byzantine, Islamic and other knowledge transmissions; not one event or a universal historical stage.

topics.title: The petrol automobile
topics.dates: 1886 · Benz motor-car patent, among a longer development
topics.note: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen is an early practical petrol automobile. Earlier steam road vehicles and parallel work by other inventors mean “first automobile” needs qualification.

topics.title: Special and general relativity
topics.location: Switzerland and Germany; wider scientific community
topics.note: These are two connected theories, not a single publication. Einstein’s work developed within a wider mathematical and physical research community.

topics.title: The Classical period in Western music
topics.shortTitle: The Classical period in Western music
topics.note: “Classical music” also names a much broader Western tradition. These dates refer to the Classical period associated with Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, not all classical traditions worldwide.

topics.title: Ancient and modern Olympic Games
topics.dates: 776 BCE · traditional first recorded ancient Games; 1896 · modern revival
topics.note: 776 BCE is the traditional recorded starting point, not proof that athletic festivals began then. Modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896.

topics.title: Development of Athenian democracy
topics.dates: 508/507 BCE · Cleisthenes’ reforms; further changes in the 5th century BCE
topics.note: Athenian democracy developed in stages. Political participation excluded women, enslaved people and resident foreigners; the date does not describe modern universal suffrage or every participatory tradition.

topics.title: Justinian’s codification of Roman law
topics.note: The Code is one part of the wider Corpus Juris Civilis, alongside the Digest and Institutes and later Novels. It compiled and revised a long Roman legal tradition.

topics.title: Egyptian pyramid building
topics.dates: From the 27th century BCE · major Old Kingdom building
topics.note: Djoser’s Step Pyramid precedes the great Giza pyramids. Pyramid-shaped monuments also arose in other societies; the poster’s Egyptian marker is not a universal beginning.

topics.title: Code of Hammurabi
topics.dates: 18th century BCE · often dated c. 1750 BCE
topics.note: A major surviving Babylonian legal collection, not the world’s earliest law code. Earlier Mesopotamian legal collections survive.

topics.title: Yoga traditions
topics.dates: Ancient roots; documented traditions in the first millennium BCE onward
topics.note: Yoga developed across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and other traditions. There is no agreed single origin date; interpreting Indus images as proof of modern yoga is uncertain.

topics.title: Zero: placeholders and a number
topics.dates: Multiple developments; 628 CE · Brahmagupta’s arithmetic rules
topics.note: Distinguish placeholder symbols from zero as an arithmetic number. Babylonian, Maya and South Asian developments cannot be reduced to a single inventor or place; 628 is an anchor for one important Indian text.

topics.title: Papermaking in early China
topics.dates: Earlier Han-period evidence; 105 CE · traditional Cai Lun report
topics.note: Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving and reporting the process, not necessarily making the very first paper. Archaeological paper predates 105 CE.

topics.title: Magnetic compasses and navigation
topics.dates: Earlier magnetic direction-finding; navigational use documented by the late 11th–early 12th centuries
topics.note: Ancient lodestone direction-finding and medieval navigational compasses are distinct stages. The approximate year 1100 is an ordering anchor for documented Song-era navigation, not a single invention date.

topics.title: Toyota Production System and lean manufacturing
topics.shortTitle: Toyota Production System and lean manufacturing
topics.dates: Mid-20th-century development; earlier roots and later international adoption
topics.note: Toyota’s just-in-time and jidoka practices developed over decades and drew on earlier production ideas. “Lean” is a later term; no single invention year is adequate.

topics.title: Tōkaidō Shinkansen opens
topics.note: The Shinkansen opened a purpose-built high-speed passenger railway; this does not mean trains or high-speed experiments began in 1964.

topics.title: Pyramids of Giza
topics.note: The poster names the Great Pyramid; the linked complex includes the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. These were built in the Old Kingdom, not at its opening boundary.

topics.title: Karnak temple complex
topics.dates: From the Middle Kingdom, with major later additions
topics.note: A temple complex expanded over many reigns, especially in the New Kingdom, rather than one Middle Kingdom construction.

topics.title: Abu Simbel temples
topics.dates: 13th century BCE · reign of Ramesses II
topics.note: Ramesside rock-cut temples, relocated during the UNESCO Nubian monuments campaign in the 20th century.

topics.title: Great Ziggurat of Ur
topics.dates: c. 21st century BCE, with later restorations
topics.note: Associated with Ur-Nammu and the Third Dynasty of Ur, not the entire loosely named “Sumerian Renaissance.”

topics.title: Mohenjo-daro
topics.note: The city belongs to the Mature Harappan phase. A poster placement near 3000 BCE should not imply that every surviving structure dates to then.

topics.title: Chogha Zanbil
topics.note: An Elamite sacred complex built under Untash-Napirisha, not a monument constructed by later Iranian-speaking tribes.

topics.title: Taxila archaeological sites
topics.dates: Multiple settlement phases · from the first millennium BCE onward
topics.note: A serial archaeological landscape with different cities and Buddhist institutions, not one Vedic-period monument.

topics.title: Persepolis
topics.note: Founded under Darius I and expanded by successors; damaged in Alexander’s conquest.

topics.title: Great Wall of China
topics.dates: Earlier regional walls; Qin linking c. 220 BCE; major Ming work 1368–1644
topics.note: A network built and rebuilt across many periods. The familiar surviving brick sections are largely Ming, not all Zhou or Qin.

topics.title: Terracotta Army
topics.dates: Late 3rd century BCE · First Qin Emperor’s mausoleum
topics.note: Belongs to the Qin imperial burial complex, not a Zhou-period monument.

topics.title: Hallstatt salt mines and cemetery
topics.dates: Bronze Age mining; cemetery principally c. 800–400 BCE
topics.note: Hallstatt is an archaeological site and the name used for a broader material-culture period. The site’s long history should not be compressed into one culture-start date.

topics.title: Temple of Saturn
topics.dates: Early 5th century BCE dedication; later rebuilding
topics.note: Traditionally dedicated in 497 BCE. The visible remains reflect later rebuilding; it was also associated with Rome’s treasury.

topics.title: Parthenon
topics.note: A Classical Athenian temple on the Acropolis, with a long subsequent history of religious use and transformation.

topics.title: Cave of Altamira
topics.note: The paintings predate the Celtic/Iberian societies beside which the poster places them. BP/years-ago dating must not be copied directly as BCE; this site predates the chart’s range.

topics.title: Lascaux cave art
topics.note: Not a monument built by Iron Age Gauls. Research has proposed different prehistoric dates; all are many millennia before 3500 BCE and the chart’s range.

topics.title: Antequera Dolmens
topics.dates: Neolithic and Bronze Age · principally 4th–3rd millennia BCE
topics.note: Prehistoric megalithic tombs, not monuments constructed by the much later Lusitanian tribes beside which the poster places them.

topics.title: Stonehenge
topics.dates: c. 3000 BCE · earthwork; c. 2500 BCE · principal stone setting
topics.note: Built long before the Celtic era. The poster’s Celtic attribution and late placement should be corrected, not reproduced.

topics.title: Chichén Itzá
topics.note: The monument icon’s placement high in the poster’s ancient column is not its construction date. Major flowering was much later than the earliest Maya communities.

topics.title: Teotihuacan archaeological city
topics.dates: c. 1st century BCE–7th century CE · major urban phase
topics.note: The city predates the Mexica/Aztec Empire; later peoples named and revered its ruins.

topics.title: Uluṟu cultural landscape
topics.dates: Living Aṉangu cultural landscape · no single founding date
topics.note: A natural landform and sacred cultural landscape, not a constructed monument or a place founded around year 1. Aṉangu custodianship and Tjukurpa continue.

topics.title: Colosseum
topics.note: Built under the Flavian emperors; inaugurated in 80 CE and altered later.

topics.title: Roman Forum
topics.dates: Developed from the early city through the Republic and Empire
topics.note: A civic and religious area with buildings of many dates. It is not a single building erected at the poster marker’s vertical position.

topics.title: Mesa Verde Ancestral Pueblo sites
topics.dates: c. 600–1300 CE · principal Ancestral Pueblo occupation
topics.note: The celebrated cliff dwellings largely belong to the final centuries of this sequence. Living Pueblo communities maintain connections with these ancestral places.

topics.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
topics.note: A communal bison-hunting landscape associated with Plains Indigenous peoples, especially Blackfoot histories. Its use long predates its low placement in the poster.

topics.title: Chaco Culture archaeological sites
topics.dates: c. 850–1250 CE · major Chacoan building and influence
topics.note: Chaco is a network of Ancestral Pueblo places, connected to living Pueblo peoples; not a vanished single tribe.

topics.title: Cahokia Mounds
topics.note: A major Indigenous urban and ceremonial centre. Its significance must not be reduced to generic pre-US background.

topics.title: Mont-Saint-Michel
topics.dates: Traditional foundation 708; major abbey construction from the 10th century
topics.note: Its buildings span many centuries and should not be dated solely by the Frankish block in which the icon appears.

topics.title: Hagia Sophia
topics.note: The surviving main building is Justinianic, with earlier churches and later alterations; its religious use changed over time.

topics.title: Windsor Castle
topics.dates: From c. 1070; rebuilt and enlarged over centuries
topics.note: Founded under William the Conqueror; it is not a single completed Norman building.

topics.title: Notre-Dame de Paris
topics.dates: From 1163 · principal medieval construction into the 14th century
topics.note: A Gothic cathedral with later restorations. The construction dates must be distinguished from modern reopening dates.

topics.title: Louvre palace and museum
topics.dates: Fortress from c. 1190; public museum inaugurated in 1793
topics.note: The poster places the museum in the medieval French kingdom, but the public museum opened during the Revolution. The medieval date belongs to the fortress.

topics.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa
topics.note: The tower was built in medieval Pisa; its placement beside a later Sicilian kingdom must not imply that kingdom constructed it.

topics.title: Cologne Cathedral
topics.note: Started in the Holy Roman Empire and completed in the German Empire. It was not wholly constructed in one medieval period.

topics.title: St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna
topics.dates: 1147 · earlier church consecration; later Romanesque and Gothic building
topics.note: The current cathedral combines phases; substantial Gothic works date to the later Middle Ages.

topics.title: Alhambra
topics.dates: From the 13th century · major Nasrid palaces
topics.note: The Alhambra is associated principally with Nasrid Granada, rather than being a monument created by the Christian “Reconquista.”

topics.title: Jerónimos Monastery
topics.note: The foundation stone is dated to 1501 or 1502 in official accounts. Its 16th-century building should not be dated by its earlier vertical position in the poster.

topics.title: Belém Tower
topics.note: A fortified tower from the reign of Manuel I, not a 15th-century monument.

topics.title: Kinkaku-ji
topics.dates: 1397 · villa origin; present pavilion rebuilt in 1955
topics.note: The Golden Pavilion is associated with Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. The present pavilion is a reconstruction following the 1950 fire.

topics.title: Forbidden City
topics.note: Built under the Ming Yongle emperor and subsequently used and altered under Qing rule.

topics.title: Sultan Ahmed Mosque / Blue Mosque
topics.note: An Ottoman mosque commissioned by Sultan Ahmed I; the familiar name refers to its blue interior tiles.

topics.title: Naqsh-e Jahan Square
topics.note: The square and its surrounding monuments developed under Safavid patronage, especially Shah Abbas I.

topics.title: Taj Mahal
topics.note: Commissioned by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal; different parts of the complex were completed at different times.

topics.title: Himeji Castle
topics.dates: Earlier fortress; principal surviving complex c. 1601–1609
topics.note: The famous surviving castle is largely early Edo construction with earlier roots, rather than a single generic Tokugawa monument.

topics.title: Palace of Versailles
topics.dates: Earlier hunting lodge; major expansion from 1661
topics.note: Versailles was expanded across several reigns. Louis XIV’s court moved there in 1682.

topics.title: Schönbrunn Palace
topics.note: The present palace reflects Habsburg construction and major rebuilding, including Maria Theresa’s reign.

topics.title: Parliament Hill
topics.note: The original Centre Block was destroyed by fire in 1916 and rebuilt. The complex has several construction phases.

topics.title: Statue of Liberty
topics.note: A French-designed gift to the United States; its modern placement must not be read as an 18th-century independence-era construction.

topics.title: Obelisco de Buenos Aires
topics.note: The monument commemorates the fourth centenary of the first Spanish foundation; it was not constructed at Argentine independence.

topics.title: Big Ben and Elizabeth Tower
topics.dates: 1859 · clock and Great Bell begin service
topics.note: Strictly, Big Ben is the Great Bell. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012; the familiar name is often used for the whole structure.

topics.title: Eiffel Tower
topics.note: Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle; not a general marker for every French republic.

topics.title: Sagrada Família
topics.dates: Construction began in 1882; continued across later eras
topics.note: The foundation predates Francoist Spain and modern constitutional Spain. No unsupported completion date should be inferred from the poster.

topics.title: Sydney Opera House
topics.note: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon with contributions by later teams; the cultural landmark is not evidence of one nation’s isolated invention.

topics.title: Second Temple Judaism
topics.location: Southern Levant and wider Jewish communities
topics.summary: A religious and cultural period under successive Persian, Hellenistic, Hasmonean and Roman authorities. Roman forces destroyed the Jerusalem temple in 70 CE.
topics.note: This is a period of Jewish religious and cultural history, not one sovereign state. Temple destruction ended the Second Temple period, rather than Jewish life or Judaism. Jewish communities and different traditions continued.

topics.title: Jewish communities and diaspora
topics.location: Southern Levant, Babylonia, Mediterranean and communities worldwide
topics.summary: Jewish communities developed across Babylonia, the Mediterranean and subsequently many other regions, while communities also continued in the southern Levant. Their histories include scholarship, languages, worship, commerce and cultural exchange as well as persecution.
topics.note: Diaspora communities existed centuries before 70 CE. There was no single moment when all Jews left the southern Levant. This overview concerns diverse, continuing communities across many states; it is neither an empire nor an unbroken state succession into modern Israel.

topics.title: The Holocaust
topics.location: Europe under Nazi rule and wider consequences
topics.summary: Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators systematically persecuted and murdered six million European Jews.
topics.note: The Holocaust unfolded through changing policies, persecution, deportation and mass murder between 1933 and 1945. It is one part of Jewish history, alongside long histories of communal life, scholarship and culture.

posterItems.label: Celtic Era
posterItems.correction: Selected pre-Roman Iron Age frame; Celtic languages and identities did not disappear in 43 CE. Stonehenge belongs to the much earlier Neolithic and Bronze Age, rather than to the origin of a Celtic state.

posterItems.label: Lusitanians and Other Tribes
posterItems.correction: An approximate Iron Age frame, not a single kingdom founded in 600 BCE. Roman writers attest Lusitanians later; the Lusitanian War ended in 139 BCE but regional conquest continued.

posterItems.label: Iberian & Celtic Tribes
posterItems.correction: A broad grouping of distinct peoples, languages and regional societies. Iberian culture is usually identified from the first millennium BCE; Rome completed its wider Iberian conquests in 19 BCE, not in 218 BCE.

posterItems.label: Carthaginian Era
posterItems.correction: Selected Barcid territorial phase beginning with Hamilcar Barca in 237 BCE. Phoenician and Punic settlements predate it; Rome expelled the main Carthaginian forces from Iberia in 206 BCE.

posterItems.label: Gaul
posterItems.correction: An approximate regional Iron Age frame, not one Celtic state. Caesar campaigned in 58–50 BCE; southern Gaul had already come under Roman rule.

posterItems.label: Italic Tribes
posterItems.correction: An approximate early grouping of several languages and peoples. Etruscans were not linguistically Italic, Greek colonies were distinct, and Italic communities continued after the Roman monarchy began.

posterItems.label: Roman Kingdom
posterItems.correction: 753 BCE and 509 BCE are traditional foundation and transition dates transmitted by later Roman historians, not archaeologically proven day-one boundaries.

posterItems.label: Roman Republic
posterItems.correction: Traditional republican frame; the Republic conquered territories at different times rather than inheriting all the coloured columns at its foundation.

posterItems.label: Roman Republic
posterItems.correction: Roman intervention began in 218 BCE, but conquest lasted into the Augustan period. This is a regional phase of the Republic, not a second Roman state.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Roman Republic
posterItems.correction: The poster marks 58 BCE. Caesar’s wars ran through 50 BCE, while Roman rule in southern Gaul began earlier.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Celtic & Germanic Tribes
posterItems.correction: A regional, approximate cultural frame spanning many communities. These categories are linguistic and historical labels, not one government or an unbroken ethnic ancestry.

posterItems.label: Hallstatt Culture
posterItems.correction: The selected Iron Age Hallstatt C–D phases date approximately 800–450 BCE. Broader Hallstatt A–B material belongs to the earlier Bronze Age; the culture was not a unitary state.

posterItems.label: Celtic Kingdom of Noricum
posterItems.correction: The Norican kingdom or federation consolidated around the second century BCE; the poster’s c. 400 BCE better describes earlier regional Celtic culture. Roman annexation began in 15 BCE; later provincial institutions continued.

posterItems.label: Aegean Civilizations
posterItems.correction: An archaeological umbrella including Cycladic, Minoan and Mycenaean cultures with different chronologies; it was not one empire or an exclusive origin story for later Greeks.

posterItems.label: Mycenaean Civilization
posterItems.correction: An archaeological period of multiple mainland palace centres, rather than a single uniformly governed Greek nation.

posterItems.label: Greek Dark Age
posterItems.correction: A conventional archaeological period following palace collapse. The label does not imply an absence of communities, creativity or contact; boundaries vary between regions.

posterItems.label: Classical Greek City-States
posterItems.correction: The poster starts this label around 800 BCE, combining Archaic and Classical Greece. Classical Greece conventionally begins around 480 BCE; city-states were independent and often at war.

posterItems.label: Macedonian Empire
posterItems.correction: 338 BCE marks Philip II’s victory at Chaeronea. Alexander’s Asian conquests began in 334 BCE; his death in 323 BCE initiated succession struggles, rather than instantly creating stable successor states.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Hellenistic Age
posterItems.correction: The poster’s Greek column ends at Roman conquest in 146 BCE. Hellenistic kingdoms elsewhere continued; 31 BCE is a common wider period endpoint, with Egypt annexed in 30 BCE.

posterItems.label: Roman Republic
posterItems.correction: The destruction of Corinth in 146 BCE is a conventional marker; incorporation and provincial organisation occurred in stages. This is a regional phase of the Roman Republic.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Roman Empire
posterItems.correction: 27 BCE marks the conventional beginning of the principate. 476 CE concerns western imperial government; the Eastern Roman state continued. The poster’s cross-column shape is not a precise territorial map.

posterItems.label: Sub-Roman Britain
posterItems.correction: Approximate transition after the withdrawal of Roman imperial administration, conventionally around 410. Regional British polities continued alongside incoming and established communities; 500 is not a universal end date.

posterItems.label: Anglo-Saxon Era
posterItems.correction: Approximate settlement and early English kingdom frame. It overlaps British polities, Scandinavian rule and the later unified kingdom, rather than replacing every inhabitant.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Wessex Dynasty
posterItems.correction: 802 marks Ecgberht’s accession in Wessex; 829 was a temporary supremacy, not the founding of a united England. The selected dynasty frame includes interruptions by Danish rulers; unification is conventionally placed in 927.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Norman Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The Norman conquest began in 1066. This selected royal period ends with Henry II’s accession in 1154 and does not mean England and Normandy always had identical institutions.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Plantagenet Dynasty
posterItems.correction: A broad dynastic convention including Angevin, Lancaster and York branches. It does not describe a single stable government or peaceful succession.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Tudor Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The Tudor royal period runs from Henry VII’s victory in 1485 to Elizabeth I’s death in 1603. Wales, Ireland and England had different relationships to royal government.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Stuart Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The shared crowns began in 1603; England and Scotland remained separate kingdoms until 1707. Republican rule interrupted the monarchy in 1649–1660, and William III was of the House of Orange.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Hanoverian Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The British Hanoverian royal period runs 1714–1901, not to the poster’s 1917 boundary. Shared monarchy with Hanover ended in 1837 because succession laws differed.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: United Kingdom
posterItems.correction: The United Kingdom was created in 1801, not 1917. Most of Ireland left in 1922; the present state name dates to 1927. The royal family adopted the Windsor name in 1917.

posterItems.label: United Kingdom
posterItems.correction: 1917 marks the adoption of the royal house name Windsor. It is a dynastic phase within the United Kingdom, not the state’s foundation.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First County of Portugal
posterItems.correction: A conventional first-county frame beginning with the recovery of Porto in 868. The first comital line ended with Nuno Mendes’s defeat in 1071. Royal administration and later reorganisation preceded Henry of Burgundy’s county around 1096; this was not an uninterrupted independent state.

posterItems.label: Second County of Portugal
posterItems.correction: The second county is usually dated from Henry of Burgundy’s appointment around 1096. Afonso Henriques’ kingship in 1139 and recognition in 1143 and 1179 mark different steps toward independence.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Portugal
posterItems.correction: 1139 is a traditional royal foundation convention; Zamora in 1143 and papal recognition in 1179 are other milestones. The kingdom’s institutional and territorial extent changed considerably.

posterItems.label: Iberian Union
posterItems.correction: Portugal and the Spanish crowns shared Habsburg monarchs. Separate laws, institutions and overseas possessions persisted; this was not complete administrative fusion.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Restored Kingdom of Portugal
posterItems.correction: 1640 began the restored Portuguese monarchy and the war for recognition, which Spain accepted in 1668. The restored kingdom continued beyond this war and was not newly founded again in 1807.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Constitutional Monarchy
posterItems.correction: The Liberal Revolution of 1820 began the constitutional transition; the first constitution followed in 1822. Civil war and absolutist restoration interrupted constitutional government before 1834. The poster’s 1807 start belongs to the French invasions.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First Portuguese Republic
posterItems.correction: The First Republic began with the revolution of 5 October 1910 and ended in the military coup of 1926; it did not continue unbroken until Estado Novo in 1933.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Estado Novo
posterItems.correction: The authoritarian Estado Novo was institutionalised in 1933 and overthrown in the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974. A military dictatorship preceded it in 1926–1933.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Portugal
posterItems.correction: A modern country frame including the First Republic, military and Estado Novo dictatorships, and the democratic transition. Democracy began after 1974; the present constitution took effect in 1976.

posterItems.label: Portugal
posterItems.correction: The democratic transition began in 1974 and the constitution took effect in 1976; the poster uses the constitutional date.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Suebi Kingdom
posterItems.correction: The Suebi established rule in northwestern Iberia after crossing the Rhine and entering Iberia. The Visigoths annexed their kingdom in 585; this was not a kingdom encompassing all Iberia.

posterItems.label: Visigothic Kingdom
posterItems.correction: The kingdom began in Aquitaine in 418 and shifted toward Iberia. The Suebi were annexed in 585; Byzantine-controlled southern areas remained separate until the seventh century. After 711, remnants continued in Septimania into the 720s.

posterItems.label: Al-Andalus
posterItems.correction: An umbrella for changing Muslim-ruled Iberian territories, not a single state lasting throughout 711–1492. The emirate, caliphate, taifas and later dynasties overlap with northern Christian kingdoms.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Asturias
posterItems.correction: 718 is a traditional royal origin date. The court and political centre shifted to León in 910, while distinct Asturian royal claims continued to 924; chronology depends on whether one tracks title, court or territory.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of León
posterItems.correction: A selected independent royal frame. León and Castile were joined and separated at several points; permanent dynastic union in 1230 did not erase León’s regional institutions.

posterItems.label: Late Reconquista
posterItems.correction: 1238 marks the Nasrid foundation convention selected by the poster. Reconquista is a retrospective, contested umbrella rather than one continuous national war; Christian and Muslim rulers also allied across religious boundaries.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Unification of Spain
posterItems.correction: 1479 marks the shared rule of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon after Ferdinand’s Aragonese accession. The crowns retained separate institutions; this was not instant state or territorial unification.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Habsburg Spain
posterItems.correction: A composite monarchy under the Spanish Habsburgs. Charles I’s accession in 1516 is the selected start; the crowns and territories retained distinct laws and institutions.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Bourbon Reforms
posterItems.correction: A selected eighteenth-century reform frame under Bourbon rulers, with a major overseas dimension. The reforms were introduced in different territories at different times; not every reform began in 1700.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Constitutional Era
posterItems.correction: Spain’s first national constitution dates to 1812, not 1808; the Bayonne Statute was imposed under Napoleonic influence. The period includes restored absolutism, constitutional monarchies, republics and dictatorship.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Francoist Spain
posterItems.correction: The regime emerged during the Civil War from 1936 and controlled the whole country after 1939. Franco died in 1975, followed by a democratic transition; the 1978 constitution is a separate milestone.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Spain
posterItems.correction: Country-level frame that distinguishes the late medieval dynastic union from later monarchy, republican, dictatorial and democratic governments.

posterItems.label: Spain
posterItems.correction: The democratic transition followed Franco’s death in 1975; the constitution was approved in 1978. This frame does not imply that Spain came into existence in 1978.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Frankish Kingdom
posterItems.correction: 481 marks Clovis I’s accession, not the first existence of Franks. Frankish realms were repeatedly divided; imperial coronation in 800 and partition in 843 are distinct events.

posterItems.label: West Francia
posterItems.correction: The western share established at Verdun in 843; 987 is a conventional Capetian transition, not an instant replacement of population or institutions.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of France
posterItems.correction: 987 marks Hugh Capet’s accession and the selected royal frame. France was not a uniformly centralised nation-state throughout this period.

posterItems.label: Bourbon France
posterItems.correction: Henry IV’s accession in 1589 begins the selected Bourbon royal frame. Bourbon restoration in 1814–1830 is a later phase, interrupted by Napoleon’s Hundred Days.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Republic
posterItems.correction: The monarchy was abolished in 1792. The republic included the Convention, Directory and Consulate before Napoleon’s imperial title in 1804.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Empire
posterItems.correction: Napoleon’s empire lasted 1804–1814 and returned during the Hundred Days in 1815. The poster’s long black band crosses countries with different occupation dates and incorrectly suggests uniform annexation.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Empire
posterItems.correction: Three French invasions occurred in 1807–1811. Portugal was not permanently annexed to the First French Empire; the royal court moved to Brazil and Anglo-Portuguese forces resisted.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Empire
posterItems.correction: Joseph Bonaparte’s imposed monarchy and French occupation faced competing Spanish governments and armed resistance. The whole country was never securely governed as one French province.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Empire
posterItems.correction: A northern Italian kingdom under Napoleon, not the whole peninsula. Other areas were annexed to France, governed by allied states or remained outside his rule.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First French Empire
posterItems.correction: A confederation of German states under Napoleon’s protection, not wholesale French annexation of Germany. The Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Republican France
posterItems.correction: The poster’s label is inaccurate: restored monarchies ruled in 1815–1848 and the Second Empire in 1852–1870. The period also includes the Second and Third Republics, occupation, Vichy and provisional government.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: France
posterItems.correction: Modern France includes republics, empires and restored monarchies. The poster’s 1946 boundary is the Fourth Republic; the Fifth Republic began in 1958.

posterItems.label: France
posterItems.correction: The Fourth Republic lasted 1946–1958, followed by the Fifth Republic. This country phase is not a single unchanging constitution.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Western Roman Empire
posterItems.correction: The 395 division concerned imperial courts and administration, not a clean cultural split. The western imperial title ended conventionally in 476, with Julius Nepos retaining a claim until 480.

posterItems.label: Ostrogothic Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Theodoric took control of Italy in 493. 553 is a conventional endpoint after Byzantine victories; warfare and residual resistance continued.

posterItems.label: Byzantine Italy
posterItems.correction: Justinian’s reconquest began in 535; Byzantine rule survived in changing parts of Italy until Bari fell in 1071. The poster’s 553–774 band is only a selected phase, not the full duration.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Lombard Kingdom
posterItems.correction: The Lombard kingdom ruled much of the peninsula after 568 and was conquered by Charlemagne in 774. Southern Lombard duchies continued afterward.

posterItems.label: Medieval Italian States
posterItems.correction: A regional umbrella for many states, cities and jurisdictions, not one state. Venice, Genoa, the Papal States, imperial territories and southern kingdoms had distinct histories.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Sicily
posterItems.correction: Founded in 1130. After 1282 the island and mainland crowns were politically divided, with both claiming Sicilian titles; they were formally combined as the Two Sicilies in 1816. The poster’s 1494 boundary is not the kingdom’s end.

posterItems.label: The Age of Divided Italy
posterItems.correction: 1494 marks the start of the Italian Wars, not the first division of Italy. Regional states and competing foreign powers continued through the early modern period, with major changes during the Napoleonic wars.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Bourbon Sicily
posterItems.correction: The poster’s 1815 restoration relates to the post-Napoleonic settlement. The unified Kingdom of the Two Sicilies was formally created in 1816 and incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Italy
posterItems.correction: The kingdom was proclaimed in 1861; Venice joined in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Fascist dictatorship developed within the monarchy; the republican referendum took place in 1946.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Italy
posterItems.correction: A modern country frame beginning with proclamation of the kingdom. The republic dates to 1946, and the republican constitution entered into effect in 1948.

posterItems.label: Italy
posterItems.correction: The referendum of 2 June 1946 chose a republic; official confirmation followed in June, and the constitution took effect on 1 January 1948.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Germanic Tribes
posterItems.correction: A selected late antique migration frame encompassing many groups and political formations. Language labels do not imply one people, one kingdom or an unbroken ancestry for modern Germany.

posterItems.label: Migration Period
posterItems.correction: A broad conventional span used by the Metropolitan Museum; other historians use narrower fourth-to-sixth-century ranges. Migration involved warfare, settlement, Roman service and changing identities rather than a single population replacement.

posterItems.label: Post-Roman Germanic Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: A selected regional transition among successor authorities, including Ostrogothic influence and emerging Bavarian power. It is not a single named kingdom founded in 476.

posterItems.label: Duchy of Bavaria
posterItems.correction: The first Bavarian duchy is conventionally traced to the mid-sixth century; Charlemagne deposed Tassilo III in 788. Later Bavarian duchies continued under different political arrangements.

posterItems.label: East Francia
posterItems.correction: The eastern realm created at Verdun in 843 developed into the medieval German kingdom. The 962 imperial coronation is a selected transition, not the disappearance of its people or institutions.

posterItems.label: Holy Roman Empire
posterItems.correction: Otto I’s 962 coronation is the selected start; some imperial narratives begin with 800. This was a changing framework of many states and cities, not a modern German nation-state.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Prussia
posterItems.correction: The royal title was adopted in 1701. Prussia did not cease in 1871: it became the largest constituent kingdom of the German Empire and its monarchy ended in 1918.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: German Confederation
posterItems.correction: A loose confederation established at Vienna in 1815 and dissolved in 1866; it was not a united Germany. The North German Confederation followed in 1867 before imperial unification in 1871.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: German Empire
posterItems.correction: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 and its monarchy fell in 1918. The 1919 constitution belongs to the subsequent republic, not the continuation of imperial monarchy.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Weimar Republic
posterItems.correction: Republican government was proclaimed in November 1918; the Weimar constitution followed in 1919. Nazi dictatorship developed after Hitler’s appointment in January 1933.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Nazi Germany
posterItems.correction: Nazi rule lasted 1933–1945, with escalating dictatorship, aggressive war and genocide. Territorial extent changed; occupation zones followed military defeat.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: East and West Germany
posterItems.correction: Allied occupation began in 1945; the Federal Republic and German Democratic Republic were founded separately in 1949. The poster’s 1945 label must not imply that both states already existed then.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Germany
posterItems.correction: A broad modern frame including empire, republic, dictatorship, occupation, two states and reunification in 1990. It is not one uninterrupted government.

posterItems.label: Germany
posterItems.correction: The GDR acceded to the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Federal Republic itself dates from 1949; modern German history did not begin in 1990.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Margraviate of Austria
posterItems.correction: The Babenberg march was established in 976 and elevated to a duchy in 1156. This was a frontier territory within a wider imperial framework, not an independent modern Austria.

posterItems.label: Duchy of Austria
posterItems.correction: The Privilegium Minus elevated the march to a duchy in 1156. The archducal title was invented in the fourteenth century but officially recognised in 1453.

posterItems.label: Habsburg Austria
posterItems.correction: 1453 marks formal recognition of the archducal title, not the beginning of Habsburg rule in Austria (which dates to the late thirteenth century). The wider Habsburg monarchy accumulated distinct crowns and territories.

posterItems.label: Austrian Empire
posterItems.correction: The Austrian imperial title was proclaimed in 1804, while the Holy Roman Empire still existed until 1806. The Dual Monarchy replaced this framework in 1867.

posterItems.label: Austria-Hungary
posterItems.correction: The 1867 Compromise established a dual monarchy with separate Austrian and Hungarian institutions and shared affairs. Its dissolution in 1918 produced several successor states, not simply modern Austria.

posterItems.label: First Austrian Republic
posterItems.correction: Republican Austria emerged in 1918; democratic parliamentary government was dismantled in 1933 and the authoritarian Federal State replaced the constitutional republic in 1934. Nazi annexation followed in 1938.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Second Austrian Republic
posterItems.correction: The republic was restored in 1945, not in 1955. Allied occupation ended under the 1955 State Treaty, followed by constitutional permanent neutrality.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Austria
posterItems.correction: A modern country frame covering the First Republic, authoritarian Federal State, Nazi annexation, restored republic and Allied occupation. Full sovereignty was restored in 1955, not the first existence of the republic.

posterItems.label: Austria
posterItems.correction: The 1955 State Treaty ended Allied occupation. The Second Republic had already been restored in 1945, and the neutrality law was a separate act of October 1955.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Byzantine Empire
posterItems.correction: The empire was Roman in its own identity. The poster’s 395 start marks a division of imperial courts; Constantinople’s dedication in 330 is the website’s selected frame. The Latin conquest interrupted rule in Constantinople in 1204–1261.

posterItems.label: Greek Successor States
posterItems.correction: After the Fourth Crusade, Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond were distinct successor powers. Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261; Trebizond survived until 1461. This was not one state ending uniformly in 1453.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Latin Empire
posterItems.correction: The crusader-founded Latin Empire occupied Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade. It was distinct from the Byzantine successor states and ended there with the city’s recovery in 1261.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Greece
posterItems.correction: The monarchy was established in 1832 after the independence struggle and international recognition. Borders expanded later; the Second Hellenic Republic replaced the monarchy in 1924.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Greek Republic
posterItems.correction: The republic lasted 1924–1935 and faced coups and instability. Monarchy was restored in 1935.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Greece
posterItems.correction: The restored royal period included Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation, civil war and the 1967 military coup. The junta abolished the monarchy in 1973; democratic institutions returned in 1974.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Greece
posterItems.correction: Independence was internationally recognised in 1830 and the kingdom established in 1832. The democratic Third Republic dates to 1974, with its constitution in 1975; the poster’s 1973 marker refers to a junta-controlled abolition of monarchy.

posterItems.label: Greece
posterItems.correction: The junta proclaimed a republic in 1973, but democratic transition began in July 1974; a free December 1974 referendum rejected monarchy and the constitution followed in June 1975.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Restored Byzantine Empire
posterItems.correction: Michael VIII recovered Constantinople in 1261. The restored empire occupied a reduced and changing territory and ended in Constantinople in 1453; some Byzantine successor territories survived later.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Early Dynastic Period
posterItems.correction: Approximate dynastic chronology. Egypt had substantial predynastic societies before unification; this is not the beginning of Egyptian culture.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Old Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Approximate traditional chronology; the pyramid-building era, not an uninterrupted ethnic or national founding.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: First Intermediate Period
posterItems.correction: Regional dynasties overlapped. Alternative chronologies put the Middle Kingdom reunification around 2030 BCE.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Middle Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Approximate Egyptian ministry periodization; other scholarly chronologies begin around 2030 BCE or use a narrower end date.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Second Intermediate Period
posterItems.correction: Regional courts, including Hyksos rule in the north and the Theban kingdom in the south, coexisted; not a single dynasty.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: New Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Approximate dynastic period, traditionally Dynasties 18–20.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Third Intermediate Period
posterItems.correction: Competing royal lines and regional powers overlapped; the poster’s 1070 is a rounded alternative.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Late Period
posterItems.correction: The poster truncates this at the first Persian conquest 525 BCE. The full Late Period conventionally includes Persian and restored native dynasties through 332 BCE.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Ptolemaic Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Ptolemy took the royal title 305 BCE; his Egyptian governorship began 323 BCE. Ends with Roman annexation 30 BCE.

posterItems.label: Arab Caliphate
posterItems.correction: The poster uses 633,641 and 651 for regional conquests. The Rashidun 632–661 and Umayyad 661–750 states are separate, already represented histories; Egypt conquered 639–642 and Sasanian defeat unfolded 633–651.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Fatimid Caliphate
posterItems.correction: Founded in North Africa 909; conquest of Egypt and establishment of Cairo occurred 969. The poster’s 969 start represents the Egyptian phase, not the caliphate’s founding.

posterItems.label: Ayyubid Sultanate
posterItems.correction: Ayyubid government ended in Egypt 1250; regional Ayyubid rulers in Syria continued through 1260 and some local branches longer. Use 1171–1250 for a strictly Egyptian subperiod.

posterItems.label: Mamluk Sultanate
posterItems.correction: Egyptian rule began 1250; control of Syria expanded by 1260. Ottoman conquest 1516–1517 ended the sultanate, although Mamluk elites persisted.

posterItems.label: Muhammad Ali Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The dynasty continued across the British occupation, protectorate and Kingdom of Egypt; these were overlapping political dimensions. The poster cuts the dynasty at 1882.

posterItems.label: Colonial Egypt
posterItems.correction: Occupation began 1882; the formal protectorate lasted 1914–1922. British influence, treaty rights and forces persisted after limited independence 1922.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Egypt
posterItems.correction: Independence declared 1922 with important British reservations; monarchy abolished 1953.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Egypt
posterItems.correction: Republic proclaimed 1953. The existing broad modern-Egypt entry begins 1922; this adds its republican phase explicitly.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Hittite Empire
