posterItems.correction: Kingdom begins around 1650 BCE, not simply 1700; the imperial New Kingdom is a narrower phase.

posterItems.label: Neo-Hittite Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: Multiple Luwian and Aramaean kingdoms followed the Hittite imperial collapse; no single successor empire. Final incorporation into Assyria varied by kingdom.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Lydia
posterItems.correction: Selected well-attested Mermnad phase begins around 680 BCE. Earlier Lydian traditions and rulers predate it; Cyrus’s conquest is conventionally dated 547/546 BCE.

posterItems.label: Sumerian Civilization
posterItems.correction: Selected urban Sumerian cultural history, not a single united empire. The poster’s 4500 BCE start is an overly precise ethnic-cultural founding date: Ubaid settlement traditions are earlier, while Uruk urbanization and writing developed during the fourth millennium. Ur III ended 2004 BCE; Sumerian language and traditions persisted.

posterItems.label: Akkadian Empire
posterItems.correction: Middle-chronology conventional dates; competing chronologies differ. Existing chart uses rounded 2350–2150 BCE.

posterItems.label: Sumerian Renaissance
posterItems.correction: The poster’s 2154–1894 frame conflates several post-Akkadian dynasties. Ur III is 2112–2004 BCE; earlier Lagash II and later Isin-Larsa states are distinct.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Old Babylonian Kingdom
posterItems.correction: Selected First Dynasty of Babylon, not all southern Mesopotamian states in this era.

posterItems.label: Kassite Babylon
posterItems.correction: Traditional period boundary 1595 BCE reflects the Hittite sack; the earliest establishment of Kassite rule is imperfectly documented.

posterItems.label: Assyrian Empire
posterItems.correction: The poster’s broad Assyrian band combines Middle and Neo-Assyrian periods. This earlier phase complements existing Neo-Assyria; power and territory fluctuated.

posterItems.label: Assyrian Empire
posterItems.correction: Nineveh fell 612 BCE; remaining Assyrian royal resistance at Harran continued until 609 BCE. Existing entry uses 612 for the fall of its capital.

posterItems.label: Neo-Babylonian Empire
posterItems.correction: Nabopolassar’s kingdom began 626 BCE; imperial expansion followed Assyria’s collapse 612–609. Conquered by Cyrus 539 BCE.

posterItems.label: Elamite Civilization
posterItems.correction: A sequence of kingdoms and cultural phases, not one uninterrupted empire. Elamite history did not simply end 1500 BCE with the appearance of Iranian-speaking groups; these histories overlapped.

posterItems.label: Iranian Tribes
posterItems.correction: A selected approximate pre-Achaemenid frame, not a state or a single dated migration. Western-Iranian groups are securely attested in Assyrian records by the ninth centuryBCE; their languages and societies continued after 550 BCE.

posterItems.label: Median Empire
posterItems.correction: Conventional traditional frame only. The extent, political unity and chronology of a Median empire remain debated; no claim that a securely documented empire was founded in 678 BCE.

posterItems.label: Persian Empire
posterItems.correction: The poster steps conquest dates across regions: Lydia 546, Egypt 525, Babylon 539. These are accessions of territory, not multiple founding dates; Iranian rule continued under successor powers.

posterItems.label: Macedonian Empire
posterItems.correction: Alexander became king 336 BCE; Asian invasion began 334, Babylon fell 331 and Achaemenid kingship ended 330. This selected personal reign must not be equated with the full earlier Macedonian kingdom.

posterItems.label: Hellenistic Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: A family of rival states following Alexander; selected separate Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Parthian histories are required for the poster’s named blocks.

posterItems.label: Seleucid Empire
posterItems.correction: Conventional era starts 312 BCE; Seleucus assumed royal title 305. Territory contracted in stages, especially with Parthian expansion.

posterItems.label: Parthian Empire
posterItems.correction: Arsacid origins conventionally 247 BCE;141 BCE in the poster is conquest of Babylonia, not the empire’s foundation.

posterItems.label: Sasanian Empire
posterItems.correction: Founded 224. Arab conquest proceeded over several decades;651 marks the death of YazdegerdIII, not the disappearance of Iranian society.

posterItems.label: Abbasid Caliphate
posterItems.correction: Cairo-based Abbasid caliphs later continued under Mamluk patronage 1261–1517; Baghdad’s fall 1258 ends this selected ruling phase.

posterItems.label: Sultanate of Rum
posterItems.correction: An Anatolian Seljuk state distinct from the Great Seljuq Empire already in the chart. Autonomy weakened after defeat by the Mongols 1243.

posterItems.label: Post-Abbasid Regional Dynasties
posterItems.correction: A regional overview, not a single successor state. Includes Ilkhanid, Jalayirid, Timurid and Turkmen powers with different and overlapping dates; Ilkhanid rule began before 1258 and several regional histories continued after 1501.

posterItems.label: Post-Abbasid Regional Dynasties
posterItems.correction: Specific state within the poster’s broad regional band; rule begins before the 1258 sack of Baghdad. Later rival Ilkhan claimants continued after 1335.

posterItems.label: Post-Abbasid Regional Dynasties
posterItems.correction: Specific major power within the poster’s umbrella band; western Iranian territory also passed to Turkmen dynasties. Their dates do not define a single 1258–1501 empire.

posterItems.label: Safavid Empire
posterItems.correction: Conventional dynasty 1501–1736. Effective control collapsed after the Afghan conquest 1722; residual Safavid claimants and restoration attempts continued until Nader’s coronation.

posterItems.label: Afsharid Empire
posterItems.correction: Nader Shah’s empire fragmented after his death 1747. Afsharid government in Khorasan survived until 1796, overlapping the Zands and rising Qajars.

posterItems.label: Qajar Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Start dates 1786,1789,1794 and 1796 reflect different stages of consolidation and coronation. Use conventional 1789 for the dynasty and explain 1796 coronation; the poster selects 1796.

posterItems.label: Pahlavi Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Reza Khan’s 1921 coup preceded the foundation of the Pahlavi monarchy 1925. Monarchy overthrown 1979.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Iran
posterItems.correction: Revolution and Islamic Republic established 1979; the broader history of Iran and its society long predates this constitutional phase.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Ottoman Empire
posterItems.correction: Conventional origin around 1299; Ottoman expansion into Byzantine, Mamluk and Iraqi territories occurred at different dates. Sultanate abolished 1922; republic proclaimed 1923.

posterItems.label: Turkey
posterItems.correction: Republic proclaimed 1923; the empire and republic are distinct phases.

posterItems.label: Kingdom of Iraq
posterItems.correction: Monarchy established 1921 under British control; mandate ended and independence recognized 1932. Monarchy overthrown 14 July 1958.

posterItems.label: Iraq
posterItems.correction: A succession of republics and regimes, with major changes 1968,2003 and 2005. The state and Iraqi society did not originate 1958.

posterItems.label: Indus Valley Civilization
posterItems.correction: The poster’s 3300 BCE start is Early Harappan, while the existing chart shows Mature Harappan 2600–1900 BCE. Add Early and Late phases explicitly; decline of urban centres did not end all Harappan traditions 1500 BCE.

posterItems.label: Vedic Period
posterItems.correction: Conventional textual-cultural frame 1500–500 BCE; dates are approximate, regional and debated. Vedic cultures coexisted with Late Harappan and other traditions; not a single state.

posterItems.label: Mahajanapadas
posterItems.correction: Multiple kingdoms and oligarchic republics, principally in northern South Asia; conventional sixth–fourth centuryBCE frame. Mauryan expansion incorporated different states at different times.

posterItems.label: Maurya Empire
posterItems.correction: Traditional dates 322/321–185 BCE; exact founding chronology varies. Not an empire covering every part of the Indian subcontinent.

posterItems.label: Post-Mauryan Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: Period overview containing Shunga, Kanva, Indo-Greek, Shaka, Satavahana and Kushan powers; many coexisted. Existing Kushan history provides one named example.

posterItems.label: Gupta Empire
posterItems.correction: Conventional imperial/art-historical phase; political decline and regional artistic influence have different end dates.

posterItems.label: Post-Gupta Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: A selected transition frame, not one polity. Regional kingdoms and post-Gupta artistic traditions began before and continued after Harsha; avoid a blanket replacement at 606.

posterItems.label: Harsha’s Empire
posterItems.correction: Harsha ruled parts of northern India 606–647, not all South Asia; southern powers including the Chalukyas remained independent.

posterItems.label: Regional Kingdoms
posterItems.correction: A broad selected frame, not one state or a cultural vacuum. Includes Pala, Pratihara, Rashtrakuta, Chalukya, Chola and Rajput polities with overlapping dates; southern kingdoms continued after 1206.

posterItems.label: Delhi Sultanate
posterItems.correction: Several ruling dynasties with shifting territories; a northern Indian political frame rather than all-India rule.

posterItems.label: Mughal Empire
posterItems.correction: Interrupted by the Sur dynasty 1540–1555. Imperial power contracted greatly before 1858, while regional kingdoms and Company rule overlapped.

posterItems.label: Colonial India
posterItems.correction: The poster correctly uses 1858 for Crown rule. Company territorial rule began earlier and is separately represented; princely states had distinct arrangements.

posterItems.label: Pakistan
posterItems.correction: Independence 1947; East Pakistan became Bangladesh 1971. Constitutions and political regimes changed within this continuing national history.

posterItems.label: India
posterItems.correction: Independent Dominion 1947–1950, Republic from 1950. Independence is a political milestone, not the beginning of Indian cultures.

posterItems.label: Liangzhu Culture
posterItems.correction: Archaeological culture 3300–2300 BCE; the poster uses 3000 and extends it toward Xia. Liangzhu is not a dynastic predecessor ruling all China.

posterItems.label: Xia Dynasty
posterItems.correction: These are traditional/modelled dates, not secure contemporary attestations. No surviving contemporary inscription securely identifies Erlitou as Xia; historicity and archaeological identification remain debated.

posterItems.label: Shang Dynasty
posterItems.correction: The later Shang is securely attested by oracle-bone writing. The beginning around 1600 BCE and transition date 1046 are conventional archaeological-historical dates.

posterItems.label: Zhou Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Western and Eastern Zhou with changing royal power; Spring and Autumn and Warring States polities coexisted under increasingly nominal Zhou kingship.

posterItems.label: Qin Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Unification 221 BCE, correcting the poster’s tiny 217 BCE label. Qin as a regional state existed much earlier.

posterItems.label: Han Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Western and Eastern Han, interrupted by the Xin dynasty 9–23 CE and subsequent civil war. Territorial reach and rule varied.

posterItems.label: Age of Division
posterItems.correction: An umbrella period, not one government. Includes Three Kingdoms, Western/Eastern Jin, Sixteen Kingdoms and Northern/Southern dynasties; brief Western Jin reunification 280–316 interrupts any claim of continuous division.

posterItems.label: Sui Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Dynasty founded 581; reunification of north and south 589. The poster uses 589 for the territorial milestone.

posterItems.label: Tang Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Interrupted by Wu Zhou 690–705; regional warlords and rival states increasingly constrained late-Tang rule.

posterItems.label: Five Dynasties Period
posterItems.correction: Northern Five Dynasties traditionally end 960 with Song’s foundation, while southern independent kingdoms continued until 979. A network of concurrent states, not five rulers of all China.

posterItems.label: Song Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Northern Song 960–1127 and Southern Song 1127–1279 coexisted with Liao, Western Xia and Jin powers. Yuan proclaimed 1271 before Song’s final defeat 1279.

posterItems.label: Yuan Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Proclaimed 1271, Southern Song conquered 1279. Ming seized Dadu 1368 but Northern Yuan rule continued beyond the poster’s endpoint.

posterItems.label: Ming Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Beijing fell 1644, while Southern Ming regimes continued to 1662 and related resistance longer. Ming did not simply become Qing everywhere at once.

posterItems.label: Qing Dynasty
posterItems.correction: Qing dynastic name proclaimed 1636 before its 1644 seizure of Beijing; conquest continued regionally thereafter. Abdication 1912.

posterItems.label: Republic of China
posterItems.correction: Founded 1912. The government relocated to Taiwan 1949 and the Republic of China continues there; it did not cease to exist with the PRC’s mainland victory.

posterItems.label: China
posterItems.correction: PRC proclaimed 1949. Its government has never administered Taiwan; the site’s separate Taiwan/ROC history preserves this distinction.

posterItems.label: Jōmon Period
posterItems.correction: Starts many millennia before the chart window. The transition to Yayoi was regionally gradual from roughly 900 BCE; Jōmon traditions persisted later in northern areas. This is not Japan’s first human occupation.

posterItems.label: Yayoi Period
posterItems.correction: Dates vary by region and dating method. Newer chronologies place wet-rice-based Yayoi society from around 900 BCE in northern Kyushu, while older general surveys use 300 BCE. Do not present the poster’s 300 BCE as a universal secure start.

posterItems.label: Yamato State
posterItems.correction: A broad conventional Kofun/Asuka frame; the Yamato court consolidated gradually.250 is an archaeological-period anchor, not a known single state-founding date.

posterItems.label: Nara Period
posterItems.correction: Capital established at Heijō-kyō710; court moved to Heian-kyō794, with a brief intervening Nagaoka phase 784–794.

posterItems.label: Heian Period
posterItems.correction: Conventional ending 1185 with the emergence of warrior government;1192 is another common boundary emphasizing the shogunal appointment.

posterItems.label: Kamakura Shogunate
posterItems.correction: 1185 marks military victory and establishment of rule;1192 marks Minamoto no Yoritomo’s shogunal title. Shogunate ended 1333.

posterItems.label: Muromachi Shogunate
posterItems.correction: Ashikaga regime 1336–1573, with a rival Southern Court 1336–1392. The later Sengoku wars overlap it; the shogunate did not continue to 1603.

posterItems.label: Sengoku Period
posterItems.correction: Conventional broad Warring States frame from the Ōnin War; proposed end dates 1568,1573,1600 or 1615 depend on the event emphasized.1603 is the Tokugawa establishment, not a universally agreed period end.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Tokugawa Shogunate
posterItems.correction: Tokugawa shogunal rule began 1603 and ended 1867–1868. International contact was controlled and restricted, never wholly absent.

posterItems.label: Meiji Era
posterItems.correction: Meiji is an imperial era within modern imperial Japan, not a separate state preceding the empire.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Empire of Japan
posterItems.correction: The poster starts 1912, which omits the Meiji imperial state. Broad constitutional-political frame 1868–1947; defeat 1945 and constitutional change 1947 are distinct endpoints.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Japan
posterItems.correction: Current constitution effective 3 May 1947. Allied occupation began 1945 and ended 1952 for most of Japan;1947 is not independence or the creation of Japan.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Indus Valley Civilization
posterItems.correction: A regionalization period including Ravi/Hakra and Kot Diji phases; dates and material traditions vary by site. Complements the existing Mature Harappan band.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Indus Valley Civilization
posterItems.correction: Urban decentralization and regional cultural continuities after the Mature phase; site chronologies vary. This does not imply the disappearance of people or traditions.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Indigenous Era · Native American Civilizations (Iroquois, Pueblo, etc.)
posterItems.correction: The poster groups many peoples into one band. Indigenous histories long predate the United States and continue today. There is no single founding year or collective end at European settlement; archaeological societies and living nations have their own histories.

posterItems.label: Iroquois
posterItems.correction: Haudenosaunee is the confederacy’s own name. Oral traditions and scholarly chronologies differ about its foundation; no disputed date is treated as settled. The Six Nations and their political and cultural traditions continue.

posterItems.label: Pueblo
posterItems.correction: Pueblo peoples include distinct contemporary communities with ancestral ties to sites such as Mesa Verde and Chaco. The abandonment of a settlement is not the disappearance of its people.

posterItems.label: Indigenous Era · Inuit, First Nations & Métis
posterItems.correction: First Nations, Inuit and Métis are distinct groups, not one ancient state or a culture that ended at colonisation. Métis communities formed in particular colonial-era historical contexts; their identity should not be projected unchanged into antiquity.

posterItems.label: Inuit
posterItems.correction: Inuit histories span different Arctic regions and communities. This cultural entry has no single founding year and does not date all earlier Arctic peoples as Inuit.

posterItems.label: First Nations
posterItems.correction: First Nations is a collective term for many distinct Indigenous peoples in Canada; it does not include Inuit or Métis and is not the name of a single ancient state.

posterItems.label: Métis
posterItems.correction: Métis peoples and nationhood developed in specific historical communities, particularly in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The poster’s continuous ancient-to-colonial band must not be read as a date for Métis origins.

posterItems.label: Indigenous Era · Olmec, Maya, Aztec & Other Civilizations
posterItems.correction: Olmec traditions, Maya societies, Teotihuacan and the Mexica-led Triple Alliance belong to different places and periods. The poster’s shared band is not one uninterrupted empire, and Indigenous societies continue after Spanish conquest.

posterItems.label: Olmec
posterItems.correction: Olmec is an archaeological designation, not proof of one empire controlling all Mesoamerica.

posterItems.label: Maya
posterItems.correction: 900 CE marks a period boundary, not the disappearance of Maya peoples. Maya communities and languages continue today.

posterItems.label: Aztec
posterItems.correction: 1521 marks conquest of Tenochtitlan by Spanish and Indigenous allied forces; it did not end Nahua people or culture.

posterItems.label: Teotihuacan
posterItems.correction: Selected monumental urban phase; settlement and later engagement with the site extend beyond this range.

posterItems.label: Indigenous Era · Māori & Other Indigenous Cultures
posterItems.correction: Māori settlement of Aotearoa New Zealand dates to approximately the late thirteenth century; other Pacific populations have their own earlier and later settlement histories. This broad label is not a single state, people or shared founding date.

posterItems.label: Māori
posterItems.correction: First settlement is dated to approximately 1250–1300 CE. The bar uses 1250 as a plotting anchor, not an exact arrival date.

posterItems.label: Indigenous Era · Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultures
posterItems.correction: Aboriginal peoples and Torres Strait Islander peoples are distinct cultural groups comprising many communities. European colonisation and federation did not end their histories or identities.

posterItems.label: Aboriginal
posterItems.correction: The deep-time date is an approximate archaeological anchor, not a precise founding year. The bar extends before and beyond the displayed window.

posterItems.label: Torres Strait Islander
posterItems.correction: Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct island homelands, languages and histories. They are not simply another name for Aboriginal Australians.

posterItems.label: Colonial America
posterItems.correction: This groups English and later British colonies before the 1783 peace settlement. Britain retained colonies afterward. It is not a state called Anglo-America, and it does not replace Indigenous histories.

posterItems.label: Colonial Canada · French and British Colonial Settlements
posterItems.correction: 1608 marks the founding of Quebec, not the first European presence or the beginning of the region’s history. French and British rule followed different territorial timelines; Canada’s Confederation in 1867 was a later partial union, not immediate full independence. See New France and British northern colonies for distinct frames.
posterItems.representation: Named period in the index and related history reader

posterItems.label: Colonial Era · Mexico
posterItems.correction: 1521 marks the fall of Tenochtitlan; the Viceroyalty of New Spain was established in 1535. Its jurisdiction extended far beyond present-day Mexico and changed over time. Spanish conquest did not end Indigenous peoples or cultures.

posterItems.label: Colonial Era · Argentina
posterItems.correction: 1536 marks the first, short-lived Buenos Aires settlement, not continuous control of present-day Argentina. The second foundation was in 1580. The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata existed only from 1776, and the independence process began in 1810 before the 1816 declaration. Indigenous territories were not uniformly controlled.

posterItems.label: Colonial Australia
posterItems.correction: The British colony of New South Wales began in 1788; other colonies were established or separated later. Six colonies federated in 1901. Colonial expansion involved dispossession and conflict, while Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories continued.

posterItems.label: United States
posterItems.correction: 1776 marks the declaration of independence; British recognition followed in 1783 and the present Constitution took effect in 1789. Anglo-America is a variable cultural-geographic term, not a unified country, empire or description of every inhabitant.

posterItems.label: Canada
posterItems.correction: Confederation in 1867 created the Dominion of Canada. Autonomy and territory developed in stages, including the Statute of Westminster in 1931 and constitutional patriation in 1982. Canada is not wholly English-speaking.

posterItems.label: Mexico
posterItems.correction: 1821 marks independence from Spain. Empires, republics, civil conflicts and changing borders followed; this is not the beginning of the region’s peoples or cultures.

posterItems.label: Argentina
posterItems.correction: 1816 marks the declaration of independence by the United Provinces, following the 1810 revolution. The Argentine state, its constitutional arrangements and territorial control developed through later conflicts and agreements. This is not an unchanged republic from 1816.

posterItems.label: Australia
posterItems.correction: 1901 marks federation of six British colonies. Constitutional independence developed gradually; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories long predate the federation and continue alongside it.

posterItems.label: Bronze Age
posterItems.correction: An archaeological period defined by particular technologies and social changes, with different dates in different regions. A single global date band cannot describe every society on this timeline.

posterItems.label: Early Bronze Age
posterItems.correction: A regional subdivision of the Bronze Age, especially used in Near Eastern and European chronologies. It does not begin and end everywhere at the same date.

posterItems.label: Iron Age
posterItems.correction: An archaeological period whose chronology varies regionally. Ironworking spread through different societies over a long period; it is not a global change occurring in one year.

posterItems.label: Classical Antiquity
posterItems.correction: A conventional period focused on the ancient Mediterranean. Its boundaries are approximate and it should not be treated as the name for every contemporary society worldwide.

posterItems.label: The Middle Ages
posterItems.correction: A conventional European period, often approximately the fifth to fifteenth centuries. Histories elsewhere use their own periodisations; the chart’s common date scale allows comparison without assigning all societies to a European age.

posterItems.label: The Modern Era
posterItems.correction: A broad historical convention, often beginning around 1500 in European periodisation. The Modern era chart starts at 1450 to include major transitions; this is a viewing window rather than a single worldwide beginning.

posterItems.label: BCE / CE date axis
posterItems.correction: BCE and CE use the same year numbering as BC and AD. There is no year zero. Approximate dates and scholarly disagreements are explained in individual entries; the chart uses one linear scale.

posterItems.label: Historical Landmark · legend
posterItems.correction: Landmarks have their own construction, use and alteration histories. Their placement beside a political period in the reference poster is not evidence that the place originated in that period. Select Landmarks in the index for the dated entries.

posterItems.label: Landmark illustrations and symbols
posterItems.correction: The poster’s decorative monument illustrations are not chronological evidence. In particular a later Japanese pagoda should not be read as a Jōmon-period building. This atlas separates monument histories from the surrounding political and archaeological periods.

posterItems.label: National flags · country labels
posterItems.correction: The flags identify the modern countries in the poster’s bottom row. They do not represent ancient polities, imply continuous borders or establish direct descent from every earlier society. The country shortcuts in the index open the corresponding modern histories.

posterItems.label: Moon Landing
posterItems.correction: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July UTC; the first steps followed on 21 July UTC. Earlier robotic lunar missions were uncrewed.

posterItems.label: Digital Revolution
posterItems.correction: A long worldwide transition involving electronics, computers and networks, not a single national invention or founding date. The transistor of 1947 is one precursor.

posterItems.label: Discovery of Insulin
posterItems.correction: The Toronto work involved Frederick Banting, Charles Best, J. J. R. Macleod and James Collip, alongside earlier international research; not the achievement of one person alone.

posterItems.label: Maize Cultivation
posterItems.correction: A gradual Indigenous domestication process, not an invention by one later empire. Its beginning predates this timeline’s 3500 BCE start.

posterItems.label: Maya Astronomy
posterItems.correction: No single invention date is justified. Maya observations, calendars and eclipse tables developed over centuries; surviving Dresden Codex astronomy reflects a later manuscript tradition.

posterItems.label: Tango
posterItems.correction: Developed in Buenos Aires and Montevideo from multiple cultural traditions. It belongs to both Argentina and Uruguay, rather than one country alone.

posterItems.label: Wi-Fi Innovation
posterItems.correction: CSIRO’s Australian team made an important high-speed wireless LAN contribution. Wi-Fi as a whole involved many inventors, companies and IEEE standards; “Australia invented all Wi-Fi” overstates it.

posterItems.label: Laws of Motion & Gravity
posterItems.correction: Newton formulated these in the Principia, building on earlier mathematical and physical work. This is not the first human awareness of motion or gravity.

posterItems.label: Watt’s Steam Engine
posterItems.correction: Watt greatly improved steam-engine efficiency; he did not invent the first steam engine. Newcomen and other predecessors must not disappear from the account.

posterItems.label: Natural Selection
posterItems.correction: Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed explanations of natural selection and their work was jointly presented in 1858.

posterItems.label: Route to India
posterItems.correction: This opened a Portuguese Cape route to India, entering existing African, Arab, South Asian and other Indian Ocean trade networks. It was not the discovery of India or the first sea route there.

posterItems.label: Discovery of the Americas
posterItems.correction: The Americas already had diverse Indigenous populations; Norse voyagers reached North America earlier. The label describes Columbus’s voyage and its consequences, rather than a universal “discovery.”

posterItems.label: Rights of Man
posterItems.correction: This French revolutionary declaration is a particular document, not the beginning of all rights traditions. Its stated universality coexisted with exclusions in political and colonial practice.

posterItems.label: Metric System
posterItems.correction: The French metric reforms and modern SI are related but not identical. SI was established in 1960 and continues to develop.

posterItems.label: Renaissance
posterItems.correction: A broad cultural and intellectual period with regional variation, drawing on classical, Byzantine, Islamic and other knowledge transmissions; not one event or a universal historical stage.

posterItems.label: Printing Press
posterItems.correction: Gutenberg’s European metal-type system transformed European printing. Chinese woodblock printing and East Asian movable type preceded it by centuries.

posterItems.label: Automobile
posterItems.correction: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen is an early practical petrol automobile. Earlier steam road vehicles and parallel work by other inventors mean “first automobile” needs qualification.

posterItems.label: Theory of Relativity
posterItems.correction: These are two connected theories, not a single publication. Einstein’s work developed within a wider mathematical and physical research community.

posterItems.label: Classical Music
posterItems.correction: “Classical music” also names a much broader Western tradition. These dates refer to the Classical period associated with Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, not all classical traditions worldwide.

posterItems.label: Olympic Games
posterItems.correction: 776 BCE is the traditional recorded starting point, not proof that athletic festivals began then. Modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896.

posterItems.label: Birth of Democracy
posterItems.correction: Athenian democracy developed in stages. Political participation excluded women, enslaved people and resident foreigners; the date does not describe modern universal suffrage or every participatory tradition.

posterItems.label: Justinian Code
posterItems.correction: The Code is one part of the wider Corpus Juris Civilis, alongside the Digest and Institutes and later Novels. It compiled and revised a long Roman legal tradition.

posterItems.label: Pyramids
posterItems.correction: Djoser’s Step Pyramid precedes the great Giza pyramids. Pyramid-shaped monuments also arose in other societies; the poster’s Egyptian marker is not a universal beginning.

posterItems.label: Code of Hammurabi
posterItems.correction: A major surviving Babylonian legal collection, not the world’s earliest law code. Earlier Mesopotamian legal collections survive.

posterItems.label: Yoga
posterItems.correction: Yoga developed across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and other traditions. There is no agreed single origin date; interpreting Indus images as proof of modern yoga is uncertain.

posterItems.label: The Concept of Zero
posterItems.correction: Distinguish placeholder symbols from zero as an arithmetic number. Babylonian, Maya and South Asian developments cannot be reduced to a single inventor or place; 628 is an anchor for one important Indian text.

posterItems.label: Papermaking
posterItems.correction: Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving and reporting the process, not necessarily making the very first paper. Archaeological paper predates 105 CE.

posterItems.label: Compass
posterItems.correction: Ancient lodestone direction-finding and medieval navigational compasses are distinct stages. The approximate year 1100 is an ordering anchor for documented Song-era navigation, not a single invention date.

posterItems.label: Lean Manufacturing
posterItems.correction: Toyota’s just-in-time and jidoka practices developed over decades and drew on earlier production ideas. “Lean” is a later term; no single invention year is adequate.

posterItems.label: Bullet Train
posterItems.correction: The Shinkansen opened a purpose-built high-speed passenger railway; this does not mean trains or high-speed experiments began in 1964.

posterItems.label: Great Pyramid of Giza
posterItems.correction: The poster names the Great Pyramid; the linked complex includes the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. These were built in the Old Kingdom, not at its opening boundary.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Karnak
posterItems.correction: A temple complex expanded over many reigns, especially in the New Kingdom, rather than one Middle Kingdom construction.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Abu Simbel
posterItems.correction: Ramesside rock-cut temples, relocated during the UNESCO Nubian monuments campaign in the 20th century.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Ziggurat of Ur
posterItems.correction: Associated with Ur-Nammu and the Third Dynasty of Ur, not the entire loosely named “Sumerian Renaissance.”
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Mohenjo-daro
posterItems.correction: The city belongs to the Mature Harappan phase. A poster placement near 3000 BCE should not imply that every surviving structure dates to then.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Chogha Zanbil
posterItems.correction: An Elamite sacred complex built under Untash-Napirisha, not a monument constructed by later Iranian-speaking tribes.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Taxila
posterItems.correction: A serial archaeological landscape with different cities and Buddhist institutions, not one Vedic-period monument.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Persepolis
posterItems.correction: Founded under Darius I and expanded by successors; damaged in Alexander’s conquest.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Great Wall of China
posterItems.correction: A network built and rebuilt across many periods. The familiar surviving brick sections are largely Ming, not all Zhou or Qin.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Terracotta Army
posterItems.correction: Belongs to the Qin imperial burial complex, not a Zhou-period monument.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Hallstatt
posterItems.correction: Hallstatt is an archaeological site and the name used for a broader material-culture period. The site’s long history should not be compressed into one culture-start date.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Temple of Saturn
posterItems.correction: Traditionally dedicated in 497 BCE. The visible remains reflect later rebuilding; it was also associated with Rome’s treasury.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Parthenon
posterItems.correction: A Classical Athenian temple on the Acropolis, with a long subsequent history of religious use and transformation.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Cave of Altamira
posterItems.correction: The paintings predate the Celtic/Iberian societies beside which the poster places them. BP/years-ago dating must not be copied directly as BCE; this site predates the chart’s range.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Lascaux Cave
posterItems.correction: Not a monument built by Iron Age Gauls. Research has proposed different prehistoric dates; all are many millennia before 3500 BCE and the chart’s range.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Dolmens of Antequera
posterItems.correction: Prehistoric megalithic tombs, not monuments constructed by the much later Lusitanian tribes beside which the poster places them.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Stonehenge
posterItems.correction: Built long before the Celtic era. The poster’s Celtic attribution and late placement should be corrected, not reproduced.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Chichen Itza
posterItems.correction: The monument icon’s placement high in the poster’s ancient column is not its construction date. Major flowering was much later than the earliest Maya communities.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Teotihuacan
posterItems.correction: The city predates the Mexica/Aztec Empire; later peoples named and revered its ruins.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Uluru
posterItems.correction: A natural landform and sacred cultural landscape, not a constructed monument or a place founded around year 1. Aṉangu custodianship and Tjukurpa continue.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Colosseum
posterItems.correction: Built under the Flavian emperors; inaugurated in 80 CE and altered later.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Roman Forum
posterItems.correction: A civic and religious area with buildings of many dates. It is not a single building erected at the poster marker’s vertical position.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Mesa Verde
posterItems.correction: The celebrated cliff dwellings largely belong to the final centuries of this sequence. Living Pueblo communities maintain connections with these ancestral places.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
posterItems.correction: A communal bison-hunting landscape associated with Plains Indigenous peoples, especially Blackfoot histories. Its use long predates its low placement in the poster.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Chaco Culture
posterItems.correction: Chaco is a network of Ancestral Pueblo places, connected to living Pueblo peoples; not a vanished single tribe.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Cahokia Mounds
posterItems.correction: A major Indigenous urban and ceremonial centre. Its significance must not be reduced to generic pre-US background.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Mont-Saint-Michel
posterItems.correction: Its buildings span many centuries and should not be dated solely by the Frankish block in which the icon appears.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Hagia Sophia
posterItems.correction: The surviving main building is Justinianic, with earlier churches and later alterations; its religious use changed over time.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Windsor Castle
posterItems.correction: Founded under William the Conqueror; it is not a single completed Norman building.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Notre-Dame de Paris
posterItems.correction: A Gothic cathedral with later restorations. The construction dates must be distinguished from modern reopening dates.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Louvre Museum
posterItems.correction: The poster places the museum in the medieval French kingdom, but the public museum opened during the Revolution. The medieval date belongs to the fortress.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Leaning Tower of Pisa
posterItems.correction: The tower was built in medieval Pisa; its placement beside a later Sicilian kingdom must not imply that kingdom constructed it.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Cologne Cathedral
posterItems.correction: Started in the Holy Roman Empire and completed in the German Empire. It was not wholly constructed in one medieval period.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: St. Stephen’s Cathedral
posterItems.correction: The current cathedral combines phases; substantial Gothic works date to the later Middle Ages.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Alhambra
posterItems.correction: The Alhambra is associated principally with Nasrid Granada, rather than being a monument created by the Christian “Reconquista.”
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Jerónimos Monastery
posterItems.correction: The foundation stone is dated to 1501 or 1502 in official accounts. Its 16th-century building should not be dated by its earlier vertical position in the poster.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Belém Tower
posterItems.correction: A fortified tower from the reign of Manuel I, not a 15th-century monument.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Kinkaku-ji
posterItems.correction: The Golden Pavilion is associated with Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. The present pavilion is a reconstruction following the 1950 fire.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Forbidden City
posterItems.correction: Built under the Ming Yongle emperor and subsequently used and altered under Qing rule.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Blue Mosque
posterItems.correction: An Ottoman mosque commissioned by Sultan Ahmed I; the familiar name refers to its blue interior tiles.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Naqsh-e Jahan Square
posterItems.correction: The square and its surrounding monuments developed under Safavid patronage, especially Shah Abbas I.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Taj Mahal
posterItems.correction: Commissioned by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal; different parts of the complex were completed at different times.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Himeji Castle
posterItems.correction: The famous surviving castle is largely early Edo construction with earlier roots, rather than a single generic Tokugawa monument.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Palace of Versailles
posterItems.correction: Versailles was expanded across several reigns. Louis XIV’s court moved there in 1682.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Schönbrunn Palace
posterItems.correction: The present palace reflects Habsburg construction and major rebuilding, including Maria Theresa’s reign.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Parliament Hill
posterItems.correction: The original Centre Block was destroyed by fire in 1916 and rebuilt. The complex has several construction phases.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Statue of Liberty
posterItems.correction: A French-designed gift to the United States; its modern placement must not be read as an 18th-century independence-era construction.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Obelisk of Buenos Aires
posterItems.correction: The monument commemorates the fourth centenary of the first Spanish foundation; it was not constructed at Argentine independence.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Big Ben
posterItems.correction: Strictly, Big Ben is the Great Bell. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012; the familiar name is often used for the whole structure.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Eiffel Tower
posterItems.correction: Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle; not a general marker for every French republic.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Sagrada Familia
posterItems.correction: The foundation predates Francoist Spain and modern constitutional Spain. No unsupported completion date should be inferred from the poster.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

posterItems.label: Sydney Opera House
posterItems.correction: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon with contributions by later teams; the cultural landmark is not evidence of one nation’s isolated invention.
posterItems.representation: Landmark article and related history reader

connectionCoverage.scope: Coverage against the current atlas timeline, not every event or relationship in world history. A linked entry may have selected contacts or context relationships rather than direct political succession. Archaeological uncertainty is retained explicitly.

entries.title: Caral-Supe
entries.reason: Shown as an early Andean urban centre. The reviewed evidence establishes its early urban and ceremonial importance but does not justify a direct political succession arrow to the much later Wari, Tiwanaku or Inca states.

entries.title: Spain · composite monarchy and modern eras
New Zealand · Dominion and later state
Lusitanians and neighbouring Iron Age communities
Central European Celtic and Germanic communities
Hallstatt culture · early Iron Age phases
Early Iron Age Greece · Greek Dark Ages
Frankish realms · Merovingian and Carolingian periods
Italian states · medieval communes and regional powers
Post-Roman kingdoms in the eastern Alpine region
Habsburg Austria · archducal and composite monarchy phases
Iran and Iraq · Mongol and regional dynasties
China · Six Dynasties and divided realms
Yamato polity · Kofun and Asuka periods
Spanish colonial Río de la Plata

regionalEntries.title: Carthage · Punic city and power
regionalEntries.location: Gulf of Tunis · present-day Tunisia, with wider Mediterranean connections
regionalEntries.note: A Phoenician-founded city developed into a major North African and Mediterranean power. The start is an approximate ninth-century plotting anchor, not the legendary foundation year treated as certain. Roman destruction in 146 BCE ended this selected Punic political phase; Roman Carthage later flourished on the site.

regionalEntries.title: Amazigh peoples · living cultures
regionalEntries.location: North Africa · communities across several present-day states and diasporas
regionalEntries.note: A selected modern reading window for diverse Indigenous North African communities and languages, not a date for their origins. Amazigh histories long predate the medieval dynasties and modern borders. Living heritage includes Zenete Ahellil traditions in Gourara; no single state or uniform identity is implied.

regionalEntries.title: Almoravid dynasty and realms
regionalEntries.location: Western Sahara, Morocco, parts of Algeria and Iberia
regionalEntries.note: A Sanhaja Amazigh movement established a realm linking Saharan routes, the Maghrib and al-Andalus. Uses UNESCO’s 1056–1147 dynastic convention. Other chronologies begin with the earlier movement or the later consolidation around Marrakesh; territorial control changed considerably.

regionalEntries.title: Almohad dynasty and realms
regionalEntries.note: An Amazigh-led religious and political movement displaced Almoravid rule and expanded across the Maghrib. This window begins with the capture of Marrakesh, rather than the movement’s earlier beginnings. Its territorial losses and collapse unfolded in stages.

regionalEntries.title: Marinid Morocco
regionalEntries.location: Centred on Fez · present-day Morocco, with wider campaigns
regionalEntries.note: The Marinids developed Fez and sponsored architecture and learning. The plotting window follows the Met’s consolidated Moroccan ruling phase after the fall of Marrakesh; the dynasty’s earlier rise began before 1269. It did not govern the entire Maghrib continuously.

regionalEntries.title: Alaouite dynasty
regionalEntries.location: Morocco · changing political institutions and territorial authority
regionalEntries.note: A dynastic frame beginning with the conventional consolidation date. The continuation of the royal house is not uninterrupted independent government: French and Spanish protectorates overlapped it in the twentieth century. The modern constitutional state is a separate, overlapping reading.

regionalEntries.title: Morocco · French protectorate
regionalEntries.location: Much of present-day Morocco · distinct from the Spanish zones and Tangier
regionalEntries.note: The Treaty of Fez established the French protectorate. Spanish-controlled zones and Tangier had different arrangements; this block does not put all Morocco under one French jurisdiction. Moroccan institutions and resistance continued, and independence was recognised in 1956.

regionalEntries.title: Morocco · independent modern era
regionalEntries.note: 1956 marks the end of the French protectorate and recognition of independence, not the beginning of Moroccan society or monarchy. Decolonisation and territorial questions unfolded through several later stages; this date does not settle disputed boundaries.

regionalEntries.title: Hausa states · late medieval and early modern
regionalEntries.location: Hausaland · principally present-day northern Nigeria and southern Niger
regionalEntries.note: Kano, Katsina, Zaria, Gobir and other states developed distinct courts, markets and political histories. This selected phase starts with their documented ascendancy by the fifteenth century and ends at the start of the Sokoto jihad. It is not one Hausa empire, nor a claim that every state began in 1400 or disappeared in 1804.

regionalEntries.title: Sokoto Caliphate
regionalEntries.location: Central Sahel · principally present-day northern Nigeria and neighbouring regions
regionalEntries.note: A jihad beginning in 1804 transformed the regional political order and established a multiethnic network of emirates. Enslavement and slave labour were central to its economy. British conquest ended independent caliphal authority in 1903; communities and some emirate institutions continued under changed conditions.

regionalEntries.title: Hausa communities · continuing histories
regionalEntries.location: Northern Nigeria, southern Niger, wider West Africa and diasporas
regionalEntries.note: A selected modern window, not an origin date. Hausa-speaking communities continued through colonial rule and independence across state boundaries. Kano’s living Durbar traditions exemplify cultural transmission and adaptation; neither the Sokoto Caliphate nor colonial Nigeria contains the whole Hausa story.

regionalEntries.title: Zulu Kingdom · independent phase
regionalEntries.location: Southeastern Africa · present-day KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
regionalEntries.note: Shaka and subsequent rulers consolidated a kingdom through alliances and force. The dates delimit the selected independent political phase to British military defeat and partition. Later resistance and institutional changes continued; 1879 did not end Zulu people or culture.

regionalEntries.title: Zulu communities · colonial and modern histories
regionalEntries.location: South Africa · especially KwaZulu-Natal, with wider communities
regionalEntries.note: This reading begins at the loss of the kingdom’s independence to make continuing history visible, not to date the origins of Zulu identity. Communities, isiZulu and royal institutions persisted through colonialism, apartheid and democratic South Africa. Language, cultural identity and political allegiance are not interchangeable.

regionalEntries.title: Madagascar · early settlement networks
regionalEntries.location: Madagascar, the Comoros and western Indian Ocean connections
regionalEntries.note: Archaeology, crops, languages and ancestry reveal African and Southeast Asian contributions to Malagasy histories. Late-first- and early-second-millennium settlements provide an important evidence window. The first human arrival, earlier foraging evidence and the timing of different migrations remain debated; 600 is not a proven first landing, and 1200 is not an end to settlement.

regionalEntries.title: Maroserana, Sakalava and Mahafaly kingdoms
regionalEntries.note: Maroserana-associated rulers consolidated several kingdoms, including Menabé and Boina, among diverse local communities. This selected seventeenth- and eighteenth-century window shows political formation and expansion, not a single island-wide state. The end of the window does not end Sakalava or Mahafaly communities and institutions.

regionalEntries.title: Merina kingdoms and Kingdom of Madagascar
regionalEntries.dates: c. 1600–1897 CE · changing kingdoms and monarchy
regionalEntries.location: Central highlands and, later, much of Madagascar
regionalEntries.note: A broad frame for highland consolidation, subsequent division and late-eighteenth-century reunification, followed by wider expansion. Not all Madagascar was always under Merina control. France annexed the island in 1896; 1897 marks the monarchy’s final colonial removal, not the disappearance of Merina communities.

regionalEntries.title: Madagascar · French colonial rule and transition
regionalEntries.location: Madagascar · changing colonial and autonomous arrangements
regionalEntries.note: French annexation in 1896 opened this selected colonial frame. Resistance, coercion and institutional change belong within it. The republic proclaimed in 1958 preceded full independence in 1960, so these dates do not describe one unchanging legal arrangement.

regionalEntries.title: Madagascar · independent eras
regionalEntries.note: Independence was proclaimed on 26 June 1960. This frame includes successive republican and political eras rather than one uninterrupted regime. Malagasy cultural histories extend across and before these modern constitutional boundaries.

regionalEntries.title: Igbo-Ukwu · archaeological metalwork
regionalEntries.note: Excavated ritual and burial contexts contain sophisticated copper-alloy vessels, regalia and imported beads. The range is an approximate archaeological plotting window; the ninth-century dating has been debated. It does not identify a documented empire or date the beginning or end of Igbo history.

regionalEntries.title: Swahili peoples and coastal cultures
regionalEntries.dates: c. 9th century CE–present · broad cultural frame
regionalEntries.location: East African coast, islands and wider Indian Ocean connections
regionalEntries.note: A broad reading frame for African coastal communities participating in Indian Ocean exchange, not a single empire. Kilwa is one selected city, not the whole coast. Coastal cultures and Kiswahili-speaking communities continued through Portuguese, Omani and European colonial interventions and remain living traditions, as at Lamu.

regionalEntries.title: Yoruba communities · living cultures
regionalEntries.location: Nigeria, Benin, Togo and wider diasporas
regionalEntries.note: A selected modern reading window, not an origin date. Yoruba histories extend beyond the political phases of Ife and Oyo. Osun-Osogbo’s living sacred landscape and evolving annual festival are one example of continuing cultural practice; no single faith or state represents all Yoruba people.

regionalEntries.title: Edo communities · continuing Benin traditions
regionalEntries.location: Benin City and wider Edo communities · Nigeria and diasporas
regionalEntries.note: The selected frame begins with British conquest and looting to show that Edo society and artistic traditions continued afterwards. The cultural community and royal institution are not the same as the formerly independent state. This is unrelated to the modern Republic of Benin’s name.

regionalEntries.title: Shona communities · living cultures
regionalEntries.location: Zimbabwe and neighbouring countries, with wider diasporas
regionalEntries.note: A selected modern window, not a date for the origins of Shona communities. Great Zimbabwe’s medieval urban phase is one part of a longer regional history. Living mbira traditions illustrate continuity and change, and are also practised by communities other than Shona; no uniform state or unchanging identity is implied.

regionalEntries.title: Tula · Toltec traditions
regionalEntries.note: Tula was a major urban and political centre with craft neighbourhoods and far-reaching exchanges. This dates its principal Tollan phase, not all occupation at Tula. The extent and nature of Toltec political control and the interpretation of later Tollan narratives remain debated; shared styles do not establish a single empire across Mesoamerica.

regionalEntries.title: Monte Albán · Zapotec capital
regionalEntries.dates: c. 500 BCE–850 CE · principal capital phase
regionalEntries.note: A major Zapotec capital developed monumental terraces, plazas, tombs and inscriptions. The dates select the main capital phase. Later use of the site and the histories of Zapotec and Mixtec communities extend beyond it; a city’s decline did not end a people.

regionalEntries.title: Mixtec kingdoms · Postclassic era
regionalEntries.location: Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero · present-day Mexico
regionalEntries.note: Multiple Mixtec lordships developed dynastic histories, alliances and artistic traditions. This conventional Postclassic frame groups distinct polities and overlapping Zapotec histories; it does not describe a single Mixtec empire or the end of Mixtec life at conquest.

regionalEntries.title: Zapotec peoples · living communities
regionalEntries.location: Oaxaca and wider diasporas · Mexico and beyond
regionalEntries.note: Distinct Zapotec communities maintain languages, institutions, traditions and new forms of cultural life. Colonial and national rule transformed their circumstances without ending their histories. There is no single founding year or one uniform Zapotec identity.

regionalEntries.title: Ñuu Savi / Mixtec peoples · living communities
regionalEntries.location: Oaxaca, Guerrero, Puebla and wider diasporas
regionalEntries.note: Mixtec communities continue across their homelands and migrant networks, sustaining varied languages and practices. This entry concerns living peoples; the separately listed Postclassic kingdoms are a selected political phase, not the whole history of Ñuu Savi.

regionalEntries.title: Chavín · ceremonial traditions
regionalEntries.note: Chavín de Huántar was a ceremonial and pilgrimage centre whose imagery and religious networks circulated widely. The broad range follows UNESCO’s introductory chronology; construction phases and regional chronologies differ. Cultural influence does not by itself demonstrate a territorial empire.

regionalEntries.title: Taíno heritage · continuing communities
regionalEntries.location: Caribbean · including Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and diasporas
regionalEntries.note: Colonial disease, enslavement and violence devastated Indigenous Caribbean societies. Descendants, families and community organisations nevertheless sustain and renew Taíno heritage and identities. The common claim of total extinction is misleading; identities and experiences differ across islands and communities.

regionalEntries.title: Poverty Point · hunter-fisher-gatherer earthworks
regionalEntries.location: Lower Mississippi Valley · present-day Louisiana, United States
regionalEntries.note: Hunter-fisher-gatherers created an extensive earthwork landscape used for residence and ceremony. Monumental construction and long-distance exchange were possible without a farming empire. These dates describe the principal site, not the beginning or end of Indigenous history in the lower Mississippi Valley.

regionalEntries.title: Hopewell · ceremonial and exchange networks
regionalEntries.location: Eastern North America · especially the Ohio valleys
regionalEntries.note: Communities built geometric earthworks and exchanged materials across extensive networks. Hopewell is an archaeological label derived from a later landowner, not a known Indigenous nation’s own name or one empire. The date range is a broad Ohio Valley convention.

regionalEntries.title: Mapuche · continuing peoples and cultures
regionalEntries.location: South-central Chile and neighbouring Argentina · wider diasporas
regionalEntries.note: Mapuche communities continue their languages, place-based knowledge and varied political and cultural practices. Their history extends through resistance, changing relationships with colonial and national states, dispossession and contemporary renewal. This is no single kingdom or founding date.

regionalEntries.title: Guaraní peoples · continuing communities
regionalEntries.location: South America · including Paraguay, Brazil and neighbouring countries
regionalEntries.note: Guaraní identifies multiple related Indigenous peoples and languages, rather than one state. Living communities maintain and adapt knowledge, institutions and cultural practices. Colonial mission histories form only one part of those histories and do not mark their beginning or end.

regionalEntries.title: Central American Federation
regionalEntries.location: Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica
regionalEntries.note: The United Provinces formed after separation from Mexico in 1823 and adopted a federal constitution in 1824. Civil conflict and secessions broke the union apart from 1838 onward. 1841 is a rounded endpoint for a gradual process, not a single simultaneous independence date for all five states.

regionalEntries.title: Bolivia · independent eras
regionalEntries.location: South America · Andean highlands and eastern lowlands
regionalEntries.note: Bolivia declared independence in 1825. Its later history includes the Peru–Bolivian Confederation and changing constitutional and political orders. This state-history frame does not date the origins of the region’s Indigenous peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Uruguay · independent state eras
regionalEntries.location: Río de la Plata · southeastern South America
regionalEntries.note: An 1825 declaration preceded the 1828 settlement securing a separate Uruguayan state after war with Brazil. The constitution followed in 1830. These political milestones are distinct from earlier histories of the region and its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Paraguay · independent eras
regionalEntries.location: South America · Paraguay River region and Chaco
regionalEntries.note: Paraguay asserted independence in 1811; wider international recognition came later. This frame groups changing governments and borders. Guaraní and other Indigenous histories are not reducible to the modern state’s founding.

regionalEntries.title: Guatemala · postcolonial state eras
regionalEntries.note: Regional independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Mexican rule and membership in the Central American federation. Guatemala’s separate statehood consolidated as the federation dissolved; U.S. recognition followed in 1844. This broad frame is not a claim of uninterrupted separate sovereignty from 1821, and does not date the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Honduras · postcolonial state eras
regionalEntries.note: Regional independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Mexican rule and membership in the Central American federation. Honduras became a separate state as the federation dissolved in 1838. This broad frame is not a claim of uninterrupted separate sovereignty from 1821, and does not date the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: El Salvador · postcolonial state eras
regionalEntries.note: Regional independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Mexican rule and membership in the Central American federation. El Salvador’s 1841 constitution followed the federation’s collapse. This broad frame is not a claim of uninterrupted separate sovereignty from 1821, and does not date the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Nicaragua · postcolonial state eras
regionalEntries.note: Regional independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Mexican rule and membership in the Central American federation. Nicaragua separated from the federation in 1838. This broad frame is not a claim of uninterrupted separate sovereignty from 1821, and does not date the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Costa Rica · postcolonial state eras
regionalEntries.note: Regional independence from Spain in 1821 was followed by Mexican rule and membership in the Central American federation. Costa Rica separated from the federation in 1838 and proclaimed its republic in 1848. This broad frame is not a claim of uninterrupted separate sovereignty from 1821, and does not date the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Belize · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Belize became independent from the United Kingdom on 21 September 1981 after earlier British colonial rule and self-government. This dates the modern state, not its Maya, Garifuna, Creole and other communities’ beginnings.

regionalEntries.title: Cuba · republic and later eras
regionalEntries.note: The republic began in 1902 after Spanish sovereignty ended in 1898 and U.S. military occupation followed. U.S. intervention rights constrained early sovereignty. The 1959 revolution brought a major political transformation; these are different eras within a longer Cuban history.

regionalEntries.title: Dominican Republic · independent eras
regionalEntries.note: Independence from Haiti was declared in 1844. Spanish annexation interrupted sovereignty in 1861–1865; later U.S. occupations also shaped state history. The broad frame does not imply one uninterrupted political order or the disappearance of Indigenous Caribbean heritage.

regionalEntries.title: Guyana · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Guyana became independent from the United Kingdom in 1966, following British Guiana. This dates a state transition; the histories of Indigenous nations and the country’s other communities extend much further back.

regionalEntries.title: Suriname · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Suriname became independent from the Netherlands in 1975 after increasing autonomy. This state-history frame does not compress its Indigenous peoples, Maroon communities and other populations into a single political origin.

regionalEntries.title: Kingdom of Hawaiʻi
regionalEntries.note: Kamehameha consolidated most major islands in the 1790s; Kauaʻi’s ruler accepted his supremacy in 1810. The monarchy was overthrown in 1893 under duress, with U.S. involvement. These dates describe the royal state, not the duration of Native Hawaiian people or culture.

regionalEntries.title: Kānaka Maoli / Native Hawaiians · continuing community
regionalEntries.note: Native Hawaiian communities continue their languages, genealogies, cultural practices and relationships with land and sea. The monarchy’s overthrow and subsequent U.S. annexation did not end this Indigenous community. Questions of sovereignty and political status have continuing historical significance.

regionalEntries.title: Papua New Guinea · independent state
regionalEntries.location: Eastern New Guinea and neighbouring islands
regionalEntries.note: Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia on 16 September 1975 after self-government in 1973. The modern state brought together territories with different colonial histories and many distinct peoples and languages. It comprises eastern New Guinea and adjacent islands, not the entire island of New Guinea.

regionalEntries.title: Samoa · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Western Samoa became independent from New Zealand administration in 1962 and later adopted the name Samoa. This state is distinct from American Samoa. Samoan societies and cultural histories substantially predate these changes in political status.

regionalEntries.title: Vanuatu · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Vanuatu became independent on 30 July 1980 after the Anglo-French New Hebrides condominium. Its many communities developed distinct languages and kastom long before colonial administration. Independence is a state milestone, not their beginning.

regionalEntries.title: Solomon Islands · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Solomon Islands became independent on 7 July 1978 after internal self-government in 1976. This dates the modern state and does not cover all earlier island societies. The sovereign country is not identical to the whole geographical Solomon archipelago.

regionalEntries.title: Homo sapiens · African origins
regionalEntries.note: Our species emerged in Africa long before kingdoms or writing. Around 300,000 years is an approximate fossil-based age, not an exact birthday or a single founding community. Earlier human relatives extend much farther into the past; Homo sapiens continues today. Numeric BCE boundaries are omitted to avoid false precision.

regionalEntries.title: Early human migrations
regionalEntries.location: Within Africa and across Eurasia, Sahul and the Americas
regionalEntries.note: Movement occurred in many episodes, not one march along a single arrow. Fossils, archaeology and genetics illuminate dispersals and contacts; arrival dates and routes remain debated. This overview includes earlier human relatives as well as Homo sapiens. Later settlement of many Pacific islands belongs to a different, much more recent history.

regionalEntries.title: Foraging, fishing & mixed economies
regionalEntries.location: Many regions · no single society or universal sequence
regionalEntries.note: Hunting, gathering and fishing did not disappear when farming began. Communities have combined these activities with cultivation, exchange and other work in changing ways. Living Indigenous peoples maintain and renew food and land knowledge; they are contemporary societies, not unchanged examples of a prehistoric stage. This is a thematic overview, not a polity with founding and ending dates.

regionalEntries.title: Fertile Crescent · early farming
regionalEntries.location: Southwest Asia · Levant, Anatolia and the Zagros/Mesopotamian regions
regionalEntries.note: Cultivation, herding and biological domestication developed gradually, with different regional schedules. Wheat, barley and livestock histories should not be reduced to one invention day. The selected range covers important early transformations, not the full life of farming, and is not a global start date for the Neolithic.

regionalEntries.title: Göbekli Tepe
regionalEntries.note: Communities built large communal structures with carved T-shaped pillars during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic. Hunter-gatherer societies could organise complex construction and ritual life without an empire. These dates describe the monumental archaeological phase; precise functions and relationships between domestic and communal buildings continue to be researched.

regionalEntries.title: Jericho · Neolithic settlement
regionalEntries.note: By the ninth to eighth millennia BCE, a sizeable permanent settlement had communal monuments including a tower and wall. Earlier deposits reach about 10,500 BCE, and Bronze Age cities developed later. The displayed dates select the Neolithic settlement and do not give the full lifespan of Jericho or imply one continuously unchanged city-state.

regionalEntries.title: Çatalhöyük · eastern mound
regionalEntries.note: Densely built houses, burials, wall paintings and symbolic objects reveal a large Neolithic community. This dates the eighteen occupation levels of the eastern mound; the neighbouring western mound has a later history. A substantial settlement need not be presented as a territorial empire.

regionalEntries.title: Northern China · millet traditions
regionalEntries.location: Northern China · Yellow River region and neighbouring areas
regionalEntries.note: Millet exploitation, cultivation and settled farming have different chronologies. Cishan microfossils have been interpreted as evidence around 10,000 years ago, while later sites more clearly document established farming communities. Exact early domestication dates and centres remain debated. The article is one archaeological example, not the entire northern Chinese agricultural tradition.

regionalEntries.title: Yangtze valleys · rice cultivation
regionalEntries.location: Middle and lower Yangtze regions · present-day China
regionalEntries.note: Archaeological rice remains record a prolonged process of cultivation and selection, rather than a finished domesticated crop appearing at one moment. Evidence from lower-Yangtze sites spans roughly 9000–4300 years before present. This selected frame follows that evidence; earlier plant use and other Asian rice histories should not be collapsed into it.

regionalEntries.title: Mesoamerica · early crop cultivation
regionalEntries.note: Squash domestication and the beginnings of maize cultivation long predated later city-states. Maize developed from teosinte beginning about 9000 years ago in southwestern Mexico; its domestication and spread continued across communities over millennia. These are rounded early-evidence dates, not the moment every community adopted farming or a single beginning for all American agriculture.

regionalEntries.title: Andes · early horticulture
regionalEntries.note: Preceramic sites record developing horticultural economies involving plants such as squash, peanuts and cotton. The evidence places early developments in parts of the Andes around 10,000 years ago. Crops and techniques accumulated at different times; this selected regional record does not make one valley the sole source of all Andean farming.

regionalEntries.title: Kuk · New Guinea agriculture
regionalEntries.location: Upper Wahgi Valley · Papua New Guinea highlands
regionalEntries.note: Wetland mounds demonstrate cultivation around 7000–6400 years ago; later ditch systems and changing land use extend toward the present. Possible earlier plant management reaches about 10,000 years ago, but is not equivalent to unequivocal cultivation. Kuk supports an independent New Guinea agricultural history. Land use was persistent but episodic, not one unchanged system.

regionalEntries.title: West Africa · agricultural traditions
regionalEntries.location: Western Sahel and other West African ecological zones
regionalEntries.note: Pearl millet domestication in the western Sahel was one of several African agricultural developments. In northern Mali, early cultivation coexisted with herding, fishing, hunting and gathering. The date selects an early evidence horizon, not the birth of all West African farming. Different crops and environments followed different schedules; cultivated and fully domesticated forms must be distinguished.

regionalEntries.title: Mehrgarh · aceramic farming community
regionalEntries.note: A 2025 study of tooth enamel from 23 burials proposes a much later date for the aceramic Neolithic phase than the familiar c. 7000 BCE chronology. The displayed range rounds its revised model for Period I, not the full settlement history or every farming community in South Asia. The revision concerns archaeological evidence and remains open to further testing.

regionalEntries.title: Eastern North America · native crops
regionalEntries.note: Communities domesticated native seed crops independently of Mesoamerican maize farming. Archaeological changes document several domesticates by about 4500–4000 years before present, although wild foods remained important and the later shift toward crop dependence was gradual. This dates a selected evidence phase, not the full life of these food systems or the founding of a single people.

regionalEntries.title: Viking Age · Scandinavian societies
regionalEntries.location: Scandinavia, North Atlantic and wider exchange routes
regionalEntries.note: An archaeological and historical period, not a single empire or ethnicity. Farming, seafaring, trade, enslavement, migration and warfare connected diverse communities; the rounded museum convention differs from 793–1066 often used in British histories.

regionalEntries.title: Sámi · continuing Indigenous histories
regionalEntries.dates: Continuing histories · no single founding date
regionalEntries.location: Sápmi · northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula
regionalEntries.note: Diverse Indigenous communities, languages and ways of life continue across state borders. There is no defensible single founding year. Norse expansion or the creation of modern Nordic states did not end Sámi histories or rights; reindeer herding is one of several livelihoods.

regionalEntries.title: Norway · kingdoms, unions and modern state
regionalEntries.note: A broad historical frame, not uninterrupted independent sovereignty. Consolidation of medieval kingship was gradual; c. 900 rounds the late ninth-century tradition.
