Danish rule and union with Sweden intervened; the latter ended in 1905. The present kingdom’s borders and institutions developed over time.

regionalEntries.title: Sweden · medieval kingdom and modern state
regionalEntries.dates: Middle Ages–present · no single founding year
regionalEntries.note: Sweden emerged gradually as a unified medieval kingdom; no precise founding year is implied. The Kalmar Union and the 1523 election of Gustav Vasa were major political changes. A realm’s shifting boundaries should not be confused with the origins of its peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Denmark · kingdom and modern state
regionalEntries.note: A selected political frame anchored around Harald Bluetooth’s conversion and Jelling monument, rather than a founding date for Denmark or Danish people. The Kalmar Union, territorial losses, the 1849 constitution and German occupation in 1940–1945 belong to different political phases; the Danish Realm extends beyond European Denmark.

regionalEntries.title: Iceland · Commonwealth, unions and republic
regionalEntries.note: 930 marks the establishment of the Althing, not first human settlement. The Commonwealth came under Norway in 1262–1264 and later Danish rule; sovereignty in 1918 retained a common monarch, and the republic was established in 1944. These were different constitutional arrangements.

regionalEntries.title: Finland · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Parliament approved independence on 6 December 1917; the republic’s constitution followed in 1919. This dates the selected independent state, not Finnish or Sámi origins. Earlier Swedish rule and the autonomous Grand Duchy under Russia preceded independence.

regionalEntries.title: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
regionalEntries.location: Central and eastern Europe · changing multiethnic territories
regionalEntries.note: The Union of Lublin joined the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania in a common political framework. Earlier unions preceded 1569. The partitions ended the Commonwealth in 1795; its diverse populations and their histories continued.

regionalEntries.title: Poland · restored state and modern eras
regionalEntries.note: 1918 marks restoration after the partitions, not the beginning of Polish history. Nazi German and Soviet invasion and occupation from 1939, a government in exile, postwar border changes, communist government and the transition after 1989 interrupt any simple story of continuous sovereign rule.

regionalEntries.title: Kingdom of Hungary · changing royal realms
regionalEntries.note: Stephen’s coronation is conventionally dated 1000 or 1001. This umbrella covers major territorial division after 1526, Ottoman rule in central areas, Habsburg royal government and the 1867 dual monarchy; it is not one unchanged or continuously independent territory. Later restoration of the kingdom in 1920–1946 is outside this selected frame.

regionalEntries.title: Hungary · post-Habsburg and modern eras
regionalEntries.note: The Habsburg monarchy’s collapse in 1918 begins this selected modern frame. Republics, the 1920–1946 kingdom, wartime occupation, communist rule and the democratic transition after 1989 are distinct phases. Hungarian history and communities predate 1918 and extend beyond modern borders.

regionalEntries.title: Ireland · later medieval societies
regionalEntries.note: Uses the National Museum’s later-medieval convention, from church reform to the Reformation. Gaelic lordships, Anglo-Norman settlements, towns, religious communities and changing English claims overlapped. This is not a single unified Irish state, nor does 1550 mark the end of Gaelic culture.

regionalEntries.title: Dutch Republic · United Provinces
regionalEntries.note: 1588 conventionally marks the republican form after earlier revolt, the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and the Act of Abjuration in 1581. Recognition of independence followed in 1648. French invasion and the Batavian Revolution ended this republic in 1795; the modern kingdom began later.

regionalEntries.title: Netherlands · kingdom and modern state
regionalEntries.location: Northwestern Europe and the Kingdom’s Caribbean territories
regionalEntries.note: The kingdom proclaimed in 1815 initially included the southern provinces; Belgium separated in 1830 and was recognised in 1839. The present Kingdom comprises the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. It is not identical to the earlier Dutch Republic or an unchanged colonial empire.

regionalEntries.title: Medieval Bulgarian states · first and second empires
regionalEntries.location: Balkans · shifting territories around present-day Bulgaria
regionalEntries.note: Groups the First Bulgarian Empire (681–1018) and Second (1185/1186–late fourteenth century), separated by Byzantine rule. 1396 is a conventional endpoint for Ottoman conquest; regional remnants and claims complicate an exact final date. It is not one uninterrupted empire.

regionalEntries.title: Bulgaria · principality, kingdom and republic
regionalEntries.note: The autonomous principality established in 1878 remained formally under Ottoman suzerainty until independence in 1908. The monarchy, communist republic and post-1989 parliamentary republic are separate phases; 1878 is not an origin date for Bulgarian people.

regionalEntries.title: Medieval Serbian realms
regionalEntries.dates: 1217–1459 CE · selected royal and successor phases
regionalEntries.note: 1217 marks Stefan’s royal coronation, after earlier Serbian principalities. Kingdom, empire and successor despotate are grouped here; their borders and degree of control changed. The Ottoman capture of Smederevo in 1459 ends this selected frame, not Serbian society.
regionalEntries.wikiTitle: History of Serbia in the Middle Ages

regionalEntries.title: Serbia · independent republic after state union
regionalEntries.note: 2006 marks the end of the state union with Montenegro, not the first Serbian state or independence. Serbia continued the union’s UN membership. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; its international status remains contested, and this listing does not resolve that dispute.

regionalEntries.title: Medieval Kingdom of Croatia · selected phase
regionalEntries.location: Eastern Adriatic and neighbouring inland regions
regionalEntries.note: 925 is the traditional royal convention associated with Tomislav; 1102 conventionally marks rule under the Hungarian crown. Details of the union and the later Pacta conventa text require caution. The range does not imply Croatia or Croatian institutions disappeared in 1102.

regionalEntries.title: Croatia · independent republic
regionalEntries.location: Croatia · eastern Adriatic and southeastern Europe
regionalEntries.note: 1991 dates declarations and implementation of independence from Yugoslavia, followed by war and later international recognition. Croatia joined the UN in 1992. This is a modern state convention, not the beginning of Croatian communities or institutions.

regionalEntries.title: Medieval Bosnia · bans and kings
regionalEntries.location: Bosnia and neighbouring western Balkan territories
regionalEntries.note: A rounded frame following the National Museum’s mid-tenth-century emergence of the medieval Bosnian state through changing bans and royal rule. The Ottoman conquest in 1463 ends this selected state frame; local communities, religious traditions and regional institutions continued.
regionalEntries.wikiTitle: History of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Middle Ages

wikipedia.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Middle Ages

regionalEntries.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Independence and international recognition came in 1992 during Yugoslavia’s dissolution. War followed; the Dayton agreement in 1995 established the present constitutional framework. Bosnia and Herzegovina is one sovereign state with internal entities, not two independent countries.

regionalEntries.title: Yugoslav states · monarchy and changing federations
regionalEntries.note: The 1918 kingdom, wartime occupation and resistance, socialist federation, and 1992–2003 Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were different arrangements. The last became Serbia and Montenegro in 2003 and ended in 2006. The 1992 federation was not automatically accepted as the sole continuation of socialist Yugoslavia.

regionalEntries.title: Slovenia · independent republic
regionalEntries.note: The assembly adopted independence acts on 25 June 1991, followed by declaration and a short war. UN admission followed in 1992. This dates the selected sovereign state, not the origins of Slovene communities or the entire history of the territory.

regionalEntries.title: Montenegro · restored independence
regionalEntries.note: The referendum of 21 May was followed by parliament’s declaration on 3 June 2006, ending union with Serbia. Earlier Montenegrin statehood preceded Yugoslavia, so 2006 is restoration in a new constitutional setting rather than the beginning of Montenegrin history.

regionalEntries.title: North Macedonia · independent state
regionalEntries.note: The September 1991 referendum begins this selected independence frame. The state entered the UN in 1993 under a provisional designation; the country’s name changed to North Macedonia in 2019 after the Prespa agreement. Modern statehood is not a claim that one ancient polity survived unchanged.

regionalEntries.title: Pyu · urban communities
regionalEntries.note: Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra preserve a long sequence of walled settlements, water management, Buddhist institutions and exchange. This is an archaeological urban tradition, not evidence for one empire with fixed borders. Rounded century limits describe the documented sequence.

regionalEntries.title: Bagan · imperial and temple-building phase
regionalEntries.note: The Bagan landscape records a major Buddhist capital and regional empire. The range marks its best-known monumental and imperial phase, not the full occupation of the city or the beginning of Burmese history.

regionalEntries.title: Toungoo · expanding and restored courts
regionalEntries.location: Myanmar and changing areas of mainland Southeast Asia
regionalEntries.note: A dynastic umbrella for an initially local court, sixteenth-century imperial expansion and a smaller restored kingdom. The late-sixteenth-century collapse and subsequent restoration interrupt any simple picture of continuous territorial control. Shan, Mon and neighbouring powers retained distinct histories.

regionalEntries.title: Konbaung dynasty
regionalEntries.note: Konbaung kings expanded their realm and later lost territory in successive wars with British forces. British capture of Mandalay and exile of King Thibaw in 1885 ended the dynasty; formal annexation of Upper Burma followed in 1886.

regionalEntries.title: Burma · British expansion and colonial rule
regionalEntries.note: British rule spread in stages after the wars of 1824–1826, 1852–1853 and 1885. These dates do not imply the whole present-day country was colonised in 1826. Japanese occupation interrupted British control during the Second World War; independence followed in January 1948.

regionalEntries.title: Myanmar / Burma · independent state
regionalEntries.note: Independence on 4 January 1948 anchors this modern-state entry. Its broad span includes major changes in government and continuing conflicts; it does not imply an unchanged constitution, uniform central control or the disappearance of the country’s many peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Dvaravati · towns and cultural networks
regionalEntries.location: Central and northeastern present-day Thailand and adjoining areas
regionalEntries.note: Buddhist monuments, inscriptions and material culture link several early urban centres. Dvaravati is treated here as a cultural and political network rather than one securely bounded empire. Individual sites and traditions flourished at different times within this approximate range.

regionalEntries.title: Sukhothai kingdom
regionalEntries.note: An important court and group of towns supported Buddhist architecture and ceramics. The conventional kingdom range includes later dependence on Ayutthaya before annexation; it is not a claim that all of present-day Thailand was unified under Sukhothai.

regionalEntries.title: Ayutthaya kingdom
regionalEntries.location: Chao Phraya basin and changing tributary networks
regionalEntries.note: Ayutthaya became a major diplomatic and commercial capital. Sources use 1350 or 1351 for its founding. Its reach changed over time; the Burmese destruction of the capital in 1767 ended this ruling phase, not Siamese society.

regionalEntries.title: Thonburi kingdom
regionalEntries.note: King Taksin established a court at Thonburi after Ayutthaya’s fall and reconsolidated power amid competing regional centres. Bangkok became the new royal capital under Rama I in 1782.

regionalEntries.title: Siam / Thailand · Bangkok and constitutional eras
regionalEntries.note: The Bangkok era began in 1782. Absolute monarchy ended in 1932, followed by successive constitutional and military governments. The name Thailand was adopted in 1939, with a later temporary return to Siam; neither the name change nor 1782 marks the beginning of the region’s peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Champa · changing Cham polities
regionalEntries.location: Coastal central and southern present-day Vietnam
regionalEntries.note: Champa comprised changing regional centres and principalities rather than an unchanging nation-state. My Son preserves major religious monuments; southern Panduranga outlasted the fall of Vijaya in 1471 and was absorbed by the Nguyễn state in 1832. Cham people and cultural traditions continue.

regionalEntries.title: Chăm communities · living histories
regionalEntries.note: Cham history continues beyond the loss of independent principalities. Living pottery traditions in Vietnam, passed on within families and communities, offer one documented example. This entry does not assign a single founding date to a diverse people or reduce Cham life to a former kingdom.

regionalEntries.title: Butuan · maritime communities and boat-building
regionalEntries.note: Excavated lashed-lug boats attest to sophisticated boat-building and maritime connections. This selected range dates the boat evidence identified by the National Museum, not the fixed lifespan or borders of a supposed kingdom. Settlement and trade at Butuan extended beyond it.

regionalEntries.title: Sulu sultanate · political authority
regionalEntries.location: Sulu Archipelago and changing maritime networks
regionalEntries.note: A Muslim sultanate developed within older island trading societies. Its autonomy contracted under Spanish and American expansion; the 1915 agreement ended the sultan’s temporal sovereignty. Religious authority, communities and contested later claims have separate histories, and 1915 does not mark their disappearance.

regionalEntries.title: Philippines · Spanish colonial rule
regionalEntries.note: Permanent Spanish settlement began in 1565; colonial rule expanded unevenly and faced continuing Indigenous and Muslim resistance. The revolution and the 1898 transfer claimed by Spain and the United States did not amount to a consensual transfer of every community’s sovereignty.

regionalEntries.title: Philippines · revolution, U.S. rule and war
regionalEntries.note: Filipino revolutionaries asserted independence and founded the First Republic while the United States imposed colonial rule. The Commonwealth began in 1935; Japanese invasion and occupation interrupted American administration. The United States formally recognised Philippine independence on 4 July 1946.

regionalEntries.title: Philippines · independent republic
regionalEntries.note: The 1946 date marks internationally recognised independence after American colonial rule. The earlier 1898 declaration remains commemorated as Independence Day. A single modern-state entry cannot stand for every Indigenous nation, regional community or constitutional era within the archipelago.

regionalEntries.title: Melaka · Malay sultanate and trading port
regionalEntries.note: A Malay sultanate made Melaka an important multicultural trading port. Portuguese conquest in 1511 ended this selected ruling phase; the city and regional Malay courts continued under changing conditions. This is not a continuous empire connecting Srivijaya directly to Malaysia.

regionalEntries.title: Malaysia · federation
regionalEntries.note: Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963 from Malaya, Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore. Malaya had gained independence in 1957; Singapore separated in 1965. The federation’s formation does not date the beginnings of its many Indigenous, Malay, Chinese, Indian and other communities.

regionalEntries.title: Singapore · independent republic
regionalEntries.note: Singapore became a sovereign republic on 9 August 1965 after separation from Malaysia. Earlier Temasek, Malay and regional histories, the British settlement from 1819, wartime occupation and self-government preceded this modern-state phase.

regionalEntries.title: Brunei Darussalam · full independence
regionalEntries.note: Full independence resumed on 1 January 1984, ending British responsibility for external affairs and defence. This date identifies the contemporary sovereign-state phase, not the origin of the much older Brunei sultanate or its people.

regionalEntries.title: Lan Xang kingdom
regionalEntries.location: Mekong region · mainly present-day Laos and adjoining areas
regionalEntries.note: Lan Xang developed around interconnected courts and Buddhist centres, including Luang Prabang and later Vientiane. Internal divisions and external pressures changed royal power; partition produced distinct successor kingdoms. Its territory and communities do not map directly onto modern national borders.

regionalEntries.title: Laos · independence and republic
regionalEntries.note: The 1953 treaty removed the remaining French restrictions on independence, following earlier autonomy within the French Union. Civil war and extensive bombing shaped later decades. The monarchy ended with proclamation of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic in 1975.

regionalEntries.title: Timor-Leste · restored independence
regionalEntries.location: Eastern Timor, Oecusse and neighbouring islands
regionalEntries.note: Independence was declared in 1975, followed by Indonesian invasion and occupation. The 1999 referendum led to a United Nations-administered transition and restoration of independence on 20 May 2002. This modern-state date does not begin Timorese history.

regionalEntries.title: Karen communities · living heritage
regionalEntries.note: Karen is an umbrella for diverse communities rather than one state or uniform identity. Weaving, language, ecological knowledge and community institutions continue across borders and displacement. The selected sources document people sustaining these traditions today; no single origin date is assigned.

regionalEntries.title: Scythian and related steppe traditions
regionalEntries.location: Eurasian steppe · Black Sea to Siberia and Central Asia
regionalEntries.note: A broad archaeological frame for varied mobile communities, regional cultures and ruling groups. Shared horse-riding and artistic traditions do not imply one united empire or a single ancestry for later peoples. The dates are approximate.

regionalEntries.title: Xiongnu confederation
regionalEntries.dates: c. 209 BCE–93 CE · selected imperial frame
regionalEntries.location: Mongolian plateau and neighbouring Inner Asia
regionalEntries.note: An empire brought diverse communities into far-reaching political and exchange networks. The conventional 93 CE endpoint concerns the northern imperial formation; southern Xiongnu governments and communities continued. This is not an ethnic extinction date.

regionalEntries.title: First Turkic Khaganate · early imperial phase
regionalEntries.location: Mongolian plateau and Central Asian steppe
regionalEntries.note: Founded under Bumin, this imperial formation soon developed eastern and western centres. Civil conflict and separation unfolded over decades from the late sixth century; c. 603 is a conventional division marker, not an instantaneous split of a uniformly governed territory.

regionalEntries.title: Eastern Turkic Khaganate · independent phase
regionalEntries.location: Mongolian plateau and adjacent Inner Asia
regionalEntries.note: Selected post-division phase of eastern Türk rule, ending with Tang military defeat in 630. Earlier eastern government, subsequent Tang arrangements and later restored Türk rule are separate frames; these dates do not delimit all Turkic communities.

regionalEntries.title: Western Turkic Khaganate · independent phase
regionalEntries.location: Central Asia · Semirechye and neighbouring territories
regionalEntries.note: The western ruling centre connected steppe alliances and oasis societies. Separation from eastern rulers was gradual. 657 marks the defeat of a principal independent ruler by Tang forces; local rulers, contested authority and related confederations continued afterward.

regionalEntries.title: Second Turkic Khaganate
regionalEntries.note: Restored Türk imperial rule developed after rebellion against Tang dominance. A coalition including Uyghur, Basmil and Karluk forces overthrew the khaganate; final resistance continued beyond conventional 744. These are state phases, not the full history of Turkic-speaking peoples.

regionalEntries.title: Uyghur Khaganate · Orkhon empire
regionalEntries.location: Orkhon Valley and wider Mongolian plateau
regionalEntries.note: An imperial confederation centred on Karabalghasun interacted closely with Tang China. 840 marks the collapse of this steppe empire; Uyghur communities and later oasis kingdoms continued. It is distinct from those later kingdoms and from modern identities and borders.

regionalEntries.title: Sogdian cities and merchant networks
regionalEntries.dates: c. 4th–8th centuries CE · selected cultural phase
regionalEntries.location: Sogdiana · present-day Uzbekistan and Tajikistan; networks across Asia
regionalEntries.note: Agriculture, urban centres, merchants and diasporic communities supported wide cultural exchange. This selected flourishing phase groups several cities and local powers rather than one empire. Sogdian history began earlier and transformations continued after these rounded century anchors.

regionalEntries.title: Saba / Sheba · South Arabian kingdom
regionalEntries.note: A selected broad phase of Sabaean political power linked irrigation agriculture, cities, sanctuaries and incense trade. UNESCO supplies the approximate range used here; other chronologies begin earlier. The wider Marib archaeological landscape remained active beyond this kingdom frame.

regionalEntries.title: Himyar · pre-Aksumite ruling phase
regionalEntries.note: A southern Arabian kingdom expanded among neighbouring states and adopted royal monotheism in late antiquity. The approximate starting anchor selects a later portion of its early development; 525 marks Aksumite intervention, not the end of South Arabian society.

regionalEntries.title: Nabataean kingdom · royal phase
regionalEntries.dates: c. 168 BCE–106 CE · selected royal frame
regionalEntries.location: Petra, Hegra and surrounding northern Arabia / southern Levant
regionalEntries.note: Petra Museum dates this royal frame to 168 BCE–106 CE. Nabataean communities and Petra existed earlier. Roman annexation in 106 ended the independent kingdom while settlements, language and traditions continued under changing rule.

regionalEntries.title: First Saudi state · Diriyah
regionalEntries.location: Diriyah and changing territories of the Arabian Peninsula
regionalEntries.note: 1727 marks Muhammad bin Saud’s accession and the official Saudi founding convention. 1744 marks Ibn Abd al-Wahhab’s move to Diriyah and their religious-political alliance, often used as a founding date in historical writing. Ottoman-Egyptian forces captured Diriyah in 1818.

regionalEntries.title: Second Saudi state · Najd
regionalEntries.note: Saudi rule was restored from Riyadh after an interruption following the fall of Diriyah. Civil conflict and changing territorial control marked this state; Rashidi ascendancy ended it in 1891. It was not uninterrupted rule over the boundaries of today’s Saudi Arabia.

regionalEntries.title: Saudi expansion and unification
regionalEntries.location: Riyadh, Najd, al-Ahsa, Hejaz and neighbouring Arabian territories
regionalEntries.note: A formation period from Ibn Saud’s capture of Riyadh to proclamation of Saudi Arabia. Several emirate, sultanate and dual-monarchy arrangements fall within it, including the existing Hejaz–Nejd entry. This groups campaigns and state changes rather than implying a single unchanged state since 1902.

regionalEntries.title: Urartu / Kingdom of Van
regionalEntries.location: Armenian Highlands · Lake Van, eastern Anatolia and southern Caucasus
regionalEntries.note: A powerful kingdom developed around Lake Van and built fortified centres across the highlands. Its origins and collapse are approximate; this follows the History Museum of Armenia’s broad chronology. Shared territory with later Armenia does not establish a simple ethnic or political succession to any modern state.

regionalEntries.title: Arsacid Armenia · royal period
regionalEntries.location: Armenian Highlands · between Roman and Iranian spheres
regionalEntries.note: The conventional period of Arsacid royal rule includes contested authority, outside intervention and partition. The dynasty’s end in 428 in the Persian sector did not end Armenian society, churches or language. Earlier Armenian kingdoms lie outside this selected frame.

regionalEntries.title: Bagratid Armenian kingdom
regionalEntries.location: Armenian Highlands · later capital at Ani
regionalEntries.note: Ashot I’s recognition restored Armenian kingship; sources differ between 884 and 885. Ani became the capital in 961. The end of the principal Bagratid kingdom did not end other Armenian kingdoms or communities, and medieval Armenia should not be read through today’s borders.

regionalEntries.title: Cilician Armenia · principality and kingdom
regionalEntries.location: Cilicia · northeastern Mediterranean coast, present-day Türkiye
regionalEntries.note: An Armenian principality developed in Cilicia, outside the Armenian Highlands; royal coronation followed in 1198/99. Its court linked Mediterranean and Mongol worlds. The Mamluk capture of Sis in 1375 ended the kingdom, while Armenian communities and cultural traditions continued.

regionalEntries.title: Kingdom of Georgia · medieval royal frame
regionalEntries.location: Southern Caucasus · changing territory around present-day Georgia
regionalEntries.note: Bagrat III’s consolidation began a medieval royal formation whose reach changed substantially. Later invasions, subordinate rule, fragmentation and reunification prevent treating the span as continuous centralized control. By 1490 several kingdoms and principalities were recognised; Georgian history continued in them.

prominence.methodology: Editorial prominence, not a scientific index: tiers summarise selected political reach, exchange networks and lasting institutional or cultural effects. Height remains chronological duration. Context frames receive less weight to avoid duplicating concurrent named histories. Tier differences do not rank peoples or cultures in human worth. Sources support the historical narratives; neither museums nor historians supplied these numerical weights. Phase multipliers are deliberately coarse illustrative visual choices, not measured shares of territory, population or GDP. Phase boundaries can reflect conventional events, reigns or broad narrative anchors; they do not date every local change.
